This technique was widely used in bookbinding from the 17th century onward to add beauty and durability to a volume.</note> The pattern on this leaf consists of intricate, swirling designs in various shades of green, accented by small flecks and veins of yellow and reddish-brown. <note>These decorative papers often served a practical purpose by concealing the "turn-ins"—the edges of the exterior leather or cloth where they were glued to the boards.</note>

->To the Gentlemen<-

## MORITZ VOIGT
<note>Moritz Voigt (1829–1905) was a distinguished German jurist and professor at the University of Leipzig. He was a leading authority on Roman law, best known for his monumental work on the "jus naturale" (natural law) and the historical development of Roman civil procedures.</note>

## RODOLPHE DARESTE
<note>Rodolphe-Madeleine-Cléophas Dareste de la Chavanne (1824–1911) was a prominent French magistrate and legal historian. He was a pioneer in the field of comparative law, studying the legal codes of ancient Greece, Scandinavia, and the Middle Ages to understand how justice evolved across different cultures.</note>

# PREFACE

---

->I<-

In making this book available to the few people who might find interest in the subject it treats, I feel a great deal of embarrassment. The cause of this is a contradiction I have encountered, which, in my eyes, constitutes an insoluble problem. It is as follows:

The conclusion I reach is that the conquest of <term>Gaul<note>A historical region of Western Europe during the Iron Age and Roman era, primarily encompassing modern-day France and Belgium.</note></term> by the Romans bestowed upon our country the benefit of a civilization infinitely superior to <term>Celtic civilization<note>The culture and social structures of the various tribes inhabiting Gaul prior to the Roman conquest.</note></term>. I will not speak of arts and literature; of <term>Greek sculpture<note>The classical style of statues and reliefs characterized by idealized realism and specific mathematical proportions.</note></term>, for example, introduced into a region of Europe where there was no notion of the rules

The weak and the poor, whom the State did not protect against the excesses of <term>private war<note>A state of localized, constant conflict between tribal leaders or families, occurring outside the control of a central government.</note></term>, were forced to accept—even under the harshest conditions—the protection of the warrior who was the strongest, the most skillful, the best trained, the best armed, and the richest; without this support, they could not preserve their small belongings or even their lives.

Such is the social organization regretted—naturally without their realizing it—by those among us who deplore the triumph of the astute politics and the sophisticated military organization of the Romans over the ignorant bravery of our undisciplined ancestors and over the sort of <term>anarchy<note>Here used to describe a lack of centralized legal authority, which the author views as a negative state compared to Roman law.</note></term> in which the latter loved to live. # PREFACE.

has never been, like Gaul, conquered by the Romans. What was the result of this apparent superiority of the Irish over us? Here is that result: it was the maintenance of the right to murder in Ireland, in exchange for the payment of a <term>composition<note>A financial compensation or fine paid to the victim's family to settle a crime, common in early legal systems (known as "eric" in Irish law), which the author views as an inferior substitute for Roman criminal law.</note></term> fixed by custom; it was permanent civil war until an English conquest which—carried out bit by bit from the twelfth to the seventeenth century and made easy by the divisions among the Irish—resulted, on one hand, in the almost universal <term>spoliation<note>The act of plundering or stripping someone of their property and rights.</note></term> of the Irish landowner, reduced to the status of a tenant farmer; on the other hand, the transfer of almost all real estate on the island to a few hundred foreigners substituted for the ancient owners by an ultra-feudal revolution, the exact opposite of our own.

Could this then be the ideal of those who consider the fall of <term>Gallic independence<note>The period before the Roman conquest of Gaul (modern-day France) led by Julius Caesar.</note></term> a disaster—when the great patriot <term>Vercingétorix<note>The chieftain of the Arverni tribe who united the Gauls in a revolt against Roman forces but was defeated by Caesar at the Siege of Alesia in 52 BCE.</note></term> succumbed in the middle of the first century before our era?

Without having as its foundation the love of fatherland and the passion for its independence, no State can subsist and ensure the life, security, and property of its citizens. Now, when do we see for the first time in history the breath of patriotism stir the almost unanimous mass of the inhabitants of the soil that is today France? It was in the year 52 <term>BCE<note>Before the Common Era; the author uses "avant notre ère."</note></term>; when at the call of <term>Vercingétorix<note>The leader of the Arverni who united the Gallic tribes against Julius Caesar.</note></term>, the largest part of a risen Gaul undertook to drive from the territory—until then barbarian and free—the civilized legions of Rome, victorious for six years (1).

(1) The sentiment of patriotism already appears, though powerless, at the time of Caesar's first campaign in 58 BCE. <term>Liscos<note>A high-ranking magistrate or "vergobret" of the Aedui tribe.</note></term>, the supreme magistrate of the <term>Aedui<note>A powerful Gallic tribe that was initially allied with Rome.</note></term>, told Caesar that there were, among the Aedui, private individuals more influential than the magistrates; that these conspirators said to the people: "If the Aedui cannot obtain, in preference to the <term>Arverni<note>The rivals of the Aedui, who later led the resistance against Caesar.</note></term>, the leadership of Gaul, it is better to suffer the domination of the Arverni, Gauls like ourselves, than the domination of the Romans: <note>original: "praestare, si jam principatum Galliae obtinere non possint, Gallorum quam Romanorum imperia perferre"</note> *it is better, if they can no longer hold the leadership of Gaul, to endure the rule of Gauls than that of Romans.*" But, in 58 BCE, among the Aedui, the Roman party of which Liscos was a member remained in power, whereas, among the Arverni in 52 BCE, this party was overthrown by the revolt of Vercingétorix, into which, after a short resistance, the Aedui were swept.

But how can one not love this unfortunate warrior who, after having brought <term>Rome's greatest general<note>Julius Caesar.</note></term> to the brink of ruin, had to suffer the humiliation of accompanying the victor in the ceremony of the triumph and who, afterwards, struck down in the depths of a dungeon by the hand of the executioner, paid with his head for the unrealized dream of national independence!

<term>Joan of Arc<note>A 15th-century French folk heroine and saint who led the French army against the English during the Hundred Years' War.</note></term>, that popular heroine of French patriotism in the Middle Ages, had, upon the pyre at Rouen, the consoling memory of the successes achieved by her marvelous mission; she could hope for their coming completion and count on the final expulsion of the executioners who took revenge for their own helplessness through the martyrdom of a defenseless young girl.

# ADDITION

## THE ANNUAL MARRIAGE.

On pages 227 (note 1), 304, and 312, there is mention of the annual marriage of Irish <term>concubines</term> <note>In ancient Irish law, a concubine was a secondary wife with recognized legal status, though lower than that of a primary wife.</note> at the fairs of <term>Uisnech</term> <note>A site in County Westmeath traditionally regarded as the sacred center of Ireland.</note> on May 1st, and of <term>Tailtiu</term> <note>Now Teltown, known for its Great Assembly or "Fair," which featured athletic contests and legal proceedings.</note> on August 1st. An allusion to this ancient custom is also found on page 316, in the description of the fair of <term>Carman</term> <note>A site of a major regional assembly, likely in modern-day County Wexford.</note> on August 1st. An example of this marriage—which was considered dishonorable for women of high rank—is offered by the epic composition entitled: "The Murder of the Sons of Uisnech." Conchobar, the King of <term>Ulster</term> <note>One of the traditional provinces of Ireland, central to the heroic "Ulster Cycle" of Irish mythology.</note>, has a legitimate wife named Mugain Aitencaethrech, also called Ethné Aitencaethrech, daughter of Echaid Feidlech (*Course of Celtic Literature* <note>original: "Cours de littérature celtique"</note>, vol. V, pp. 89, 101, 176). He inflicts upon <term>Derdriu</term> <note>Commonly known in English as Deirdre of the Sorrows, the tragic heroine of the Ulster Cycle.</note>, the widow of Noïsé, the insult of taking her as a concubine for one year and then giving her, likewise for a year, to Eogan, the murderer of Noïsé (*Course of Celtic Literature*, vol. V, pp. 231, 235). Derdriu, who endured the first affront with immense sorrow, escaped the second through suicide.

We do not have to examine here the literary value of this moving tale, which owes its primary interest to the desolation and tragic end of Derdriu. Rather, it is from a legal perspective that we must consider this document. Why, in Ireland, does the marriage of a concubine last exactly one year?

The legal purpose of the Irish custom, by fixing the duration of the concubine’s marriage at exactly one year, must have been to prevent the husband from acquiring the pos- <meta>The text ends mid-sentence with a hyphenated word "pos-", likely "possession".</meta>

<summary>This appendix examines the ancient Irish legal practice of temporary, one-year marriages for concubines contracted at seasonal fairs. It uses the tragic story of Deirdre (Derdriu) to illustrate how these unions were used as a form of social or legal insult.</summary>

### THE ANNUAL MARRIAGE.

...annual session which would have required a year and a day <note>original: "l'an et jour"</note> (1). This annual possession would have probably allowed the husband to acquire ownership through <term>usucapion</term> <note>A legal concept where ownership is gained by possessing something or someone for a specific period of time without interruption.</note>, and consequently the right to resell the concubine and keep the price of this sale to the detriment of the concubine herself and her parents. One might compare this to the acquisition of Roman <term>manus</term> <note>In Roman law, the legal power or "hand" a husband held over his wife, placing her under his authority.</note> by usage, <term>usu</term> <note>original: "usu"; the acquisition of legal rights through continuous use or habit.</note>, continued without interruption for one year (2).

The year of marriage expired in Ireland at a pagan festival, which served as the occasion for a fair. The habit persists, in part of France, of setting the end of rural leases at either the feast of Saint John (June 24) or Saint Martin (November 11); these are the successors to the festivals of *Beltene* (May 1st) and *Samhain* (November 1st). As for the specific habit of changing concubines—rented or sold for a year—at a fair every year, we can consider the current Christian custom in the Champagne region of hiring domestic servants (both women and men) for a one-year term starting at the Saint John fair of Troyes (June 24) as a survival, to a certain extent, of this old pagan and Celtic usage.

The successive sale or leasing of a daughter by her father to several husbands (3), even when the previous husbands were not yet dead at the time of the new sales or leases, was a custom contrary to the law of the Gospel. This custom was naturally prohibited by Christianity. What remains of it is the practice of hiring a servant to a master.

(2) Gaius, *Institutes* <note>original: "Institutiones"</note>, I, § 111. See Voigt, *The Twelve Tables* <note>original: "Die XII Tafeln"</note>, vol. II, p. 226, note 13.
(3) *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 346, l. 9 and following. See vol. III, p. 314, l. 5-10; vol. IV, p. 62, l. 9-11; vol. I, p. 154, l. 11-12.

-> THE STATE, LIKE THE GODS, REMAINS UNCONCERNED WITH THE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN FAMILIES. — THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE STRUCTURE OF SOCIETY AND THE CONCEPT OF THE AFTERLIFE. <-

The earliest conception of the State is entirely different from the one that centuries of habit have imposed on our minds. The State, in our view, has two primary missions to fulfill.

The first consists of internal governance: the State acts as a dispenser of justice; it must regulate, in accordance with the law <term>droit</term> <note>The French "droit" refers to both "law" and "the right," encompassing the entire legal system and the principles of justice.</note> and, as far as possible, equit—

### FIRST PART. CHAP. I.

—ably, the relationships of citizens among themselves, to punish every crime committed by one citizen against another, and to compel anyone who has seized the property of their fellow citizen to make restitution.

The second obligation of the State concerns external relations: it is to protect the persons and property of citizens against attacks from foreigners, to defend territory threatened with invasion by the national enemy, and to punish as they deserve the traitors or cowards who do not provide their assistance in ensuring the security of the fatherland against the foreigner.

Of these two roles of the State, the second was the only one understood at the dawn of societies. At the time of the Roman conquest, the Celtic world still attributed no other function to the State than to maintain the independence of the city-state <term>cité</term> <note>While we usually think of a "city," the author uses "cité" here in the classical sense of a "civitas" or sovereign community of people.</note> and the integrity of the property of the people or the nation against the aggression of neighboring peoples or nations. The State, the city-state, was a group of families allied against the foreigner, but the families that composed the State regulated their relationships among themselves as they saw fit, without the State having the right to intervene to determine the nature of those relationships.

Political and religious conceptions are interdependent. In primitive societies, one does not have the idea of the State sentencing a citizen’s murderer to death and carrying out the execution, or compelling a thief to make restitution; nor does one have the notion of a god,

-># THE CELTS AND THE OTHER LIFE.<-

...or punishing in another life the man who in this world was guilty of a crime against his fellow, or rewarding in that other life the man who was just and charitable toward his neighbor. Among the Celts, the belief in the immortality of the soul had a power that vividly struck the minds of the Romans, but this belief was not, as it is among Christians, associated with the theological doctrine of heaven and hell. The deceased, it was thought, found in the other world a life similar to this one, and where, just as in this life, any higher justice was absent.

Regarding the Celtic belief in the immortality of the soul, ancient texts are explicit. The first Greek scholar to study the customs of the Gauls believed he recognized in Gaul a Greek doctrine: the <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>From the Greek *metempsychosis*, meaning the "transmigration of souls"—the belief that after death, a soul moves into a new body.</note> of Pythagoras. According to Pythagoras, souls are judged after death; when they are found unworthy of returning to heaven, they must be incarnated once more in this world, either in the body of a human or in that of an animal, depending on their moral state or their degree of perfection. Pythagoras, it is said, claimed to remember having lived four lives in this world, and of those four lives, there were three in which he had been a historical figure. He supposedly lived for the fifth time when, in the sixth century BCE, he founded the philosophy named after him, Pythagoreanism.

Posidonius <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher, politician, and astronomer (c. 135–51 BCE) who traveled throughout the Roman Empire and wrote extensively on the Celts.</note>, who visited Gaul around the year 100

# THE CELTS AND THE OTHER LIFE.

> » minds free from worry, in the Isles of the Blessed,

In this passage by the Greek poet [Hesiod], from the eighth century before Christ, we already recognize the faith in a god who grants rewards in another life; it is like a twilight announcing the dawn of the Christian paradise. Nothing of the sort exists among the Celts. The future life is similar to this one; there is no more a supreme power in the next world than in this one that punishes the wicked and rewards the virtuous man. The deceased finds in the other world a double of his body and of the other objects placed with his body in the tomb: weapons, horses, clients <note>In the ancient context, "clients" were free-born dependents who pledged their loyalty and service to a powerful patron in exchange for protection and support.</note>, and slaves (2). In the other world, the social and legal relationships established in this one persist without change: the client remains a client, for the slave the chain of servitude is not broken, and unpaid debts do not cease to be due (3), consequently—

# THE STATE AMONG THE CELTS AND THE EGYPTIANS.

The Celts did not have a system of <term>public prosecution</term> <note>The original French "vindicte publique" refers to the right of the state or community to punish crimes, rather than leaving punishment to the victims.</note> in this world, unless it concerned a crime against the State. In relations between individuals, private vengeance—carried out by the offended family with the support of their <term>clientele</term> <note>A group of dependents or followers who owed service to a powerful leader.</note> or their patron—was their only means of ensuring justice prevailed and repressing iniquity. In their eyes, the next world offered the wronged man no other procedure than private vengeance to ensure the observance of the laws violated by the wicked.

In Egypt, on the contrary, from the most ancient times to which we can trace back, we see the established notion of divine justice in the afterlife, and that of royal justice in this one. The *Book of the Dead*, of which we possess copies written in the sixth or perhaps even the seventh century before our era <note>Approximately 600–700 BCE.</note>, provides us with the official text of the <term>plea</term> <note>original: "plaidoyer"; here referring to the "Negative Confession" or "Declaration of Innocence" where the deceased defends their moral life before the gods.</note> that the deceased, arriving before the supreme judge, was required to deliver. The deceased did not only have to establish that he had fulfilled his obligations toward the gods; he also had to have fulfilled his duties toward men.

This epistle was carried with Christianity to Ireland, that is to say, into a portion of the Celtic world which, having escaped the beneficial influence of Roman law, still found itself in the early centuries of our era—and remained through the Middle Ages—under the rule of the right of <term>private vengeance</term> <note>A legal system where the family of a victim has the right or duty to punish the perpetrator themselves, rather than the state doing so.</note>, like Gaul in the time of <term>Poseidonius</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and traveler who observed the Celts around 100 BCE.</note> and Caesar. Homicide was therefore lawful in Christian Ireland; it was even a duty whenever, through murder, one avenged the death of a member of one's family killed by a member of another family, even if they lived within the same city. When public retribution does not exist, the conscientious fulfillment of the duty of private vengeance ensures the preservation of society, which otherwise could not exist. What, then, was the forbidden form of murder in Ireland during the Middle Ages? In a manuscript from the ninth century, the *homicida* of the Vulgate is rendered by four Irish words meaning: "He who kills the members of his
» family (1)."

# CHAPTER II.

## THE OATH BY THE FORCES OF NATURE.

For now, we will study another effect of theological and social conceptions in the Celtic world. The gods, like the State, are indifferent to the justice or injustice of human acts; such is the fundamental notion of religion and social organization among primitive peoples. From a very ancient period, two means were found to remedy this flaw in theological doctrine and political institutions. These means are the <term>oath</term> and <term>vassalage</term> <note>The system where a person of lower status (the vassal) pledges loyalty and service to a person of higher status (the lord) in exchange for protection.</note>. Through vassalage, the poor and the weak secure the support of the powerful against injustice. Through the oath, men place their contracts under the protection of the gods. Whoever fails to fulfill a contract after having sanctioned it with an oath thereby insults the gods, who will take vengeance—not out of a love for justice, but out of respect for their own dignity. When, in the third book of the *Iliad* <note>Homer's ancient Greek epic poem describing the Trojan War.</note>, a treaty concluded between the Greeks and the Trojans decides that the war will cease, that Me-

Among Christians, the oath is a formula that routine alone explains. Zeus, in Sanskrit <term>Sanskrit: an ancient Indo-Aryan language and the classical literary language of India</term> *dyâu-s*, from a primitive *dyêu-s*, is nothing other than an ancient name for "heaven"; *dyâu-s* has preserved this meaning in Sanskrit; the name of the sun, the first of the ornaments of the celestial vault, appears here to poetically complete the idea of heaven, just like the stars in the Irish oath that we will reach on p. 23.

In 336 BC, Celtic ambassadors came to find Alexander the Great, then at the beginning of his reign. They formed an alliance with him. They confirmed the treaty with an oath: "If we do not observe our engagements," they said, "may the heaven falling upon us crush us; may the earth opening up swallow us; may the sea overflowing submerge us." We shall find, on p. 23, this formula poetically developed in an Irish epic text from the early Middle Ages. From two texts by Greek authors contemporary with Alexander the Great, one must conclude

(*Iliad*, III, 276, 277; cf. *Odyssey*, XII, 323.)

After having offered the ambassadors a drink—among French peasants today there is still no good bargain made without a glass of wine (1)—Alexander asked them: “What do you fear most?” Instead of answering him: “It is you,” as Alexander had hoped, the Celts replied: “We fear no one; we dread only one thing, and that is that the sky might fall upon us.” This response has been preserved for us among the surviving fragments of a book written by one of Alexander’s most famous lieutenants, Ptolemy, who died as king of Egypt in 283 BC (2). It corresponds to the first article of the oath: “If we do not observe our engagements, may the sky, falling upon us, crush us, p. 19.”

Alexander considered the Celts' answer as an act of insolence. His teacher, Aristotle, made a different observation. The Celts, he remarked, fear only one thing, which is the sky falling on them if they do not fulfill their treaty of alliance; thus they believe they do not have to concern themselves with the last two articles of their oath: “If we do not observe our engagements, may the earth, opening up, swallow us; may the sea over—”

# CHAPTER III.

## THE JUDGMENT OF WATER.

Among the <term>Celts<note>Ancient Indo-European peoples of Central and Western Europe, specifically referring here to the Gaels of Ireland.</note></term>, the forces of nature are not transformed—as they already were for the most part in <term>Homeric Greece<note>The era of Greek history reflected in the epics of Homer, where gods were depicted with human forms and personalities.</note></term>—into characters with human forms who possess the ideas and passions of men; witnesses to this are: Zeus, the sky; Poseidôn, the sea; <term>Aidôneus<note>An archaic name for Hades, the ruler of the underworld, representing the earth.</note></term>, the earth. In Celtic belief, each of the constituent elements of the material world that we see is a mysterious being that hears our invocations and sees our acts; it is from them that, in this very life, when their intervention has been provoked, one receives the punishment deserved by those who do not observe their commitments. The sun, taken as a witness by <term>Loégairé<note>Lóegaire mac Néill, the High King of Ireland who famously broke his oath to the men of Leinster.</note></term>, burns him when the oath is violated. This is because the sun heard the oath and saw the violation. The sun "sees all and hears all," as we read in the *Odyssey* (1),

When someone concluding a contract asks them to sanction it, they hear his voice, and, if the contract is not executed, they inflict the punishment that falls within their domain; that is why the earth swallowed <term>Loégairé<note>Lóegaire mac Néill, a semi-legendary High King of Ireland who famously died after violating an oath sworn by the elements.</note></term>, and why the wind refused him the air necessary for breathing.

Water possesses the same powerful faculties, without distinction between the water of the sea, the water of rivers, or the water contained in a cauldron. "May the overflowing sea submerge us," the <term>Celtic<note>Refers here to the Gauls or tribal envoys from the Adriatic region who met with Alexander.</note></term> ambassadors said in 336 BC to the King of Macedonia, <term>Alexander the Great<note>The Greek conqueror; this famous exchange highlights the Celtic lack of fear toward men, fearing only the collapse of nature.</note></term>. "Unless the sea, with its gray and blue solitudes, comes over the hairy brow of life;" such is the poetic exclamation of the Irish king <term>Conchobar<note>Conchobar mac Nessa, the legendary King of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology.</note></term>. But water is not found only in the sea; it flows in the rivers; one can also place it over a fire in a cauldron.

# FIRST PART. CHAPTER III.

These three texts agree in observing that, in the eyes of the Celts, the Rhine was a judge of last resort; among them, the notion of a superior power—whose decision the river would have expressed through a kind of supernatural manifestation—was absent. The first of these documents is explicit on another point, on which it agrees with the formula of the oath: "May the overflowing sea submerge us." The Rhine pronounced condemnation by submerging, and acquittal by keeping the subject afloat. After the Germanic conquest, this Celtic belief was maintained on the banks of the Rhine, where the doctrine accepted in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries was still that the guilty party fell to the bottom of the water and the innocent floated (1).

Among the Germanic peoples in general, as well as among the Poles and the <term>Hindus<note>The original French "Indoux" refers to the peoples of India; the author is drawing a comparison between Indo-European legal traditions.</note></term>, an inverse practice had prevailed. If the accused stayed on top of the water, he was declared guilty; if, on the contrary, he fell to the bottom, he was considered innocent; in this latter case, it was thought that the water had graciously received him into its bosom; in the former, it was concluded that the water had rejected him as unworthy (2). ->### JUDGMENT BY WATER.<-

Germanic. In the ninth century, Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, in his treatise on the divorce of King Lothair and Queen Theutberga <note>Theutberga was a Carolingian queen accused of incest; her case became a landmark in medieval law regarding divorce and the use of "God's judgment" or ordeals.</note>, mentions the trial of cold water: *judgment of cold water* <note>original: *aquae frigidae judicium*</note> (1). “Water,” he says, “receives certain people and thereby shows them to be innocent; it rejects others and proves them guilty (2).” Before plunging the accused into the water, they were tied with a rope, one end of which remained in the hands of one of the assistants; this rope was used to pull the subject <note>The author uses "patient" in the sense of one undergoing a trial or suffering an action.</note> from the water before, for lack of breathable air, he lost his life and nothing remained of an innocent man but his corpse (3). This trial, understood in this way as the reverse of the Celtic system, remained in use in Germany and France until the end of the sixteenth century.

Belief in the magical power of water led to the creation not only of the <term>ordeal of cold water<note>Also known as *judicium aquae frigidae*, where floating was a sign of guilt (the water "rejected" the sinner).</note></term> where the accused was thrown in entirely, but also the <term>ordeal of boiling water<note>Also known as the *lebes*, where the accused had to retrieve an object from boiling water; healing without infection was seen as divine acquittal.</note></term> where they only placed their hand. ->**THE CELTIC FORMAL DUEL.**<-

primitive theory. The expression "judicial duel," established among us by long usage, is also the result of a level of civilization that the Celts of Caesar's time had not yet reached. At that time, in disputes between private individuals, there was no mandatory jurisdiction; only arbitration was known, and no magistrate could order a duel. The duel was a softened form of private war <note>a system of blood feuds where families sought their own justice</note>, a way to spare the blood of relatives, friends, and clients <note>social dependents or subordinates protected by a patron</note>; the adoption of this form resulted from a contract. Instead of a judicial duel, there was the "formal duel" <note>from the French "duel conventionnel," meaning a combat based on a mutual agreement or "convention" rather than a court order</note>. One of the oldest historical examples of this ancient type of duel is offered to us by the Celts of Spain in the year 206 BCE.

P. Cornelius Scipio, who later owed his surname *Africanus* <note>Latin: "the African," a title granted for his victory over Carthage in Africa</note> to his victory against Hannibal, was then in Spain, where he had achieved multiple successes against the Carthaginians. It was gladiatorial combat that he had promised to the gods. To this category—as strange as the other to the Roman spectators—belonged two great Spanish lords: Corbis and Orsua, both sons of kings. Their fathers were brothers and had reigned one after the other in order of primogeniture <note>the right of the firstborn to inherit the throne</note>: the question was which of the two sons should succeed the last of the two brothers to die. Corbis's father, being the eldest, had ascended the throne first; Orsua's father was the second, having succeeded his brother on the throne. Orsua claimed that the throne was included in the inheritance that his father was passing down to him. Orsua, consumed by pride—which is so often the primary passion of young people—did not realize his cousin's chances of success. Corbis, more practiced in the handling of weapons, more skillful and stronger than his opponent, had no trouble defeating and killing him (1). It was he, therefore, who obtained the crown.

This duel, so contrary to Roman customs, struck their imagination vividly. More than two centuries later, Valerius Maximus—who wrote, as we know, under the Emperor Tiberius—spoke of it in his collection of memorable examples. To make the impiety <note>A lack of proper respect for family or religious duty</note> of this deadly combat more shocking, he portrayed the two opponents as two brothers disputing their paternal inheritance. According to Valerius Maximus, the elder would have willingly followed Scipio's peaceful advice; it was supposedly the younger who refused to accept it, and his death was the just punishment for his perverse obstinacy (2).

### FIRST PART. CHAP. IV. § 1.

...found this arrangement of the ancient narrative preserved by Livy, dates from the year 32 of our era, or is slightly later than that. Fifty or sixty years later, Silius Italicus, who wrote under Domitian (81–96), further embellished this tragic anecdote. He is not content with making the combatants two brothers as Valerius Maximus had imagined: to make their struggle even more horrific, he has them kill each other; he depicts the two swords each piercing the chest opposite it; he shows us the two brothers lying dying on the ground and heaping mutual insults upon one another; cries of hatred are mixed with their final sighs. Later, says Silius Italicus, they tried to unite their corpses on the same pyre, but the flames escaping from these funeral remains rose up while dividing themselves, and the ashes of the two brothers refused to rest in the same tomb (1). <note>The image of the "divided flame" is a classical literary trope used to signify eternal hatred, famously seen in the Greek myth of the warring brothers Eteocles and Polynices.</note>

Silius Italicus notes, however, that this duel was consistent with the national customs of the two combatants:

->*This was the dire custom of that race* (2).<- <note>original: "Is genti mos dirus erat"</note>

# CELTIC CONVENTIONAL DUEL.

Corbis is the personal name that explains the place name *Corbio*. *Corbio* is a city in Spain; it belonged at that time to the *Suessetani*, and the Romans captured it twenty-two years after the duel of Corbis and Orsua (1). The *Suessetani* lived on the banks of the Ebro (2); their capital, called *Suessatium* in the *Antonine Itinerary* <note>The *Antonine Itinerary* was a famous register of stations and distances along the roads of the Roman Empire.</note> (3), is named (through a scribal error) *Suestasion* by Ptolemy. It is a place name related to that of the *Suessiones* of Gaul, whose modern French form is Soissons. *Suessatium* was located near Vitoria in Alava, a Basque province. In the time of Ptolemy, *Suessatium* belonged to the *Caristi* (4). Now, *Caristi* derives from *Caros*, a Celtic name borne by an inhabitant of Segeda who was elected general of the *Arevaci* (a Celtiberian people) in the year 153 BC (5). *Caristi* is formed with the help of a suffix *-isto-* which is found in the first part of the name of the *Tolistobogii*, a Gallic people of Asia Minor; and through the land of the *Caristi* flowed a river whose name was Gallic, the

### § 2. — *The duel, particularly the conventional duel among the Irish.*

In Irish law, which appears here to date back to a high antiquity, the duel, in two circumstances, does not expose the victor to paying the <term>composition for murder</term> <note>a legal fine or "blood money" paid to the family of the deceased to settle a blood feud, known in Irish law as 'éraic'</note> and ensures his triumph in the pending dispute; this takes place:

1° When the duel has been preceded by a contract made with the consent of the family of the defeated party and which has determined the legal effects of the victory; then, whoever the victor may be, whether it is the plaintiff or the defendant, he does not owe a composition for the murder of his adversary;

2° When the duel is caused by the defendant's refusal to allow a <term>seizure</term> <note>the legal process of distraint, where a creditor takes possession of a debtor's property to compel payment</note> to proceed against him in the forms established by custom; in this case, the seizing plaintiff who kills his debtor will not pay a composition if he had previously—

---

(1) Poseidonios <note>a Greek Stoic philosopher and historian (c. 135–51 BC) who traveled extensively in Gaul</note>, fragment 24, in Didot-Müller, *Fragments of Greek Historians* <note>original: "Fragmenta historicorum Graecorum"</note>, vol. III, p. 260. Cf. Diodorus Siculus <note>a Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note>, book V, chapter 28, section 5; Didot edition, vol. I, p. 271; and below, p. 69.

# CELTIC DUEL IN IRELAND.

The Irish plaintiff has three ways of proceeding to obtain justice: 1st, the seizure of movable property, <term>aithgabail</term> <note>the legal process of taking cattle or other goods to satisfy a debt, often called 'distress'</note>; 2nd, the seizure of land or real estate, <term>tellach</term>; 3rd, the duel, <term>comrac</term>.

> “There are,” says a legal text, “three cases where one commits an illegality among the Irish <note>original: 'la Feine', referring to the Féni, the free land-owning class of ancient Ireland governed by these laws</note>, namely when one performs a seizure of movables irregularly, a seizure of land contrary to the law, or a duel without verbal agreements (*literally, without contracts of the lips*), or without having experienced a refusal to obey the law (1).”

It is therefore lawful to challenge the debtor to a duel if they resist by force a seizure undertaken according to the rules; before Christianity arrived in Ireland, no law forbade the debtor from such resistance. Irish law prior to Christianity must have been, on this point, the same as the law of the Gauls before the Roman conquest.

The Irish collection of canons <note>known as the 'Collectio Canonum Hibernensis', a major source for early Irish ecclesiastical law</note>, which dates to around the year 700 or thereabouts, attributes two decisions to Saint Patrick that forbid a debtor from using weapons to repel someone performing a seizure. In Book XXXIV, chapter 8, we read: “Following the decision of the Irish synod—”

---

(1) “There are three times when illegality is pursued among the Irish: illegal seizure of movables, unlawful entry onto land, and combat without lip-contracts, or without a refusal to comply with the law” <note>original Old Irish: "Atait teora aimsera in-seagair éidechta la Feine : athgabail-éidechta, tellach indligtech, comrug gen curu bel, no gan elod cu n-dliged"</note> (*Legal Entry* <note>original: 'Din techtugad'</note>, in *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. IV, p. 32, lines 3-5). According to the <gloss>explanation</gloss>, the challenge to a duel was lawful after the expiration of the delay following the command to pay, <term>apad</term> <note>a formal notice period required before proceeding with legal seizure</note> (*Ibid.*, p. 32, l. 14).

Hector and Odysseus measured the field of battle and drew lots to see which of the two combatants would be the first to throw a javelin at his opponent; they were the official witnesses to this duel, which the two armies were about to witness. Paris was favored by the lot: he struck the first blow; but soon, anticipating an imminent defeat, he fled, and one of the Trojans wounded Menelaus with an arrow. One could translate <term>fetialis</term> as "Roman envoy extraordinary;" but he was more than a modern diplomat; he was a kind of priest. What predominated in him was his religious character; the formulas he uses belong to the sacred ritual. "Do you command me, O King," says the Roman <term>fetialis</term>, "to conclude a treaty with the representative," — more exactly with the fictitious and legal father, <term>with the father-delegate</term> <note>original Latin: "cum patre patrato"</note>, — "of the Alban people?"

Each people is considered as a family, and the treaty is concluded between the "fathers" created for the occasion (2). <term>Pater patratus</term>, literally "father made" <note>or "father-delegate," referring to the specific individual empowered to act as the head of the people for the treaty's purpose.</note>, is an alliterative formula which, consequently, dates back to a prehistoric era in Roman literature.

The combat of the Horatii and the Curiatii <note>Two sets of triplets—the Horatii for Rome and the Curiatii for Alba Longa—who fought as champions to decide the war between their cities without a full-scale battle.</note>, while more decisive than that of Eteocles and Polynices <note>In Greek mythology, the sons of Oedipus who killed each other fighting for the throne of Thebes.</note>, was more serious than that of Menelaus and Paris <note>A duel in the *Iliad* intended to end the Trojan War, which was interrupted by divine intervention.</note>, since five out of the six combatants lost their lives. On both sides, there were mutual grievances regarding acts of looting or the seizure of livestock carried out by peasants. Roman legend thus conceives of conventional combat <note>A pre-arranged fight between champions used to resolve a conflict between two groups.</note> in the same way as Greek legend. While there is a moral idea within the agreement itself, no moral doctrine is associated with the concept of the fight, unlike the judicial combat of the Middle Ages <note>Trial by combat, where it was believed God would grant victory to the innocent party.</note>. The same is true among the Celts.

### § 5. — *The intervention of the family in the agreement preceding the duel.*

In the Roman document, we noted the intervention of the formal and legal father, the <term>pater patratus</term> <note>The chief of the fetials, a college of Roman priests. He acted as the "father" of the Roman people for the purpose of swearing treaties.</note>. The appearance of this strange figure is the result of a legal doctrine that we find more clearly expressed in the *Iliad* and in Irish law. An interesting point of resemblance between the Homeric duel and the Celtic duel is that the head of the family for each of the two combatants intervenes in the agreement preceding the fight: this leader is Agamemnon for Menelaus, and Priam for Paris. Hector proposed the duel; Menelaus requests Priam's intervention: "Bring Priam," he says, "so that he may personally swear to the observation of the treaty (1)."

<page-num>61</page-num>
<header>THE DUEL AND THE FAMILY.</header>

Although the duel was proposed by Hector and Paris, it could be argued that the actual challenger was Menelaus; as a general rule, the challenger of a duel is the one who claims to have been offended. Furthermore, Menelaus represented the Greek army, which had come to attack the Trojans on their own territory. Now, Indo-European common law <note>The ancestral legal customs shared by various cultures across Europe and parts of Asia, such as the Greeks, Romans, Celts, and Germans.</note> appears to have been this: when the person who has challenged an opponent to a duel is killed by him, the victor—acting in legitimate self-defense—owes no <term>composition</term> <note>A financial payment, often called 'wergild' or 'blood money,' paid to a victim’s family to prevent a blood feud.</note> to the family of the deceased. However, when it is the challenger who kills, the family of the deceased has the right to demand the compensation for murder, unless they have previously given their consent to the duel. Thus, in the absence of Priam’s intervention in the treaty, Menelaus, by killing Paris in the proposed duel, might have found himself liable for the murder compensation. This is an inevitable consequence of the Indo-European theory of the family: since the family is the owner of all property enjoyed by each of its members, no member can, through an agreement to which the family was not a party, strip the family of its rights. One of the primary lucrative rights of the family is to demand the compensation due in the event of the murder of one of its members.

When a man had no family, the family was replaced by that man’s chief <term>chef</term> <note>In the context of ancient Irish or "Brehon" law, a person was always legally "tethered" to a protector, usually a tribal leader or lord.</note>. The rule here is much the same as when determining who will pay the composition <term>composition</term> <note>A financial settlement or "blood money" paid to an injured party to prevent a cycle of revenge.</note> for a crime. In cases where the culprit is insolvent, the debt falls upon his family; if the family cannot pay, the debt is the responsibility of the lord; it can, finally, go as high as the king. A legal maxim <term>brocard</term> <note>A short, authoritative legal proverb.</note> says, "every man without a chief goes to the king (2)."

Whoever challenged another to a duel was therefore required, before the fight, to notify not only the family but also the chief of his opponent. This was to put them on notice: they could either accept the duel or prevent it by settling the dispute and granting the reparation fixed by custom for the wrongful—or simply unjust—act that had triggered the duel. This notification served as a guarantee for the challenger against any future demand for a murder composition if he were to emerge victorious. Ancient Irish law, in agreement with most primitive legal systems, holds a doctrine regarding premeditated murder that is very different from the one prevailing in modern legislation. It recognizes the legitimacy of murder in circumstances where, in our modern view, it would not even be excusable. In such cases, the law employs the expression <term>necessary murder</term> <note>The author uses this term to describe a killing that is legally mandated or justified by social obligation, rather than a crime of passion or malice.</note> to designate this act of violence (1). Killing the murderer of a relative, up to and including the rank of a <term>first cousin</term> <note>Refers to the *derbfine*, a four-generation kin group central to ancient Irish social and legal structure.</note>, is considered a "necessary murder." The consequence is that the two murders offset each other. No <term>indemnity</term> <note>Financial compensation paid to the victim's family to prevent a blood feud.</note> is due for the second murder, unless the murderer's family has prevented the exercise of vengeance by paying the indemnity fixed by custom; in that case, the paid indemnity must be returned (2).

There are only two cases where Irish custom views homicide unfavorably; these are: 1st, the case

***

(1) "Necessary killing" <note>original Old Irish: "Marbhadh dethbire"</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. IV, p. 244, l. 20); "necessary wounding of a person" <note>original Old Irish: "guin duine dethbire"</note> (*ibid.*, p. 252, l. 17).

(2) "In the vengeance for a man of the <term>true kin</term> <note>original Old Irish: *derbfine*</note>, the family is entitled to the <term>body-price</term> <note>original Old Irish: *coirp-dire*; compensation for the physical loss of a person.</note> and the <term>honor-price</term> <note>original Old Irish: *einech-lann*; compensation for the loss of status or insult to the family.</note> for his killing; but if they have received the <term>fine</term> <note>original Old Irish: *eiric*</note> before they have carried out the vengeance for the man of the true kin, the family must pay back the body-price and the honor-price in equal measure": "When the murder of a first cousin is to be avenged by the death of the murderer, the family of the deceased has the right to the price of the body and the honor of that deceased; but if they received this price before exercising vengeance, they must, after the vengeance, fully restore this price" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. IV, p. 252-254; cf. below, ch. V, § 22).

children are not at all included among the relatives whose murder is prohibited. Regarding concealed murder <note>In ancient law, a killing done in the open was often treated as a legal wrong that could be settled with money, but a "concealed" murder—where the body was hidden—was seen as a treacherous crime of a higher order.</note>, the antiquity of the condemnation it faced is established by the agreement found here between Irish law and the Salic law <note>The Salic law was the ancient legal code of the Salian Franks, established during the reign of Clovis I in the early Middle Ages.</note>. Hiding a murder was the dishonest method used by those who wished to escape the payment of the fine. One had to be very careful not to fight a duel without witnesses, as this was to expose oneself to being considered guilty of concealed murder.

### § 8. — *Primitive Theory of the Duel.*

In all these combats, the victor's success is not attributed to a god of justice. Neither the Greeks of the epics, nor the Romans of royal legend, nor the Celts held this medieval belief <note>In the Middle Ages, the "Judgement of God" assumed that the heavens would intervene to ensure the righteous party won a duel. In the ancient world, victory was seen more as a sign of divine favor or raw power rather than a moral verdict.</note>. One must not believe, however, that all religious ideas were banished from the primitive conception of combat. Menelaus owes his success to the friendship of Ares, the god of war; he is <term>beloved of Ares <note>original: Ἀρηίφιλος (*Arēiphilos*)</note></term>. The weapon of war, it was once believed, possessed something divine. Before statues of Mars were erected in Rome, this god was worshipped there in the form of a spear (1). Among the Germans and the Celts, the sword seems to have been considered the most important manifestation of the power of the terrible god invoked by warriors.

Among the Germans, the god of war was the god of the sky himself: *Tivaz*, called *Ziu* in Old High German and *Tyr* in Old Norse, who gave his name to the third day of the week, *Tuesday* in English,

The Quadi <note>A Germanic tribe that lived along the Danube in what is now modern-day Austria, Slovakia, and Hungary.</note>, a Germanic people, having to conclude a treaty barely a century before Attila, drew their swords, says **Ammianus Marcellinus**, and swore upon them, for they regarded them as gods (1). The practice of the oath upon the sword persisted among the Germanic peoples after their conversion to Christianity. **Grimm** <note>Jacob Grimm, the famous scholar of folklore and legal history, whose work *Deutsche Rechtsalterthümer* remains a foundational text on ancient Germanic law.</note> has identified an example dating back to the year 889 (2). The same practice was maintained in Holstein <note>A region in northern Germany.</note> until a time very close to our own. The point of the sword was thrust into the ground, and the oath was taken upon the hilt (3). A description of Ireland, written in 1600 and published in 1887 by **Father Hogan**, notes that the custom of swearing by the sword was still used in Ireland at the end of the sixteenth century, and that the sword fixed in the ground was then attributed a sort of divine character. Here is the translation of the text:

I, p. 138, lines 9-10).

The antiquity of the oath by the sword in Ireland is proven by a passage from the epic text titled *Serglige Conculain* <note>Literal translation: *The Wasting Sickness of Cuchulainn*, a famous tale from the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology.</note>, where we see Cuchulainn held in bed by an illness. ### § 1. — Generalities.

The duel was a way to avoid war between two families and two peoples and to limit the shedding of blood. There was a way to prevent all bloodshed: it was the payment of the composition by the guilty party, by their family, or by their people. ### § 2. — *Compensation among the Celts.*

Among the Celts, the amount of compensation is generally determined by the rank of the victim, whether it concerns murder, injury, or insult; this is the common law of the Indo-Europeans. We will see in § 15 what exception this rule includes. What is specific to Celtic law is the distinction between 1st, the **body-price**, fixed invariably for all free men; 2nd, the **honor-price**, which is added to the body-price and whose amount depends on the dignity of the person who was killed, wounded, or insulted. # SETTLEMENT FOR CRIMES IN GAUL.

In Caesar’s time, the Gauls were still in a social state where, except in the case of a crime against the State, sentences were only financial for any solvent man, and where the tariff of <term>compositions</term> <note>a fixed financial payment made to a victim or their family to "compose" or settle a legal dispute and prevent a blood feud</note> was the foundation of criminal law.

### § 3. — *Exile as a means of avoiding the payment of the settlement.*

The murderer generally has a choice between the payment of the settlement and exile. Nicolaus of Damascus <note>a Greek historian and philosopher who was a tutor to the children of Marc Antony and Cleopatra</note>, born in 64 BC and died toward the beginning of the Christian era, informs us that, among the Celts, exile, *phyge* <note>original Greek: "φυγή"</note>, was the resource of the citizen who killed a fellow citizen; but, he says, whoever killed a foreigner was put to death (1). If this murder had not been severely punished, one could expect reprisals and a war with the neighboring people to whom the foreigner belonged.

The murderer of a foreigner therefore placed the security of his own homeland in great danger: he had committed a crime of high treason; he was arrested, brought before the assembly of the people, condemned to death and executed. But killing a fellow citizen could not—

***

(1) "The punishment is greater for one who kills a foreigner than for one who kills a citizen; for the penalty for the former is death, while for the citizen it is exile" <note>original Greek: « Μείζω δ' ἐστὶν ἐπιτιμία κατὰ τοῦ ξένον ἀνέλοντος ἢ πολίτην · ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὲν γὰρ θάνατος ἡ ζημία, ὑπὲρ τοῦ δὲ πολίτου φυγή »</note> (*Stobaeus, Florilegium*, book 44, chapter 41; Teubner-Meineke edition, vol. II, p. 185, lines 14-16; *Fragments of the Greek Historians*, vol. III, p. 457, fragment 105).

The author of such a murder was left free, and if he did not obtain—by paying the <term>composition</term> <note>a financial settlement used to resolve a feud</note>—the family of the deceased's abandonment of their right to vengeance, he could save his life through exile. This meant leaving the territory of his own city and taking refuge in that of another, though without being forced to leave Gaul entirely. These exiles, who were numerous in Gaul, twice provided strong contingents to the armies raised to fight the Romans: first by the Treveran <note>a member of the Treveri, a tribe from the Moselle valley</note> Indutiomarus in 55 BC (1), and later in 51 BC by the Senon <note>a member of the Senones, a tribe from the area of modern-day Sens</note> Drappes (2).

These are the customs of Homeric Greece. In the fifteenth book of the *Odyssey*, Telemachus, having taken leave of King Menelaus of Lacedaemonia, is about to board his ship to leave the Peloponnese. Before entering his vessel, he makes a sacrifice on the shore in honor of his protector, the goddess Athena; he sees someone approaching: it was Theoclymenus, a prophet and the son of a prophet; he had killed a man, and to avoid death he had left Argos, his homeland (3). "I have," he said, "departed from Ar—"

This doctrine consists of distinguishing two elements within the total amount of the composition <note>A financial settlement or "blood-price" paid to a victim or their family to end a feud.</note>. In Irish, this total amount is called *éric* (from *er-icca* or *per-yecca*), meaning “perfect payment” and “perfect healing,” for the full payment of the composition is intended to heal all the wounds inflicted by weapons and blows. The two elements that make up the *éric* are: 1st, the price of the body, in Irish *coirp-díre* <note>Literally "body-fine."</note>, or simply *díre*; 2nd, the price of honor—literally of the face—in Irish *enech-lann*, later also *lóg-eneich*, and in Old Breton *enep-uuert* (1). The price of the body is fixed, while the price of the face varies according to the dignity or social status of the person. The oldest mention we have of a fixed price for a man’s life—specifically a free man or a citizen (p. 138)—dates back to the fifth century AD.

Irish law is less severe; it limits itself to doubling the compensation, known as the *éric* <note>original: *éiric*, a general term for restitution, ransom, or blood-money in early Irish law</note>: now, the legal text says, this compensation is divided into two parts: seven female slaves, and the honor-price. A fire has caused the death of a man, says another Irish legal text. The same legal text deals with the manner in which the price of the body shall be shared. It distinguishes two elements in this price: the restitution, <term>aithgin</term> <note>literally "re-birth" or "restoration," referring to the replacement of the loss itself</note>, which consists of one female slave <note>original: *cumal*, the standard unit of value in early Ireland, often equivalent to three cows</note> who will belong to the son; in the absence of a son, to the father; in the absence of a father, to the brother; and in the absence of a brother, to the closest relative of the deceased. There remain six female slaves who constitute the <term>dîre</term> <note>the "fine" or "penalty" above the simple restitution</note> in the narrow sense of the word—that is to say, when it is distinguished from the restitution, *aithgin*. One half, meaning three female slaves, is shared between the father and the son. The other half is divided into thirds: one female slave to the brothers, one female slave to be shared between the father and the son, and one female slave to be shared among all the members of the section of the family called the <term>geilfine</term> <note>the smallest and closest circle of the Irish kin group, usually consisting of five people</note>, which is to say, among the closest relatives.

The *dîre*, or, to speak more clearly, the <term>coirp-dîre</term> <note>literally "body-fine"</note>, includes, in ordinary usage, not only the six female slaves mentioned last, but also the female slave given additionally as restitution, *aithgin*, to the family of the deceased.

### § 5. — *The price of the body in Wales. Modifications to Celtic criminal law as a result of the Roman conquest.*

*Dîre* <note>the fine or penalty paid for a crime</note> = *\*díreyá*, derives from *\*díro-s*, which in Irish is *dír*, meaning "just." This Celtic *\*díro-s* would be in Indo-European *\*dhé-ro-s* (1), which offers us the full form of the root <term>DHÊ</term> <note>a fundamental linguistic root meaning "to put" or "to place"</note>, and it is the reduced form of this root that we recognize in the Greek justice <note>original: θέμις (*themis*); referring to divine law or established custom</note>. The Irish *díre* is found again in Welsh in the form *dirui* or *dirwy*.

But this word, which before the Roman conquest must have had the same value in Britain as in Ireland, took on a different meaning in Welsh law than it had originally. In Wales, the *dirwy* <note>a fine paid to the king rather than the victim's family</note> remains a charge upon the guilty party or their family, but it is not to the family of the victim that it is paid; it is to the king (2) and his officers (3). It is, therefore, a "fine" in the sense used in our modern law; it is the equivalent of the Germanic peace-money <note>original: *fredum*; in Frankish and Germanic law, this was the sum paid to the public treasury to "buy back" the peace of the king after a crime</note>. The Germanic peace-money and the Welsh *dirwy* are the consequence of a legal doctrine that is relatively modern—

# FIRST PART. CHAPTER V. § 5.

modern one that calls upon the king and his officers to assist the injured party in obtaining punishment for the crime. However, the Welsh *dirwy* and the Irish *díre* are the same word.

Through the Roman conquest, the right of vengeance and the <term>composition</term> <note>a financial settlement paid to a victim or their family to prevent further retaliation</note> for crimes and offenses were suppressed; in Great Britain, as in Gaul, magistrates were charged with punishing men guilty of murder and violence. From this came the new meaning taken in Welsh by the Celtic **díréiâ*, which was originally "composition" and which, in Welsh (where it is written *dirwy*), means "fine."

The composition for murder is the corollary of the right of vengeance, and cannot exist without it. Now, the right of vengeance cannot be exercised without the use of force by private individuals, and the use of force to take justice into one's own hands was forbidden by Roman law at the time when Gaul and Great Britain were conquered.

The **lex Cornelia de sicariis** <note>The Cornelian Law on Assassins</note>, established by Sulla in 81 BC, punished with banishment any free man who walked about carrying a weapon with the intention of killing someone, even if he had killed no one, and even more so if his plan had been carried out (1). ->ROMAN LAW AND WELSH LAW.<-

was completed by others, notably by those passed by Julius Caesar or Augustus, who were the authors of either the **Julian law on public violence** <note>lex Julia de vi publica</note> or the **Julian law on private violence** <note>lex Julia de vi privata</note>. The first equates to banditry and punishes with exile the act of any free man who, accompanied by armed men, carries out a seizure of movable (1) or immovable (2) property. Under the Empire, the confiscation of all assets became an accessory to exile, which, first transformed into deportation to a specific place, was then, little by little, replaced by the death penalty (3).

This is why Strabo, around the year 20 of our era, recounts that the Gauls, formerly so warlike, live today in peace (4) and that they have laid down their arms (5).

Violence without arms was itself forbidden by the **Julian law on private violence**. This law punished with the confiscation of a third of one's property any free man who, by his own private authority and accompanied by unarmed men, carried out a seizure of real estate (6).

### PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 5.

The confiscation of one-third of one’s property was a fine, or *mulcta* <note>original Latin: *mulcta*</note>. Fines multiplied under the Roman Empire, and in Great Britain, the Celtic word *díréid* or *dirwy*—which had originally designated the **composition** <note>A "composition" is a legal payment made by an offender to a victim or their family to settle a grievance and prevent a blood feud</note> paid to the relatives of a deceased person—took on the meaning of the Latin *mulcta*, "a fine paid to the State." It retained this meaning in medieval Welsh law. It is contrasted with the *camlwrw*, which was payable to the king in cases of less serious crimes. The *camlwrw*, a lower fine than the *dirwy*, was owed, for example, by a Welsh creditor who, seeking payment, performed a seizure of movable property without authorization, contrary to the **Julian laws on private and public violence** <note>original Latin: *leges Juliae de vi privata et de vi publica*</note> cited on page 95. The *camlwrw* was only three cows, while the *dirwy* amounted to twelve (1).

Upon the departure of the Romans, the system of composition for murder was re-established in Great Britain, but at that time a new word designated the "price of the body": this was *galanas*. Instead of being a fixed amount, the *galanas* became variable, being higher or lower depending on the status <note>literally: "dignity"</note> of the person killed; this did not prevent it from being combined with the price of honor, called

---

...without arms" (Ulpian in the **Digest** <note>A primary source of Roman law compiled under Justinian I</note>, book 48, title 7, *Regarding the Julian law on private violence*, fragment 5; see also fragment 1).

(1) "He who has taken a pledge for a debt without permission shall lose the whole debt and shall pay three cows as a *camlwrw* <note>original: *camlury*</note> to the lord" (**Welsh Laws** <note>original Latin: *Leges Wallicae*</note>, book II, chapter 7, sections 2, 3; see also chapter 17, sections 6, 7. Aneurin Owen, *Ancient Laws and Institutes of Wales*, folio edition, pp. 784, 823; octavo edition, vol. II, pp. 778, 841).

The Welsh *saraad* is the same word as *sarugad*, which means "insult" in Irish. One-third of the *saraad* and the *galanas* <note>In Welsh law, *galanas* was the payment for homicide, while *saraad* was the payment for injury or insult</note> goes to the king and his officers, and two-thirds to the family of the deceased.

Ireland has preserved the primitive meaning of the word \* *díreiá*, a <term>composition</term> <note>A legal payment made by an offender to a victim’s family to settle a grievance and prevent a blood feud</note> for murder paid to the family of the dead; the concept expressed by this word in Ireland was one of the elements of <term>Gaulish law</term> <note>The legal customs of the Celts in mainland Europe (Gaul) before they were assimilated by Rome</note> before the Roman conquest. This conquest took away from families the right to avenge murders by the death of the murderers, or to spare the lives of the murderers by accepting from them the payment of a <term>composition</term>; it imposed on the Gauls the modern system of <term>public justice</term> <note>original French: *vindicte publique*—the principle that the state, not the individual, has the right to punish crimes</note> carried out by magistrates.

FIRST PART. CHAP. V. § 6.

Irish:
> “The Irish Synod stated: Whoever dares to steal or seize the belongings of a king or a bishop, or commit any offense against them that is an act of contempt toward them, shall pay the price of seven slave women, or perform penance for seven years under the orders of a bishop or a monastic scribe (1).”

Elsewhere, this decision is attributed to Saint Patrick (2) <note>Patrick (5th century), the patron saint of Ireland, to whom many early Irish laws and canons were later attributed to grant them authority</note>. We must distinguish two elements here: one belongs to **Celtic law**, namely the seven slave women <note>original: *ancillae*. In ancient Ireland, a female slave or *cumhal* was a standard unit of value used for large payments, roughly equal to three milk cows</note> or their value owed to a king who has been gravely insulted; to this primitive element, a new ecclesiastical element was added, in which there are again two parts to distinguish: 1st, the assimilation of the bishop to the king; 2nd, for the insolvent debtor, the substitution of **canonical penance** for the <term>composition</term> <note>A financial settlement paid to an injured party to prevent further conflict</note>, at the rate of one year of penance per slave woman. This was a softening of the primitive law which, in cases of non-payment, allowed the right of vengeance to take its course—and royal vengeance meant the death penalty.

One may read the legendary tale in which a subject of King Conchobar <note>Conchobar mac Nessa, the legendary King of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology</note>, having thoughtlessly said that

Here is what the week of an Irish king of a <term>túath (a small tribal kingdom or petty state)</term> looked like in times of peace:

> On Sunday, says the <term>Crith gablach (an 8th-century law tract on social status)</term>, he drinks beer with his subjects, in whose eyes the merit of a king depends on the generosity with which he distributes the precious beverage. On Monday he grants audience to litigants, on Tuesday he plays chess, on Wednesday he watches his dogs hunt; he dedicates Thursday to his marital duties, on Friday he takes a horse ride, and on Saturday he renders his judgments (1). But these judgments were dictated to him by his judge or <term>brehon (a professional jurist and transmitter of traditional law)</term>, so that neither the resolution of legal and factual questions nor the drafting of the verdict caused him much trouble. It was indeed a case for the saying "Happy as a king!" But, in times of war, unstable fortune reclaimed its rights.

->**PRICE OF THE HONOR OF KINGS IN IRELAND.**<-

Most Irish kings ended their lives with a violent death.

Above the king of a petty state, the *rí tuaithe* <note>literally "king of a túath" or tribal territory</note>, stands the provincial king, the *rí cóiced*, which literally means "king of a fifth of Ireland," otherwise known as *ruire* <note>reconstructed linguistic form: \*ro-airek-s</note>, meaning "great chief." The price of his honor <note>the *lóg n-enech* or honor-price: the legal compensation due for an insult or injury to one's social standing</note> is twenty-one female slaves, or sixty-three cows, or even one hundred and five horned beasts of average value, known as a <term>séd (a standard unit of value in Old Irish law)</term>.

The honor-price of the supreme king, the king of "great chiefs" (*rí ruirech* <note>reconstructed form: \*ríx ro-airecon</note>), reached twenty-eight female slaves, or eighty-four cows, or one hundred and forty horned beasts of average value, the <term>séd</term>. Thus, the honor of a provincial king was worth that of three kings of a petty state, and the honor of the supreme king equaled that of four kings of a petty state. This is what we read in the *Senchus Môr* <note>The "Great Tradition," the most important collection of early Irish law tracts</note> (1). This doctrine appears less certain than the one fixing the honor-price for the king of a *túath*. According to the *Crith gablach* <note>an 8th-century legal tract on social status</note>, the honor of the supreme king is worth exactly double the honor of a king of a *túath*, totaling fourteen female slaves (2).

### PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 7.

whose members, in Ireland, bore the title of <term>aire (a noble or chief)</term>. The first category of the <term>aire</term> was composed of those who had vassals under them. The collective body of a chief’s vassals was called the <term>déis (the jurisdiction or vassal-community)</term>, in the genitive case <term>désa</term>. The chiefs who possessed vassals were divided into four classes: the <term>aire forgill (noble of testimony)</term>, the <term>aire tuise (noble of leadership)</term>, the <term>aire ard (high noble)</term>, and the <term>aire désa (noble of the vassal-community)</term>. It was these men who formed, strictly speaking, the nobility or <term>flaith</term>; a passage from the <term>Senchus Mór (The Great Tradition)</term> states that the <term>flaith</term> extends from the <term>aire désa</term> up to the king (1). The other types of <term>aire</term> constituted a sort of lower nobility between the <term>flaith</term> proper and the simple freeman.

The <term>aire forgill</term> or "noble of testimony"—that is, the noble whose testimony carries the highest legal value—has, according to the <term>Crith Gablach (The Branched Purchase)</term>, forty vassals or <term>céile</term>, half of whom are free, <term>sóer céile (free-vassals)</term>, and half of whom are serfs, <term>céile-gialna</term> or <term>dóer céile (base-vassals)</term> (2). The price of his honor <note>the 'honor-price,' or the legal compensation due for an offense against his status</note>, says the gloss of the <term>Senchus Mór</term>, is six female slaves or <term>cumal</term> (3), which is one female slave less than the price for a king. This is the conversion into "large currency" of the figure indicated elsewhere in "small currency" by the text of the <term>Senchus Mór</term>: thirty horned beasts or <term>séd (a standard unit of value)</term>, specifically twenty-four two-year-old heifers, <term>samaisc</term>, and six cows; five horned beasts of average quality are worth one female slave. As a general rule, according to the <term>Senchus Mór (The Great Tradition)</term>, the honor-price of an Irishman determines the amount of the portion of wealth that this Irishman has the faculty to dispose of by bequest in favor of a Church (1).

The <term>*aire túise* (noble of leadership)</term> or "principal noble," so named because he precedes in dignity those who will be discussed hereafter, has twelve free vassals and fifteen serf vassals, twenty-seven in total, thirteen fewer than the <term>aire forgill</term> (2). The price of his honor is fixed at twenty head of horned cattle, <term>séd (a unit of value usually equal to a heifer)</term>, of which sixteen are two-year-old heifers, <term>samaisc</term>, and four are cows: ten head fewer than when dealing with the <term>aire forgill</term> (3). By changing the currency of account, one could have said that his honor was worth four female slaves, two fewer than that of the <term>aire forgill</term>, and three fewer than that of the king (4).

### PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 7.

The <term>aire ard (high noble)</term>—"high" in relation to the <term>aire désa (noble of vassals)</term>—has seven fewer vassals than the <term>aire túise (noble of leadership)</term>, meaning he has twenty: half are free and half are serfs (1). The price of his honor <note>In early Irish law, 'honor-price' (lóg n-enech) was the monetary value of a person's social status, used to determine legal standing and the amount of compensation due for injuries.</note>, which is five head of cattle or one female slave <note>The 'cumal' or female slave was a standard unit of value in ancient Ireland, often equivalent to three cows.</note> less than that of the <term>aire túise</term>, amounts to only three female slaves or fifteen head of horned cattle, consisting of twelve two-year-old heifers and three cows (2).

The <term>aire désa</term>, or "noble of vassals," must, according to the <term>Crith Gablach (The Branched Purchase)</term> <note>An 8th-century Irish legal tract that serves as the primary source for understanding social classes and their requirements.</note>, have ten vassals: five free and five serfs (3). The price of his honor is also represented by the number ten—ten head of cattle, including eight two-year-old heifers and two cows (4); the total is equivalent to two female slaves.

Below the <term>aire désa</term> come two classes of *aire* who possess no vassals: the <term>bó-aire (cow-noble)</term> and the <term>óc-aire (young-noble)</term>.

The <term>bó-aire</term>, or "noble of cows," possesses twelve cows (5). The price of his honor is five head of horned cattle (6) or one female slave; or, if one prefers, three cows (7). A variation of the <term>bó-aire</term> is the <term>bruighfer (hospitaller or land-man)</term> who has twenty cows, and for whom the honor-price rises to six head of cattle (8).

The <term>óc-aire (young-noble)</term> or "beginner noble," literally "young noble," has seven cows (1). The price of his honor <note>The 'honor-price' (lóg n-enech) determined a person's status in the eyes of the law; it was the maximum amount for which they could testify or act as a legal guarantor.</note> is three head of horned cattle, which is to say, three two-year-old heifers (2).

Below the *aire* <note>The general term for 'noble' in early Irish society.</note> comes the freeman of inferior condition, the <term>midboth (middle-hut dweller)</term>, who possesses nothing, or who has less wealth than the <term>óc-aire</term>. His honor is valued at a single head of horned cattle—again, a heifer—but this heifer is less than two years old (3).

### § 8. — Various Aspects of the Hierarchy: Graduated Value of Testimony and the Importance of the Retinue in Ireland.

The importance of the honor-price is considerable. The tariff of the honor-price is not only applied when it is a matter of determining the amount of a composition <note>A 'composition' was the financial settlement paid to an injured party to resolve a legal dispute and prevent a blood feud.</note>. It is to this tariff that one refers when seeking to determine the value of a testimony, an oath, a bond, or the capacity to act as a plaintiff in a lawsuit. The testimony of the freeman of inferior condition, the <term>midboth</term>, is worthless in any case where the interest at stake exceeds the price of a heifer of less than two years of age. ### § 11. — *Celtic feudalism and livestock tenure.*

Celtic feudalism is based not on the granting of land, but on the granting of <term>cheptel</term> <note>A system of leasing livestock, specifically cattle. In the Irish "base-client" system, a lord provided cattle to a commoner in exchange for labor, food-rents, and loyalty</note>. Land is, in theory, the property of the state, the city, or the people. The king may, in his capacity as a magistrate, authorize a citizen to take possession of a portion of territory to establish a home there. However, he does not act as a feudal suzerain <note>A superior lord to whom a vassal owes duties</note> when doing so. In the piece titled "The Cause of the Battle of Cnucha," we see the high king Cathair, who reigned in the second century of our era (1), assigning a piece of land to his druid to build a dwelling; he imposes no dues or services upon him, nor does he grant him this land as a fief (2). *pecus, pecudis* <note>original: "pecus, pecudis," meaning a single head of cattle</note>, and whose root is identical to that of *pecus, pecoris* <note>original: "pecus, pecoris," meaning a herd or livestock</note>. The French landed fief <term>an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term> dates only from the times when the ancient theory of vassalage <term>the system of obligations between a lord and a subordinate</term>, which had been expelled from Gaul by the Roman conquest, was brought back by the Germanic peoples (1). These Germanic tribes, upon entering Gaul, found the established Roman imperial system of land ownership, which then changed the conditions of primitive vassalage and gave it a landed basis that was originally unknown.

However, the word *fief* preserved during the French Middle Ages a meaning that remains consistent, to a certain extent, with its primitive value and its etymology.

Alongside the landed fief, which plays such a significant role in the history of monarchical France, the French Middle Ages also recognized the "money-fief" <note>original: "fief de soudée," a fief where the lord paid the vassal a regular sum of money rather than granting land</note>, which consists of a monetary income.
