### § 12. — *Two types of livestock lease. Two classes of vassals.*

Irish law distinguishes two species of livestock lease <term>cheptel: a contract where a lord provides cattle to a subordinate in exchange for service or rent</term>: the servile lease and the free lease; from which come two kinds of vassals: serf vassals and free vassals. It is the serf vassals, it seems, whom Caesar calls *ambacti* <note>vassals or attendants of a lord</note>; he gives the free vassals the title of *clientes* <note>clients or dependents</note>. In a passage from the *Gallic War* <note>original: "De bello Gallico"</note>, the phrase "servants and clients" <note>original: "servi et clientes"</note> appears to express the same idea as the phrase "vassals and clients" <note>original: "ambacti et clientes"</note> used elsewhere (1). In former times, Caesar says, they burned at the funerals of chiefs the servants and clients "whom it was known the deceased had loved (2)." "The more a knight is of high birth and wealthy," Caesar reports elsewhere, "the greater the number of vassals and clients he has around him in war (3)."

---

(1) Observation by Mr. E. Windisch, in the *Reports of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Saxony* (session of June 14, 1892), p. 159 of the year 1892.
(2) "Those whom it was established were loved by them" <note>original Latin: "Quos ab eis dilectos esse constabat" (Book VI, ch. 19, § 4)</note>.
(3) "They are engaged in war, and as each is most distinguished by birth and resources, so he has the greatest number of vassals and clients around him" <note>original Latin: "In bello versantur, atque ut eorum quisque est genere copiisque amplissimus, ita plurimos circum se ambactos clientesque habet" (Book VI, ch. 15, §§ 1, 2)</note>. *Ambactus* is therefore a kind of *servant* <note>original: "servus"</note> who is distinguished from the Roman *servant* in that he is armed and accompanies his master to war. It is with this qualification that one must accept the assertion of Festus <note>a Roman grammarian</note>, that *ambactus* is a Gaulish word meaning *servant* and was already used with this meaning by Ennius (239-169 BC) (1).

When the livestock lease <term>cheptel: a contract where a lord provides cattle to a tenant in exchange for services or rent</term> is "free," the borrower can, by returning the cattle he received, release himself from all obligations: "If the borrower is weary of his bargain," says the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," an ancient Irish law code</note>, "he is free to return [it] whenever he pleases (2)." When, on the contrary, the livestock lease is "servile," the general rule is that the borrower cannot release himself without returning the

Compare the following Greek text: "They also bring with them free servants chosen from the poor, whom they employ as charioteers and shield-bearers in battle." <note>original Greek: "Ἐπάγονται δὲ καὶ θεράποντας ἐλευθέρους ἐκ τῶν πενήτων καταλέγοντες, οἷς ἡνιόχοις καὶ παρασπισταῖς χρῶνται κατὰ τὰς μάχας."</note> Diodorus Siculus, book V, ch. 29, § 2; Didot edition, vol. How does the <term>aire: a title for various grades of freemen and nobles</term> become "unworthy," <term>eisindraic: Old Irish for unworthy or disqualified</term>? The gloss of the preface to the <term>Senchus Mór: "The Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish law</term> says that it is when he commits a theft. According to the jurist who annotated the text of the *Senchus Mór* in the treatise on servile livestock leasing <note>This refers to *daer-rath*, a form of base-tenancy where the tenant receives cattle in exchange for rent, labor, and submission</note>, the *aire* makes himself unworthy when he gives false testimony, <term>guforgell no guafiadhnnuisi: Old Irish for "false testimony or false witness"</term> (1), whether against his own vassal or against any other person; in such a case, he no longer has any right to his <term>honor-price: the legal value assigned to a person's status, determining the compensation they could receive for injuries or the weight of their word in court</term>; he is "worthless," <term>anfoltach</term>, and "unworthy," <term>esinruic</term>. We saw earlier, on page 109, that the weight of a testimony is equal to the honor-price of the witness.

The contract for servile livestock leasing is established by the delivery to the taker of:
1. The livestock which constitute the capital for the rent to be paid by him in the form of various redevances and certain services; these animals are called <term>turcreic: literally "purchase price"</term>;
2. The livestock which constitute his honor-price; these are called "exchanged cattle," <term>séuit turclóidi</term> (2).
The rule is formally stated by the *Senchus Mór*: "The honor-price of each person, these are his exchanged cattle <term>séuit turclóidi</term> (3)."

The obvious consequence of the sale of the <term>honor-price: the legal value of a person's status, determining their compensation for injuries</term> by the tenant of the **servile livestock** <note>Referring to *daer-rath*, a base-tenure agreement where the tenant accepted cattle from a lord, resulting in a loss of some legal independence</note> was that the right to be paid this portion of the <term>composition: a legal fine or restitution paid to satisfy a grievance</term> belonged to the landlord of the livestock when the tenant was killed or fell victim to a crime or offense that required the payment of such a fine.

The tenant of **free livestock** <note>Referring to *saer-rath*, a higher-status agreement where the tenant remained legally independent while paying rent for cattle</note> received only one-third of his honor-price in addition to the cattle forming the lease; in return, he owed: 1st, a rent in kind equivalent to one-third of the capital received, meaning that in Ireland the interest rate for him was thirty-three percent (1); 2nd, unpaid physical labor, <term>manchuine: manual labor or service owed to a lord as part of a tenancy agreement</term>, for example: assisting in the construction or repair of the chief’s fortress, helping with the chief’s grain harvest, and finally, serving in his wars; 3rd, an act of homage renewable every three years, which consisted of standing upright before the seated landlord (2).

The tenant of the servile livestock had similar burdens: physical labor, notably—

The servile livestock lease was therefore much more advantageous for the taker than the free livestock lease, but it resulted in a social degradation. The taker no longer had a right to his honor-price <note>In ancient Irish law, the "honor-price" (lóg n-enech) was the legal value of a person's status; losing it meant losing one's standing as a free member of the community.</note>. Like the plebeians of Gaul in the time of Caesar, he was no longer among the number of men who count and to whom some honor is rendered, <note>original: *qui aliquo sunt numero atque honore*</note> (1); he was the archetype of those unfortunate Gauls who, crushed by debt, <note>original: *aere alieno*, literally "other people's copper"</note> placed themselves into servitude under the dominion of the nobles (2); the obligation to harvest for the chief, or to build and repair his fort, is what led Caesar to say that most Gaulish plebeians were in a position identical to that of a Roman slave: "over these [men], masters have all the same rights as they do over slaves" <note>original: *in hos eadem omnia sunt jura quae dominis in servos*</note> (3). But there was a great difference between them and the Roman slave: they were the master's companions in war. The Irish text is explicit on this point. And Caesar, who uses the word <term>ambactus: a Celtic term for a dependent or vassal, usually a military follower</term> as a synonym for "slave," says that the military power of Gaulish chiefs depends, among other things, on the number of their *ambacti* (4); his doctrine is therefore on this point in agreement with Irish law. ## § 13. — *The honor-price in French Brittany and in Wales.*

The Irish theory of the **honor-price** seems therefore to have existed in Gaul. The Celtic expression used to designate this part of the legal compensation <note>original: *composition* — a payment made to settle a legal grievance or injury</note> literally means "price of the face"; such is the meaning of the words <note>original: *enech-lann*, *lóg enich*</note> in Irish, and, as we have said, it is explained by the blush that an insult brings to the face of the insulted party. # THE PRICE OF HONOR IN WALES.

under the title *Laws of Hywel the Good* <note>original: "Leges Howeli Boni"; Hywel Dda (the Good) was a 10th-century king of Wales credited with codifying traditional Welsh laws</note> (1). *Sarhaet* <note>a term for an insult or the fine paid to compensate for one</note> is the ordinary term in Welsh law to designate any <term>composition: a legal fine paid to settle a grievance</term> motivated by an insult.

But according to the terms of the *Venedotian Code* <note>the law code specific to Gwynedd, North Wales</note>, it is the *gwyneb-warth* <note>translated literally as "face-shame"</note> that the king’s gatekeeper owes to the high officers of this prince when he refuses them entry to the palace (2). The Welsh translate *gwyneb-warth* as "shame of the face;" but in this compound word, *warth* ("shame") is a faulty pronunciation of *werth* ("value" or "price"); compare the Breton *enebarz* for *enep-uuert* <note>meaning "face-price"</note>.

In the two aforementioned cases, the Welsh *gwyneb-warth* appears to have preserved the general sense of the Irish *enech-lann* <note>the "honor-price" in Old Irish law, reflecting a person's social status</note>; but, usually, this word has taken on a special meaning in Welsh law; it is used exclusively in legislative provisions relating to women; it does not designate, like its Breton equivalent, the dower <note>the portion of a husband's estate provided to his wife for her support after his death</note>, for which Wales has a technical expression, *cowyll* <note>the "maiden-fee" or morning-gift given to a bride by her husband after the consummation of the marriage</note>; it expresses the insults done to women by immoral acts, such as abduction (3), seduction followed by abandonment (4), and the infidelity of the husband (5). Breton law and Welsh law have each, and in an independent manner, restricted the use of the Celtic expression which, in Brittany and Wales, signified "face-price;" <note>referring to the legal value of a person's honor</note> this shall not prevent us from concluding that this expression must have originally held the same importance for them as the corresponding Irish expression. The Irish compound *enech-lann* and the Welsh and Breton compound *enep-uuert* have exactly the same meaning; the first term is identical, *enep* = *enech*; the final consonant is, in the first, the Gaulish representative, and in the second, the Irish representative of a primitive *q* <note>this refers to the linguistic split between P-Celtic (like Gaulish, Welsh, and Breton) and Q-Celtic (like Irish), where a primitive 'q' sound evolved into 'p' or 'ch/k' respectively</note> (1). To express the idea of honor through a word meaning "face" and to make the price of honor an element of <term>composition: a legal payment made to an injured party to settle a feud</term>, is, in both form and substance, a Celtic doctrine that must date back to the highest antiquity.

# HONOR-PRICE FOR INJURY OR INSULT.

A fatal blow gives the family of the deceased the right to demand the full <term>honor-price: the legal value assigned to a person based on their social rank</term>. For a wound that causes a simple effusion of blood and which was made in a fit of anger, the injured person is entitled to only a quarter of the honor-price (1). When the wound has produced only swelling, they can only claim the indemnity called *airer* (2); this is one-seventh of the honor-price (3); in this case, the injury takes the name *enech-ruice* <note>original: "enech-ruice"</note> (4) or *enech-griss* <note>original: "enech-griss"</note> (5). These words mean "face-shame" or "face-reddening."

The technical expression in this document is <note>original Latin: "vitam redimere, se redimere"</note> "to redeem one's life" or "to redeem oneself." He who takes a prisoner away from the magistrate called a <term>grafion: a Frankish administrative official or count</term> must redeem his life (2). The same obligation falls upon the *grafion* in the event of a denial of justice; he must redeem himself by paying the price he is worth: "As much as it costs to redeem himself" <note>original Latin: "Quantum valet se redimere"</note> (3). If he does not pay this price, he shall pay with his life, which is called "to settle with one's life" <note>original Latin: "de vita componere"</note> (4). The insolvent murderer is treated according to this system; he loses his life if none of his relatives wish to redeem him: "If no one wishes to redeem him through composition, let him pay with his life" <note>original Latin: "Si eum in compositionem nullus voluerit redimere, de vita componat"</note> (5).

This is also the doctrine of the <term>Law of the Twelve Tables: the earliest code of Roman law, established around 450 BCE</term>; according to this Roman law, the debtor—that is to say, generally the murderer (I do not mean the assassin to whom the law of <term>Numa: Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome</term> applies (1))—after having been put up for sale at three successive markets and failing to find a buyer, remains at the disposal of the creditors. -># REDEMPTION OF LIFE. SMACHT.<-

The same expression <term>smachtu rechto</term> or <term>smachtu rechta</term> <note>these terms literally translate to "penalties of the law" in Old Irish</note> reappears with the same meaning in the gloss on the Epistle to the Thessalonians (1) and the Epistle to the Colossians (2). <term>Smachtu</term>, in the sense it is used in these three places, could be the Irish translation of Caesar's "penalties" <note>original Latin: *poenas*</note> in *The Gallic War* <note>original Latin: *De bello gallico*</note>, book IV, chapter 13, paragraph 5, which we examined above on pages 80-81.

In the epic piece titled "The Sickbed of Cuchulain," <note>original Irish: *Serglige Conculainn*</note>—referring to the legendary hero of Ulster—when the author wishes to speak of a time when Ireland had no high king, he says that Ireland was without a penalty imposed by a king, literally "without a king's penalty," <term>cen smacht rig</term> (3).

This vague meaning of the word <term>smacht</term> in various texts does not prevent it from having had a very precise meaning in the oldest language of Irish law, where it designated the **composition** <note>composition: a legal payment or fine paid to compensate for a crime or to avoid a blood feud</note> that a culprit had to pay to redeem his life. The legal principle of which the word <term>smacht</term> is the expression in Irish: *redemption of life*, belongs to Germanic law and the most ancient Roman law as well as to Celtic law. It dates back to the most remote antiquity. <term>Smacht</term> = *\*smactu-s* is perhaps connected to the same root as the German *smach*, meaning "shame, outrage, affront" (1); giving to the composition the name of the injury it compensates for is a natural metaphor.

<header>THE FORTY-NIGHT DELAY.</header>

<sig>10</sig>

The importance of the forty-night delay in Frankish procedure, as in Irish procedure, is another common feature of both systems of law.

The use of the forty-night delay in Ireland is attested by the <term>Senchus Mór</term> <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of early Irish legal texts</note> when, in the treatise on <term>distraint</term> <note>The legal seizure of movable property to settle a debt; original French: "saisie mobilière"</note>, the anonymous author uses the expression "man of forty nights," <term>fer cethracat aidche</term> <note>original Old Irish</note> (1). When distraint is carried out against the "man of forty nights," this man is entitled to the longest possible legal delays: ten full days between the summons and the seizure, the same between the seizure and the removal of the objects affected by that seizure, and finally ten full days during which the seized and removed objects remain in <term>impoundment</term> <note>original French: "fourrière"</note> without becoming the property of the creditor.

The "man of forty nights" is one who, already involved in an initial lawsuit, has committed to the plaintiff of that first case to appear before arbitrators. Custom grants him, for this first trial, a delay of forty nights between the commitment to appear and the actual appearance. A third party who, without waiting for the expiration of this period, wishes to bring a new lawsuit against this litigant, begins, according to custom, with a distraint; however, he is obliged to grant the defendant the longest delays permitted by the proce-

<term>Canon law</term> <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority for the government of the Christian organization and its members</note> counts by days following Roman usage, even in Ireland. Furthermore, the three Lents of Irish canon law: 1st before Easter, 2nd before St. John’s Day, 3rd before Christmas, are mandatory for everyone (5), whereas the "man of forty nights," who in the procedure of <term>distress</term> <note>The legal seizure of property to enforce payment or performance of a duty</note> enjoys the longest delays allowed by law, appears to us as an exception to the general state of society.

<meta>This page continues the comparison between ancient Irish and Germanic legal traditions. Having previously discussed how both cultures measured legal delays in "nights" rather than days, the author now examines specific procedures for property disputes and the influence of Roman legal structures on these "primitive" systems.</meta>

<page-num>150</page-num>
<header>PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 16.</header>

The obligation to appear in court and the deadline for fulfilling this obligation is thus a common feature of both <term>Salic law</term> <note>The ancestral code of the Salian Franks, written in the early 6th century</note> and Irish law; this shared trait must date back to the era when the Germans, then subjects of the Celts, were governed by the same laws as their masters. A similar explanation can be offered for the resemblance between Salic and Irish law regarding their regulations on <term>property seizure</term> <note>The legal process of taking possession of land or expelling an unauthorized occupant</note>.

Property seizure is illustrated in Salic law through the procedure of expulsion against the ***homo migrans*** <note>original Latin: "migrating man"—someone attempting to settle in a community where they were not born</note>. The *homo migrans* is one who has come to settle in a ***villa*** <note>In this context, a rural township or communal settlement rather than a single house</note> of which he is not a native; he requires the consent of all the inhabitants of the *villa*. If there is any opposition, even if there is only a single objector, the *homo migrans* is expelled. The procedure against him begins with *three* formal commands made in the presence of witnesses, each followed by a delay of *ten* nights. After the expiration of the third delay of *ten* nights—that is, at the end of *thirty* nights—the claimant has the right to call upon the ***grafio*** <note>A Frankish administrative official, often translated as "count," who acted as a judge or enforcer</note> or count to expel the *homo migrans*, and the *grafio* is bound to grant this request (1).

The petition to the count or *grafio* and the intervention of the magistrate are, in Salic law, innovations; they represent a conquest of the Roman legal spirit over the legislation of primitive peoples.

# PROPERTY SEIZURE.

If we therefore set aside the petition to the count and the intervention of that magistrate, the procedure against the ***homo migrans*** <note>original Latin: "migrating man"—a stranger attempting to settle in a community without unanimous permission</note> of <term>Salic law</term> <note>The ancestral legal code of the Salian Franks, compiled around the 6th century</note> takes on an archaic character that it lost under the pens of its Latin editors.

If we open Volume IV of the *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, we find there the procedure for property seizure as it was practiced in one of the European legal systems that has been least influenced by Roman law. We see that the procedure for property seizure involves a delay of ***thirty nights*** divided into ***three periods of ten nights each*** (1), and that it requires ***three notifications*** (2). In its general features, this is the same procedure prescribed by Salic law for the expulsion of the *homo migrans*. It features the same number of delays, the same duration for each, and the same number of notifications.

The primary difference between the Irish procedure and that of Salic law is that the former, being more archaic, is also more solemn. Salic law requires the claimant, when making each of these three notifications, to be accompanied by witnesses and to formulate the command through...

---

(1) In three legal decades: "<note>original Irish: i teora dechmadaib dliged</note>." *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. IV, p. 18, lines 17-18. Neither the word *day* nor the word *night* is in the text, which speaks only of decades or, more literally, tenths; but the word ***teora*** ("three") is feminine, referring to the feminine ***aidchib*** ("nights") which is implied; ***laithib*** ("days"), which is neuter, would require ***trib***. See above, pp. 145-149.
(2) *Ibid.*, vol. IV, p. 18, line 20 and following; p. 20, lines 1-4.

The Irish law tells the claimant the exact terms he must use: "You shall demand of him right according to law, if there be justice." <note>original French: "Tu lui demandas droit selon droit s'il y a justice." This reflects the ritualistic oral tradition of the *Senchus Mor*, or the Great Custom of Ireland.</note> But the number of witnesses, which is not fixed in <term>Salic law</term> <note>The law of the Salian Franks</note>, is set in Ireland with a characteristic solemnity: one witness at the first command, two at the second, and three at the third.

Finally, in Ireland, witnesses alone are not enough; the claimant must bring horses with him: two the first time, four the second, and eight the third. These horses are harnessed; the first time, he stops with them at the entrance of the property; the second time, entering the property, he unharnesses them there; the third time, he advances with the eight horses as far as the house built on the property, or, if there is no house, to the far edge of the estate. At the end of thirty nights, the claimant—by right and without the intervention of a magistrate—becomes the owner of the **seized estate**, unless the defendant has halted the effect of this procedure by responding to one of the notifications, either by a challenge to a **duel**, by a <term>distress of movable property</term> <note>original: "saisie mobilière"—the seizing of personal goods like livestock to satisfy a debt or legal claim</note>, or by an offer to appear before an arbitrator with a commitment to comply with the judgment that will be rendered.

Thus, the procedure for the **seizure of real estate** in Ireland differs from the procedure for the seizure of real estate...

<page-num>153</page-num>
# SEIZURE OF REAL ESTATE.

Irish law differs from real estate seizure in <term>Salic law</term> <note>The ancestral law of the Salian Franks, a Germanic tribe, dating back to the early 6th century</note> in two ways: 1st, it is carried out without the authorization of a magistrate; 2nd, it is subject to a much more rigorous formalism. These are two ancient characteristics that the law of the Salian Franks must have also possessed prior to the written versions that have reached us. On the other hand, the two laws show an absolute agreement regarding the number of formal demands—three—and the length of the three waiting periods following them—ten nights each, totaling thirty nights.

The long period of dominance the Celts exercised over the Germans explains this agreement, just as it explains the similarity we noted regarding the forty-night delay. It also explains the correspondence we see in the meaning of the names given to the **ordeal of boiling water** in Ireland and in the Germanic laws, as these names simply mean "cauldron" (1). <note>original: "chaudron." In medieval trials by ordeal, a person would reach into a cauldron of boiling water to retrieve an object; healing without infection was seen as proof of innocence.</note>

This same historical reality accounts for the identical nature of certain fundamental elements in the Frankish and Irish rates for **composition** <note>A legal system of fines paid to a victim or their family to settle a grievance and prevent a blood feud</note>; it helps us understand why, in both legislations: 1st, the slave or serf is valued at one-seventh the worth of a free man (p. 142-143); and 2nd, the temporary use of someone else's horse without the owner's consent gives the owner the right to demand a compensation equal to the value of a slave or serf in the rate established by law (p. 144).

### PART ONE. CHAP. V. § 16.

The Germanic rule, which assigns a portion of the <term>composition</term> <note>A legal payment made to settle a grievance and prevent a blood feud</note> to the king—called *frithus* or *fredum*, literally "peace"—and leaves only two-thirds, known as *faidus* (in German *fehde*, meaning "hatred" or "contest"), to the victim or their family (1), is foreign to primitive Celtic law. Nevertheless, it is quite ancient, as it is already found in the *Germania* of <term>Tacitus</term> <note>A Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) who wrote one of the earliest accounts of Germanic tribes</note> (2). From the end of the first century of our era, the State intervened among the Germans in private disputes and required payment for this intervention in the interest of peace—*frithus* (in modern German *Friede*); by then, the more advanced laws of Egypt (p. 9-11), Greece, and Rome had already begun their conquest of Germany, whereas Ireland preserved the rules of primitive law until the beginning of the seventeenth century.

Yet there was something in Ireland analogous to the *fredum*: the fees of the <term>brehon</term> (3) <note>An ancient Irish judge or legal expert who interpreted the complex Brehon Laws</note>, that is to say, the jurist upon whose report the king and the assembly of the people delivered their sentence. These fees were already a Homeric custom. One of the scenes sculpted by Hephaestus on the

# ARBITRATION IN THE ODYSSEY.

Greek civilization of the <term>Homeric age</term> <note>The period of Greek history described in the works of Homer, roughly the 8th century BCE</note>, around eight hundred years before Jesus Christ, was, in its fundamental aspects, nearly identical to that of independent <term>Gaul</term> <note>The region of Western Europe inhabited by Celtic tribes, corresponding mainly to modern-day France</note> seven centuries later; it could have often provided subjects for paintings similar to those left to us by <term>Poseidonius</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and historian (c. 135–51 BCE) who wrote extensively on the customs of the Celts</note>. Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus, the protagonist of the Odyssey</note>, having returned to Ithaca, kills—in concert with his son Telemachus—the rivals who, believing him dead, were seeking the hand of his wife, Penelope. He is by no means reassured when he reflects on the probable consequences of the daring massacre that his jealousy as a husband drove him to commit.

> "If someone," he says to Telemachus, "among the people has taken the life of a single man who leaves behind avengers even in small numbers, he flees, abandoning his relatives and his homeland (1); yet we have put to death the most distinguished young men of Ithaca, those who were the pillars of the State. I ask you to give this your serious attention (2)."

Indeed, the relatives of the dead gather together. Eupeithes, the father of one of the victims, takes the floor.

### ARBITRATION IN THE ODYSSEY.

The *Odyssey* does not tell us what the specific clauses of this treaty were. It was unnecessary to state them. One can assert without fear of error that Ulysses undertook the commitment to pay the blood money <note>original: *τὰ ὑποφόνια*</note> (1), which he owed for the numerous murders he had committed; but from this was deducted what the suitors owed him for the acts of plundering they had committed in his house during his absence, and for the feasts they had held at his expense without his consent; the total had been valued at twenty oxen per suitor. This sum had been offered to him in the name of the suitors before he killed them (2), and he had refused to accept it; it remained due to him after their death. Now, once this sum was subtracted from the blood money for murder, the latter must have been reduced to a very low figure (3).

What is particularly remarkable in the Homeric narrative is the intervention of a goddess, and the threat she addresses to Ulysses when she tells him that, if he wishes to continue the war against the relatives of the dead suitors, he will incite against himself the almighty wrath of Zeus. In his

We know where the Druids came from. The Belgae, accompanied by some Celts—the *Parisii* (1), for example—had conquered Great Britain in the second century BC (2). There they had found and subdued the *Góidel* <note>Also known as the Gaels, the early Celtic inhabitants of Ireland and parts of Britain</note>, that is to say, a Celtic population more anciently installed on that island. Among this population was a teaching priesthood that recruited from among its students; these were the Druids. The Druids, defeated along with their compatriots, in turn conquered their conquerors, the Gauls of Great Britain; then, not content with this success, they extended their dominance over the Gauls of the continent (3). At the same moment, Greece, subjected to the political domination of the Romans, imposed upon its barbarian masters the poetry of its religious fables, its literary methods, and its philosophy:

# THE DRUIDS AS ARBITRATORS.

Two centuries later, one saw emerging from Jerusalem—which was then under the authority of a Roman *praeses* <note>original: "praeses"; a Roman governor or administrative official</note>—a religion which, in Rome, caused the national gods to fall from their altars, and which imposed its spiritual domination upon its conquerors.

The importation into Gaul of Druidism, which was born among the *Góidel* <note>The Gaels, or early Celtic inhabitants of the British Isles</note> in Great Britain, was like the conquest of Rome by the literature and arts of Greece or by Christianity: a peaceful revenge of the vanquished.

The Druids became in Gaul, like Mentor in Ithaca, the arbitrators of legal disputes. 

> "Each year, at a fixed date," says Caesar, "they sit together as judges in the territory of the Carnutes <note>A Celtic people living in the region of modern-day Chartres, considered the religious center of Gaul</note> in a consecrated place, and there, from all sides, all those who have disputes gather to ask them to render judgments to which these litigants submit." 

"**All those who have disputes**," OMNES *qui controversias habent* (1) <note>original Latin: "All who have controversies/disputes"</note>, is an expression that must not be taken in an absolute sense. **All**, OMNES, means "a great many people." If **all those** who had disputes had them judged by the Druids, Caesar could not have informed us that, before his time, there were wars between the Gauls almost every year...

---

(1) *The Gallic War*, Book VI, ch. 13, § 10. Regarding this passage from Caesar, cf. Strabo, Book IV, ch. 4, § 4, who, speaking of the Druids, says: "They are entrusted with both private and public disputes, such that in the past they even mediated wars and stopped those about to draw up for battle; and cases of murder, in particular, were turned over to them for judgment." <note>original Greek: "Πιστεύονται τάς τε ἰδιωτικὰς κρίσεις καὶ τὰς κοινάς, ὥστε καὶ πολέμους διήτων πρότερον, καὶ παρατάττεσθαι μέλλοντας ἔπαυον, τὰς δὲ φονικὰς δίκας μάλιστα τούτοις ἐπετέτραπτο δικάζειν."</note> Didot edition, p. 164, lines 24-27.

# IMMOLATION OF PRISONERS OF WAR.

Posidonius <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher and polymath who traveled through Gaul around 100 BC</note>, at the beginning of the first century before our era, found the same custom in Gaul. He notes that, in this country, "wrongdoers"—that is to say, murderers who cannot ransom their lives—"are held in prison for five years,"—evidently to give their relatives plenty of time to collect a ransom, if they wish or are able to;—"then," tied to stakes in honor of the gods, "they are burned with other offerings on immense pyres (1)." He adds: "The Gauls also use prisoners of war as victims in honor of the gods. Some among them kill, along with the men, the animals captured in war; they take their lives either by burning them or by employing another kind of torture (2);" it is Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian whose work often preserved lost writings of earlier travelers like Posidonius</note> who, copying Posidonius, gives us these details.

Another echo of Posidonius is found in Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note>. After having recounted how the druids, striking a man with a sword blow in the back, claimed to divine the future by his movements

tor, what we would certainly find in the texts relating to triumphs would be, instead of secular decapitation, human sacrifice; and the oldest documents would teach us that in Rome, in the first centuries, the prisoners who had been part of the victor’s procession were sacrificed to Capitoline Jupiter <note>The supreme Roman deity, whose temple stood on the Capitoline Hill.</note> just like the animals that had appeared with them in the ceremony. Among the Gauls, the ancient conception was maintained into the historical period, and the execution of a prisoner of war—like that of an insolvent murderer or a thief (1)—is considered a religious act; it is carried out through the ministry of the druids in the form of a sacrifice in honor of the gods.

### § 19. — *Druidism, incompatible with the fundamental principles of classical Roman law, is suppressed by the Roman conquest.*

The Roman conquest brought an end to human sacrifices in Gaul (2). A decree of the Senate <term>sénatus-consulte: a formal decree or resolution issued by the Roman Senate</term> of—

Among the early Romans, as among the Ossetians <note>an Iranian ethnic group from the Caucasus mountains</note>, vengeance for murder was a religious duty. An example of the application of this doctrine is offered to us by the legend of Romulus <note>the legendary founder of Rome</note> and Tatius. Relatives of Tatius, king of the Sabines and co-ruler with Romulus, robbed and killed ambassadors sent to Rome by the inhabitants of Laurentum. Tatius having refused all reparation, vengeance was exercised against him, and he was killed by the relatives of the ambassadors. Romulus judged that the death of Tatius and that of the ambassadors compensated for one another; but the gods did not approve of this way of thinking; they sent an epidemic which took the lives of men; they struck the livestock and the fields with sterility; to calm the celestial anger, it was necessary to punish with the <term>ultimate penalty</term> <note>death</note> the murderers of the ambassadors and the murderers of Tatius (2).

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of blood vengeance, transitioning from the legendary examples of the previous page to a formal comparison between the "law of nations" (international relations between tribes or cities) and "private law" (internal matters) in both Celtic and Roman societies.</meta>

<header>PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 20.</header>

The crime of some and the reprisals carried out by others fell under the <term>law of nations</term> <note>the legal principles governing the interactions between different sovereign peoples</note> and not private law, since, in both cases, each perpetrator belonged to a different city than his victim; the exercise of vengeance for the first and second murder therefore fell within the jurisdiction of public authorities. We have seen, on page 83, that in similar circumstances in independent Gaul, the State to which the perpetrator belonged had him arrested and put to death, whereas in the case of the murder of a fellow citizen, the State left the perpetrator free to escape by flight and abandoned the exercise of the right of vengeance to the relatives of the deceased. There is thus a concordance here between Celtic law and the law of Rome under the kings.

Here is a point on which the two legislations contradict each other.

A law of Numa <note>the second legendary king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious and legal institutions</note> seems to have assigned to the State the punishment of every murderer, even a citizen of Rome, when he had acted with premeditation and the victim was a free man. The text is well known: *If anyone knowingly and with [malicious] intent puts a free man to death, LET HIM BE DECLARED A MURDERER* <note>original Latin: "Si quis hominem liberum dolo [malo] sciens morti duit, PARICIDAS ESTO"</note>; *PARICIDAS* refers to the murderer of an equal, *par* <note>the Latin root for "equal"</note>; his punishment was the <term>law of retaliation</term> <note>also known as "lex talionis," or an eye for an eye</note>, that is to say the death penalty, inflicted by order of the magistrate, and the execution of the culprit was considered a religious act (1). Numa had taken away from the family the right

<header>THE DUTY OF VENGEANCE AND NECESSARY MURDER.</header>

The right to accept a <term>composition</term> <note>a financial payment made to the victim's family to settle a feud; similar to the Germanic "wergild"</note> for murder was only upheld in cases where the murder was not premeditated: *If someone should kill a man unintentionally* <note>original Latin: *Si quis imprudens occidisset hominem*</note>; in such a case, the guilty party could be replaced by a ram sacrificed to <term>Janus</term> <note>the two-faced Roman god of beginnings and transitions, who oversaw the religious cleansing of the community</note>, and the religious duty was fulfilled (1).

Celtic law, in contrast to Roman law, never involves a magistrate to ensure the punishment for a murder committed by a citizen against a fellow citizen. In this case, regardless of aggravating or mitigating circumstances, the law makes no distinction and allows the relatives of the victim the right to accept a composition without exception.

However, in the Celtic theory of composition, a trace of the rigor of primitive law remains: the expression "necessary murder," or "murder of necessity," <note>original Old Irish: *marbad dethbire*</note>.

<header>PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 20.</header>

been "by necessity" or not, <term>dethbire</term> <note>original Old Irish: meaning "necessary" or "justifiable"</note> or <term>indethbire</term> <note>original Old Irish: "unnecessary" or "unjustifiable"</note>. A murder "of necessity" is one that was not premeditated, or if premeditated, has a legitimate cause: the duty of vengeance. A murder that is not of necessity is one that is not motivated by the duty of vengeance and which is the result of a prior intent provoked by the desire for gain (1).

When a murder has been "of necessity," the murderer is not the sole debtor for the entire composition. Of the seven female slaves <note>The "cumal" or female slave was a standard unit of value in ancient Irish law</note> who make up the price of the composition, he alone owes only the female slave whose value the family of the deceased has the right to demand as restitution, <term>aithgin</term> <note>original Old Irish: "restitution" or "replacement," referring to the basic value of the loss</note>. The debt for the remainder of the composition is shared between him and his closest relatives, for example, his son or his father; that is to say, a part

If the murder is not necessary—that is to say, if it was premeditated and, furthermore, is not motivated by the duty of vengeance—the entire composition <note>a financial settlement or blood-money paid to settle a legal claim</note> is owed by the murderer alone. His son and his father may, like the rest of his close relatives, be called upon to contribute to the expense, but only after the murderer's own resources have been exhausted.

Thus, the duty of vengeance makes a murder "necessary"; this is the theory of antiquity.

To the category of murder that the duty of vengeance makes "necessary," in accordance with an ancient doctrine that seems to have been common to all humanity, the Irish jurists have equated non-premeditated murder (1). That is to say, <term>unintentional</term> murder <note>original Greek: ἀκούσιος (*akousios*)</note>, which among the Athenians was punished by exile without granting the relatives of the deceased the right to kill the murderer as long as he did not return to Attica (2). This is the same type of murder which, in Rome, according to a law of Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious and legal rites</note>, was expiated by the sacrifice of a ram (p. 181). -># NECESSARY MURDER IN IRELAND.<-

of an imprudence, or a lack of precaution, is not, strictly speaking, "necessary;" "necessary" murder, in the precise sense of the word, is that which is imposed upon the murderer by the sacred duty of vengeance; and as the duty of vengeance was imposed on all close relatives, by order of kinship, the closest relatives bore all the consequences of the act that this duty required. This principle was extended in Ireland to the consequences of unpremeditated murder <note>homicide resulting from an accident or lack of foresight</note> which was assimilated to murder motivated by the duty of vengeance, and the composition <term>composition: a financial settlement or "blood money" paid to a victim's family to prevent further feuding</term> was partly owed by the family in both cases.

How, one might ask, does a murder that avenges another give rise to the payment of a composition? Evidently, for the first murder that the necessary murder avenged, a composition is already owed to the family of the first victim, but this composition may be lower than the composition owed for the victim whose life was taken by the fulfillment of the duty of vengeance; in this case, the perpetrator of the second murder owes the difference between the two compositions; it is this difference that is borne concurrently with him by his closest relatives.

This law imposes the duty of vengeance upon: 1st, the father, the son, and the grandson; 2nd, the brother, the uncle, and the nephew (2). This is the Irish *geilfine*, plus the uncle and the nephew; it is the *derbfine*, minus the first cousin; it is the merging into a single group of the two groups distinguished by the law of Draco. ### § 22. — *Who is the debtor of the composition? The distinction between necessary and unnecessary crimes.* ###

With this explanation finished, let us return to a question posed in § 20. By whom is the <term>composition <note>A financial payment made to an injured party or their family to settle a feud and prevent further violence.</note></term> owed? There are two scenarios to distinguish. Is the composition being claimed for a <term>necessary murder <note>In the context of ancient law, this refers to a homicide that was either legally/socially mandatory (such as an act of blood vengeance) or one that was accidental/unpremeditated.</note></term> (1st, in the strict sense of the word, meaning an obligatory murder; 2nd, for an unpremeditated murder)? Or is it being claimed for any other cause?

Usually, the composition is not requested for a necessary murder. It is requested for a wound that was not fatal, for a blow, for an insult, for any wrong done to another, and finally for a premeditated murder that the duty of vengeance does not justify. In all these cases, the composition is owed in its entirety by the guilty party; his family is only a debtor in his absence, and it can discharge itself of all debt by handing over the culprit either to the surviving victim or to the victim's family, if that victim has lost their life (2). This is <term>noxal surrender <note>Original French: *abandon noxal*. A legal principle where a family head could avoid liability for a crime committed by a dependent by surrendering the wrongdoer to the victim's family.</note></term>. From this rule, there—

### PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 22.

The responsibility of the king is not unique to Irish law. It is also found in India: a Brahmanic code <note>This refers to ancient Hindu legal texts, such as the Laws of Manu.</note> obliges the king to compensate a victim of theft when he cannot find and return the stolen object (1). The king’s responsibility is merely one form of the collective responsibility of the commune or the district, which is encountered in a large number of ancient legal systems (2). The liability of relatives is also a matter of common law in primitive legislations; it certainly existed in Gaul, as did the option for relatives to escape this responsibility by surrendering the culprit. The same principles are found in the Salic law <note>The Salic Law (*Pactus Legis Salicae*) was the ancient civil law code of the Salian Franks, established during the reign of Clovis I in the early Middle Ages.</note>.

> ” where the murderer finds himself unable to

> ” twelve co-jurors must swear that he possesses
> ” nothing on the surface of the earth, nor in the depths
> ” of the earth, other than what he offers as
> ” **composition** <term>composition<note>A financial settlement paid to atone for a crime or injury, intended to "compose" or settle the dispute between parties.</note></term>... He then summons his close
> ” relatives to pay in his place. If the relatives
> ” are, in their turn, unable to provide the sum
> ” required, the culprit is handed over to his creditor.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal liabilities of the Irish kinship group (fine). # WHO OWES THE COMPOSITION IN IRELAND.

When the **necessary crime** <term>necessary crime<note>In Old Irish law, a *cin dethbire* was a "crime of necessity"—an act that, though harmful, was committed under justifiable or unavoidable circumstances, such as self-defense.</note></term> is not a murder, the family is only obliged to contribute after the criminal’s own resources are exhausted. The remainder of the debt is divided in the same way as a profitable inheritance left by the murderer would be shared (1). The family’s situation, when the necessary crime is not a murder, is the same as when the crime—though a murder—is not "necessary" <note>This refers to the principle that for non-necessary murders, the individual’s assets are seized first, or the family may "extinguish" their debt by surrendering the murderer.</note>. The reason why the family contributes to the **composition** <term>composition<note>Known as *éiric* in Irish law, this was the financial payment made to settle a legal claim or crime, effectively compensating the victim's family to prevent a blood feud.</note></term> due for a **necessary murder**, even if the murderer is personally solvent, is, according to the Irish **legal experts** <term>legal experts<note>The *Brehons*, the professional class of jurists in early medieval Ireland who maintained and interpreted the complex traditional laws.</note></term>, that the family would have received a share of the composition if the murderer had been the one who lost their life. But if the murderer had only received a wound, the composition would have belonged to them in its entirety (2).

III, p. 68, l. 7-11). "Every crime of necessity that a man commits, except murder, results—if that man is solvent—in the payment of **composition** <term>éiric<note>The Irish term for compensation for a crime.</note></term> by him until his movable property and land are exhausted; what he still owes [for a crime of necessity] except for the composition [for a crime of necessity that is not murder] is to be paid by his family in the same way they share an inheritance." ### § 23. — Murders for which the family cannot demand composition. The killing of a thief.

There are a certain number of murders for which no **composition** <term>composition<note>A financial payment (*éiric* in Irish) made to the family of a victim to settle a legal claim and prevent a blood feud.</note></term> is owed.

Thus Gaius <note>A celebrated Roman jurist who lived in the 2nd century CE; his *Institutes* is a primary source for understanding early Roman law.</note> stated: "The penalty for manifest theft was capital, according to the Law of the Twelve Tables; the thief, when he was a free man, was adjudged to the victim (1)." Gaius adds that the legal experts who preceded him had questioned whether, despite this adjudication, the thief remained a free man or if he became a slave. It is evident that the second hypothesis is the correct one. The sentence that adjudged the thief as a slave to the victim gave the victim the power of life and death over the thief.

From the comparison between these various civilized and barbarian legislations, there is reason to conclude that in Gaul, in the time of Caesar, the victim who arrested his thief—either at the moment of the theft or while the thief was still in possession of the stolen object—had the right to take his life. This explains the death of thieves who were burned and offered in sacrifice to the gods by the Druids (2) <note>Druids were the high-ranking religious and legal authorities in ancient Celtic cultures.</note>.

The Roman legislation of the Empire, that is to say, the Praetorian legislation <note>Law developed by the Roman Praetors (magistrates), which was more flexible and equitable than the rigid ancient laws of the Twelve Tables.</note>, was much less harsh—

(1) "The penalty for manifest theft according to the Law of the Twelve Tables was capital; for a free man, after being whipped, was handed over to the person he had robbed. Whether he truly became a slave by this handover, or was placed in the position of one handed over, was a question among the ancient jurists." <note>original: « Poena manifesti furti ex lege XII Tabularum capitalis erat, nam liber verberatus addicebatur ei cui furtum fecerat. (2) *The Gallic War*, Book VI, Chapter 16, § 5: "Those who... have been caught in the act of theft." <note>original: « Qui in furto... sint comprehensi. »</note> These words seem to imply the case of **flagrant délit** <term>flagrant délit<note>From the French, meaning "in the very act" of committing a crime.</note></term>.

rigorous against <term>manifest theft<note>Theft where the perpetrator is caught in the act or while still in possession of the stolen goods.</note></term> than the Law of the Twelve Tables; it replaced the penalty of <term>adjudication<note>A legal process where a person was handed over to their victim as a slave to settle a debt or penalty.</note></term> with a fine of four times the value of the stolen object (1), while for non-manifest theft, the penalty remained double the value, as it had been in the Law of the Twelve Tables.

Such was the law that the Romans brought to Great Britain. After their departure, there was a return to ancient severity. A Welsh legal text proposes the scenario of a thief who, at the moment of being hanged (2), denounces an accomplice. This testimony of a man about to appear before God is held as decisive. The accomplice revealed in this way is thus convicted of theft, but he has the option to redeem himself from the <term>final punishment<note>A historical euphemism for the death penalty.</note></term> (3); for, says the legal text, one cannot put to death someone who was not found in possession of the stolen object (4).

Indeed, being found in possession of a stolen object constitutes one of the aggravating circumstances which, according to certain Roman legal scholars, were sufficient to constitute <term>flagrante delicto<note>Latin: "in a blazing offense." The thief found in possession of the stolen object had, according to Welsh law, the option to redeem himself; when, possessing the necessary resources, he did not redeem himself (2), he paid for this thrift with his life. In such a case, the <term>composition for murder<note>Known as "galanas" in Welsh law; a financial payment made to a victim's family to prevent a blood feud.</note></term> could not be claimed from the victim of the theft by the relatives of the thief. A legal text affirms this, adding that the death of the thief cannot give rise to a lawsuit between two families (3).

<header>THE PENALTY OF THE DOUBLE IN ROME AND IRELAND.</header>

Norwegians (1) pronounced the death penalty against thieves; it was the application of the law given to the Athenians by <term>Draco<note>An early Greek lawmaker (c. 7th century BCE) known for the extreme severity of his punishments, from which we get the word "draconian."</note></term> seven centuries before Jesus Christ (2), and old French law was likewise much more rigorous toward them than our modern Penal Code. There is therefore no reason to be surprised if one finds in the provisions of <term>Celtic law<note>The traditional legal systems of the Celtic-speaking peoples, such as the Irish and Welsh, before they were fully replaced by English or Roman-influenced systems.</note></term> regarding theft a harshness that is no longer present in our customs.

What is strange is that in medieval Irish law, which preserves the harshest rules of primitive penalty against theft, we find, alongside this rigorous severity—and by a flagrant contradiction—the gentler provisions of Roman law. Roman law during the Imperial era punished <term>manifest theft<note>Theft where the thief is caught in the act or in possession of the goods.</note></term> by a <term>composition<note>A legal payment made by an offender to the victim to settle a claim and avoid further punishment or feuding.</note></term> payable to the victim which was to be worth four times the stolen object, the *penalty of the fourfold* (3). If the theft was not manifest, the thief owed the victim twice the value of the stolen object, the *penalty of the double* (4).

Now, this penalty—the restitution of double the stolen object—passed from canon law into Irish civil law, not as a general rule, it is true, but in one specific case. The author of the treatise on distraint <note>The legal act of seizing someone's property to force them to pay a debt or fulfill an obligation.</note>, the first book of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish laws.</note>, provides for a case where the seized object has been left in the defendant's custody, but the defendant then removes it. For example, according to the <term>gloss<note>A brief marginal or interlinear note explaining a difficult word or passage in a manuscript.</note></term>, the defendant might move it to the enclosure of one of those great lords where the plaintiff is legally unable to carry out a seizure. In this case, the defendant incurs the penalty—literally "the debt"—of theft, *fiach gaiti* <note>original Old Irish: *fiach gaiti*</note> (1), which is to say, restitution of double the value, *taisiuc diabul-aithgina* <note>original Old Irish: *taisiuc diabul-aithgina*</note> (2). Despite the similarity of this text with the <term>Law of the Twelve Tables<note>The earliest attempt by the Romans to create a code of law (c. 450 BC).</note></term>, which concerns "non-manifest" theft <note>A category of theft in Roman law where the criminal was not caught in the act, resulting in a fine rather than physical punishment.</note>, this provision appears modern within the context of Celtic law (3).

<header>MURDER IN A DUEL.</header>

[The object] stolen does not give rise to the payment of a <term>composition<note>A financial payment (known in Old Irish as *éraic*) made by an offender to a victim or their family to settle a legal claim and prevent a blood feud.</note></term>. Nor is a composition paid when one has killed their opponent in a regularly initiated duel. A duel is considered regularly initiated in two circumstances: 1st, when it has been preceded by a contract concluded with the participation of the family, which has determined the consequences of the duel; 2nd, when its cause is the defendant’s refusal to allow the plaintiff to proceed with a <term>seizure<note>The legal act of taking possession of property to satisfy a debt, known in Irish law as *athgabáil*.</note></term> in the forms determined by custom.

The first of these two scenarios was already discussed on page 47. In this case, both parties—speaking in a loud and intelligible voice before witnesses—determine what the consequences of defeat will be for both the winner and the loser. This might include, for example, the restitution of a specific object to the plaintiff if they are victorious, or the final abandonment of that object to the defendant if the latter wins. In general, this involves fixing both the object of the dispute and the resolution that the outcome of the fight will provide for the legal question at hand (1).

# FIRST PART. CHAP. V. § 24.

We have seen, on pages 61 and 64, that the contract by which a duel becomes "agreed-upon" is not valid without the consent of the family; by giving this consent, the family forfeits its right to a <term>composition for murder<note>A financial settlement, or blood-price, paid to a victim's family to prevent a cycle of revenge killings.</note></term>. Likewise, when a duel is caused by the defendant's refusal to submit to the consequences of an <term>extra-judicial procedure<note>Legal actions taken outside of a formal courtroom, such as a private seizure of goods to settle a debt.</note></term> initiated by the plaintiff, the plaintiff must be careful. If he wishes to be certain of avoiding claims from the defendant's family after the duel, he must first give that family <term>formal notice<note>A legal demand (*mise en demeure*) requiring the family to settle the debt themselves if the defendant refuses.</note></term> to pay the debt. Otherwise, after killing his opponent, he risks having to pay the full composition for murder (1).

A regular duel gave the victor ownership of the body, the weapons, and the clothing of his opponent (2). The body belonged to him, meaning he had the right to cut off the head of the vanquished and carry it home as a trophy. In Ireland, epic legends and history offer numerous examples of this barbaric practice (3). The same custom must have existed in Gaul; it was

The duel was abolished in Gaul and Great Britain by the Roman conquest. In the laws of Wales—which are a mixture of old Celtic customs, Roman law, and innovations following the Roman period—the duel, when it does not result in a man's death, is punished by a fine, <term>dirwy<note>A specific fine in medieval Welsh law, typically twelve cows, paid to the king for serious offenses like assault or theft.</note></term>, of twelve cows to the benefit of the king and royal officers (2); see above, p. 94, 96. The death of a man in a duel leads to the payment of <term>galanas<note>A blood-price or compensation for homicide paid by the killer's family to the victim's family to prevent a blood feud.</note></term>, one-third of which also belongs to the king and his officers (3), while the remainder goes to the family of the deceased. The total amount of <term>galanas</term> for a free man, a <term>bonhedic<note>A Welsh term for a man of noble lineage or a gentleman of birth.</note></term>, is 309 and two-thirds cows, namely:

<header>MURDER OF A WIFE IN GAUL.</header>

The right to kill, as a consequence of a regular duel, was also present among the Gauls, if we are to believe Caesar, as a result of marital authority and paternal authority. According to him, furthermore, when a high-born head of a household dies and his wives are suspected, his gathered relatives subject his wives to the <term>question<note>A historical term for judicial interrogation involving torture to extract a confession.</note></term> just as they would slaves; in cases where their guilt is proven, they are put to death by fire after being subjected to all kinds of tortures (1).

It would be a mistake to conclude from this text that polygamy was the norm in the Celtic world, or that every husband could dispose of his wife’s life as he pleased without facing the exercise of the right and duty of vengeance by the deceased woman's relatives—or at least without having to pay the wife's family a <term>composition<note>A "blood price" or financial settlement paid to a victim's family to prevent a blood feud.</note></term> like any other murderer. We say "his wife" and not "his wives."

Common Indo-European law does not recognize polygamy. Monogamy is one of its fundamental principles. It requires the wife to be of equal status to her husband; it imposes marital fidelity upon the wife; it does not impose it upon the 

---

(1) "Husbands have the power of life and death over their wives, as they do over their children; and when a father of a family born in a more illustrious position has died, his relatives assemble, and if the circumstances of his death come under suspicion, they hold an investigation into the wives in the manner of slaves, and if proof is found, they kill them, tortured by fire and all manner of torments" <note>original: "Viri in uxores, sicuti in liberos, vitae necisque habent potestatem; et cum paterfamiliae inlustriore loco natus decessit, ejus propinqui conveniunt, et, de morte si res in suspicionem venit, de moribus in servilem modum quaestionem habent, et, si compertum est, igni atque omnibus tormentis excruciatas interficiunt"</note> (Caesar, *The Gallic War*, VI, c. 19, § 3).

Odysseus, the Homeric hero, has only one legitimate wife, Penelope, daughter of Icarius, king of a part of Acarnania (2). Penelope is faithful to him; but when the hero refuses the <term>composition<note>A financial settlement or "blood price" paid to settle a grievance and avoid a blood feud.</note></term> of twenty oxen per head, which is offered to him in the name of the suitors; when he inflicts the ultimate punishment on the twelve female slaves who yielded to the solicitations of those reckless young men, it is easy to guess the cause of this pitiless severity. These twelve female slaves were so many concubines whom Odysseus had maintained in the conjugal home, under the eyes of Penelope, and whose presence this model wife was constrained by custom to endure. These concubines were unfaithful to Odysseus; their death and that of their accomplices is the vengeance that Odysseus takes for this outrage to his jealous authority (3).

<page-num>213</page-num>
# MONOGAMY AMONG THE INDO-EUROPEANS.

The household of most great Greek and Roman lords must have resembled that of Odysseus. In Rome, two categories of women were distinguished: 1st, those with whom it was lawful to contract a marriage; 2nd, those with whom marriage was prohibited. The former were those with whom one had the <term>*connubium*<note>A Roman legal term referring to the capacity to enter into a valid civil marriage (justae nuptiae).</note></term>. Originally, the Roman patrician had the *connubium* only with patrician women. He did not obtain it with plebeian women until the year 445 before our era (1).

It was a principle in Rome that children followed the condition of their mother (2). This was a fundamental rule to which successive exemptions were made, but of which certain remnants have always remained. The children that a master had with his slave were born slaves: their father could not, even through manumission <note>The formal process of freeing a slave.</note>, erase the stain of their original servitude and raise them to the rank of <term>freeborn<note>Latin: *ingenui*; citizens born free, as opposed to those who were freed from slavery.</note></term> to which the sons of the legitimate wife were entitled from birth. The children that, in the early days of Rome, a patrician would have had with a plebeian woman would be

---

see Kovalevsky, *Contemporary Custom and Ancient Law*, p. 155-161; cf. p. 187, 201-203, where he notes that the sons of the legitimate wife alone continue the family, and that they alone inherit from the father.

Similarly, children born of the union of a Roman citizen and a Latin woman were born Latins, so long as the Latins did not possess the <term>connubium<note>The legal right to enter into a valid Roman marriage (justae nuptiae) which granted the father legal power over his children.</note></term>; and the children that a <term>foreign woman<note>original: *peregrina*</note></term> had with a Roman citizen were born <term>foreigners<note>original: *peregrini*</note></term>. Of these children, whose mother was of a condition inferior to that of the father, none entered into the paternal family or had any right to the father’s inheritance.

A remnant of this ancient conception survives in the <term>left-handed marriage<note>original: *mariage de la main gauche*; also known as a morganatic marriage, a legal arrangement among European royalty where the spouse of "inferior" status and any children born of the union have no claim to the father's titles or property.</note></term> contracted by German princes. The children who owe their lives to these marriages cannot succeed their father and do not enter into his family.

The Indo-European conception of marriage is entirely different from the Christian conception, which imposes equal fidelity on both parties, and it also stands in opposition to the Semitic conception, which shows us in Constantinople the son of an enslaved woman rising, by right of his father, to the highest dignity in the Muslim world.

The distinction made by the Greco-Roman world between the free woman and the enslaved woman gives the former a sense of self-respect that the Semitic woman did not know in antiquity. On this subject, one can compare two equally legendary tales, one Roman, the other Jewish.

wife of Sinatus <note>original: "Sinatos"</note>, tetrarch <term>tetrarch: a ruler of one of the four administrative districts of a province</term> of Galatia—that is to say, one of the four kings who governed each of the three small nations among which the Gauls of Asia Minor were divided. to speak of his love, his riches, and his power, which gave him superiority over Sinatus; and he had the audacity to confess to Camma that he was the murderer of her so-deeply-mourned husband. "But, if I killed him," he added, "it was for love of you; my only wickedness is to have loved you too much."

Camma repelled him; he returned to the charge several times, each time in vain. But the refusals offered to him did not take the harsh form one might have expected. Camma, who at first had seemed to think only of avenging her husband, appeared to soften; for her parents and friends, seeking to please the all-powerful Sinorix, used every means of persuasion and even almost of constraint to decide her to consent to this union. She finally even told them that she was yielding, and she made an appointment with Sinorix in the temple to celebrate their marriage solemnly in the presence of the goddess.

Sinorix arrived at the appointed hour; all the nobility of Galatia <note>An ancient region in central Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey) settled by Celtic tribes.</note>, both men and women, accompanied him. Camma went toward him with a gracious air, offered him her right hand, and led him to the altar of the goddess. Then, performing the traditional rite, she seized a golden cup full of mead <term>mead: an alcoholic drink made from fermented honey and water, referred to here as "hydromel"</term>: after having poured a few drops on the ground in honor of the goddess, she drank part of it and invited Sinorix to drink the rest. He, having reached the height of his desires, finished the cup in total delight.

While he drank, Camma watched him do it.

Before the guests’ arrival, she had mixed a deadly poison into the mead <note>original: "hydromel"</note> in the cup. When Sinorix had finished drinking, she let out a great cry in which the witnesses could distinguish the name of her late husband; then she prostrated herself at the foot of the altar.

> “I call the venerable goddess to witness,” she said,
> “that if I was able to survive you, dear Sinatos, it was
> thanks to the hope I had of seeing this beautiful
> day arrive. My only joy in life was thinking that
> I would avenge you. Now that I have done so, I
> go down to join you in the abode of the dead.
> As for you, Sinorix, the most wicked of all men,
> instead of a wedding feast, let your friends and
> servants prepare a tomb for you.”

Hearing these words, Sinorix already felt the poison acting and inflicting the first convulsions throughout his body. He leapt into his chariot, believing that the movement and the jolts would relieve him. But he could not bear them; he had himself placed in a litter <note>A portable, couch-like vehicle carried by servants, often used by the wealthy or the sick in antiquity.</note> and ceased to live that very evening. The news of his death reached the temple of Artemis toward the end of the night. Camma was in her death throes. She was told that the murderer of her husband no longer existed. She still had the strength to express her joy, then, with satisfaction etched upon her features, she expired. In the absence of her husband’s relatives, who did not know the name of the murderer, it was she who had fulfilled the duty of vengeance.

<page-num>222</page-num>

<header>PART ONE. CHAPTER V. § 25.</header>

Plutarch was captivated by the beauty of this charming story <note>The author uses the word "roman" (romance/novel) here to suggest that the story of Camma has a literary or legendary quality.</note>. He included it twice in his *Moral Works* <note>original: "œuvres morales," commonly known by the Latin title *Moralia*</note>, once in his treatise *On the Bravery of Women* (1), and again in his short book *On Love*; this latter work presents Camma as the model of a well-born widow who would prefer, says Plutarch, the embraces of a bear and the coils of a serpent to the marriage bed of a new husband (2). Polyaenus also included the story of Camma in the collection of anecdotes he titled *Stratagems* (3). This dramatic narrative displays all the hallmarks of a legendary composition, and we do not know if it has any foundation whatsoever in historical reality. We do not even know if Camma, Sinatos, and Sinorix ever existed. But the certainly Celtic names of Sinorix and Sinatos show us that this legendary tale is Celtic in origin.

Here is another story, less fantastic, in which fable seems to play no part; it is the one that made the name of Chiomara famous. Polybius <note>A famous Greek historian of the Hellenistic period, known for his objective approach to history.</note> recounted that he had met this woman in Sardis, and that he had spoken with her. Here, then, even the most skeptical are forced to believe; but what is reported of Chiomara is far less miraculous than the heroism of Camma.

# FIDELITY OF THE WOMEN OF GALATIA.

Chiomara, a Gaul of Asia <note>The "Gauls of Asia" refers to the Galatians, Celtic tribes who migrated to and settled in central Anatolia (modern Turkey) in the 3rd century BCE.</note> like Camma, was the wife of Ortiagon, king of the *Tolistobogii* <note>The Tolistobogii were one of the three principal tribes of the Galatians.</note>. She was taken prisoner in a war against the Romans in the year 189 BCE; along with the other captives whose lives had been spared, she was led into the Roman camp near Ancyra <note>Modern-day Ankara, Turkey.</note>, and she remained there for some time under the guard of soldiers commanded by a centurion. This military leader, whom *Livy* <note>original: "Tite-Live"; Titus Livius was a famous Roman historian who recorded these events in his history of Rome.</note> presents as a model of avarice and bad morals, first sought to seduce Chiomara, and having failed to do so, he raped her. Next, through a second breach of his duties as a soldier, he wished to sell her back to her husband. Ortiagon accepted the bargain, and one night, the centurion, accompanied by Chiomara, went secretly to an agreed-upon place to receive from Ortiagon’s messengers the promised sum, and to hand over to them the prisoner whom the leader of the Roman army had entrusted to his care. When he arrived at the destination, he found Ortiagon’s messengers with an Attic talent of gold <note>An Attic talent was a massive unit of weight/currency; a talent of gold would have been an extraordinary ransom.</note>, which was the price settled in advance, and he began to weigh it with a scale to ensure he was not being cheated. While he was thus occupied, Chiomara gave an order in her own language to the Gauls who had come for her. These men, obeying her, drew their swords from their scabbards, and one of them cut off the centurion’s head. Chiomara picked up this bloody head, wrapped it in a fold of her robe and, arriving before her husband, let it roll at his feet. “Oh, my wife,” cried Ortia-

<sig>15</sig>

Irish epic literature understands the right of the king <note>A reference to the *jus primae noctis*, or the legendary right of a king to sleep with a bride on her wedding night.</note> Conchobar <note>Conchobar mac Nessa, the legendary King of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology.</note> and the duty of hospitality <note>In some ancient Irish traditions, hospitality could include providing a female companion to a guest, a custom the author identifies as contrary to later standards of modesty.</note> in a way that is contrary to the most elementary laws of modesty (1); but the Irishwoman Derdriu <note>Better known as Deirdre of the Sorrows, a tragic heroine who fled her betrothal to King Conchobar to be with her lover Naoise.</note>, like the Galatian Chiomara, does not accept that a woman should have two living husbands at the same time (2). Derdriu and the wife of the King of Leinster, Mesgégra, would rather die than marry the murderer of their husband (3), and are thus peers of the Galatian Camma <note>Camma was a priestess of Artemis who poisoned herself and her husband's murderer to avoid a forced marriage.</note>. Blathnat, wife of Cú Roí <note>original: "Cûroï"</note>, King of Munster, betrays her husband to the hero Cúchulainn who kills him, then gives herself to Cúchulainn, but she pays for her crime with her life, heroically avenged by the poet Fercertné who, dragging her with him into a precipice, causes her a fatal fall; and the great warrior of Ireland, an accomplice of Blathnat, also atones for the murder of Cú Roí with his death. It is Lugaid, son of Cú Roí, who, after having killed Cúchulainn’s charioteer, gives the hero himself the mortal blow, and finally cuts off his head (4). Thus, Irish epic literature, like other literatures, recognizes marital fidelity and feminine modesty.

It would therefore be an injustice to judge the Celts of the British Isles by ancient and medieval texts, according to which it would seem that, as a general rule, women in these islands were shared by several men (1). ->**LEGITIMATE WIFE AND CONCUBINE IN IRELAND.**<-

Ideals constitute the greatness of peoples, and the Celts held an ideal of the married woman equivalent to those offered by Greece and Rome in antiquity.

This ideal is lacking among the Semitic peoples, as is the Roman vestal virgin <note>A priestess of the goddess Vesta in Rome, dedicated to maintaining the sacred fire and sworn to celibacy.</note>; compare the Galatian cult of the virgin Artemis, pp. 219, 221.

The technical term in Irish law to designate the wife proper is *cétmunter* <term>cétmunter: literally "first of the household," referring to the primary, legal wife</term>. She is contrasted with the concubine, literally a “woman of contract,” *ben urnadma* (1). She must possess the same wealth and the same social rank as her husband; she and her children can annul disadvantageous contracts made by her husband without her consent. When she has not given her husband a legitimate reason for divorce and he purchases another wife, the purchase price belongs to the first wife, to the detriment of the second wife and her parents. The second wife owes the "honor-price" <note>In early Irish law, the "honor-price" was a specific monetary value assigned to an individual based on their social status; any offense against them required payment of this amount.</note> to the first, and the first marriage is dissolved; a husband who reconciles with his first wife owes her a new purchase price (2).

The legend of Saint Brigit provides us with a characteristic example of the rights of the legitimate wife, the *cétmunter*, in Ireland. The druid Dubthach, who had a legitimate wife, purchased an enslaved woman, made her his concubine, and she became pregnant; the

The legitimate wife, jealous of the concubine, threatened Dubthach with divorce; now, in the event of a divorce, she was entitled to take with her the dower <note>Property or money settled on a woman by her husband at the time of marriage.</note> that her husband had given her. Thus, after a long resistance, the druid eventually sold his concubine to another master (1). Thus, the Irish married woman has the right to divorce in cases of the husband's infidelity.

Under Irish civil law, divorce by mutual consent is legal (2), despite what is stated in Irish canon law <note>The internal religious laws governing the Christian church.</note> which, at first, allowed a husband to divorce on the grounds of a wife's adultery (3), and which later prohibited divorce even in cases of adultery. This latter rule is the one that found its way into the "Irish Collection of Canons," where it is placed under the patronage of Saint Patrick—even though, according to another document, Saint Patrick held to the former system. The Collection of Canons expresses it thus:
