Through purchase, <term>coibche</term> <note>The Irish term for the marriage-gift or bride-price.</note> (the Latin <term>coemptio</term> <note>original Latin: "coemptio" — A Roman legal process where a woman was symbolically purchased to enter her husband's family and legal power.</note>), the married woman in Ireland did not enter her husband’s family as she would have in Rome. When her husband was killed, she had no right to the compensation <note>original: "composition" — the legal fine or "blood money" paid to a family to settle a murder.</note> for a murder that she could not have avenged (2). If she remarried, it was with her birth family, and not with her late husband's family, that she shared the price of her sale to her second husband (3). From this resulted an independence for the married woman, the oldest example of which is given to us by *Medb*, Queen of *Connaught*, one of the most important characters in the primary work of Irish epic literature, which tells us how this queen seized the bull of *Cûailngé* <note>This refers to the *Táin Bó Cúailnge* or "The Cattle Raid of Cooley," the central epic of the Ulster Cycle.</note>.

# CELTIC DOWER.

Roman law does not recognize the <term>dower</term> <note>Property settled on a bride by her husband; the reverse of a dowry</note>: in Roman law, the husband receives a dowry and gives none in return. An eleventh-century Irish scholar, who had studied Roman law, imagined that the dower, or *tinnscra*, was a custom unknown to the entire world except for Ireland. When the sons of Milé <note>The Milesians, the mythical ancestors of the Irish people</note>—that is, the ancestors of the Irish—arrived in Ireland, they found, it is said, a colony of Jewish women who had preceded them. They proposed marriage to these women, who replied that they would not consent without receiving a *tinnscra*.

> "That is why," adds the Irish scholar, "men buy
> and will always buy their wives in Ireland,
> while everywhere else it is the women
> who buy the men (1)."

But the dower existed outside of Ireland; we have seen above that the Bretons brought the custom from their great island <note>Great Britain</note> to the French continent. There, they referred to it in the ninth century by the name *enep-uuert* <note>Literal translation from Old Breton: "face-price"</note>, in the eleventh century as *enep-guerth*, and in the eighteenth century as *enebarz* (2). We also find the—

<page-num>239</page-num>
<header># DOWER AND DOWRY AMONG THE GERMANS #</header>

This absolute assertion required a certain degree of qualification. One would be wrong to conclude that among the Germanic peoples the use of the <term>dowry</term> <note>property brought by the wife to the marriage</note>, given by the wife's parents and brought by her, was absolutely unknown.

Undoubtedly, among the Germans, the <term>dower</term> <note>property or a gift provided by the husband to the bride</note> was of great importance; it could include a number of horses, horned cattle, even slaves (1), and, once the concept of landed property was established, it could consist of real estate. In the sixth century of our era, Chilperic, the Frankish king of Soissons, upon marrying Galswintha—daughter of Athanagild, the Visigothic king of Spain—gave her as a dower, or *morganegiba* <note>The "morning-gift" given by a husband to his wife the morning after the wedding</note>, five cities: namely, those of Bordeaux, Limoges, Cahors, Béarn, and Bigorre (2).

On the contrary, the dowry—the Roman *dos*—among the Germans was of minimal value. According to Tacitus, it consisted of "some arms offered by the woman, that is to say by her father, to the husband (3)"; this represents the primitive Germanic law, although among the Germans

### § 26. — *The killing of children by the father. Paternal power in Celtic law.*

There are no reservations to be made regarding the right of life and death that Caesar's *Commentaries* attribute to the Gallic father over his children (1). We find this same right in Ireland, where Tadg—a druid serving the high kings <note>The "High King" or *Ard Rí* was a historical title for the supreme ruler of Ireland.</note> Cathair and Cond in the second century of our era—intends to burn his daughter. Her crime was allowing herself to be abducted by a lover; Tadg spares her only because she is protected by the king, for whom her husband had served as the primary warrior (2).

In Wales, one of the miraculous stories recorded in the *Book of Llandaff* <note>original: *Livre de Llan Dav*; a 12th-century manuscript containing the history and hagiography of the diocese of Llandaff.</note> tells of a king who sentences his pregnant daughter to death. The unfortunate woman is first enclosed in a leather bag and thrown into a river, but the river carries her safely to the bank. The father then has her placed on a pyre which is set ablaze, where she miraculously gives birth without being harmed by the flames (3).

One can compare to this Christian narrative the pagan legend of the Irish high king Cairbré "Cat-Head," who is said to have lived in the first century of our era. He ordered his three deformed sons to be successively cast into the sea immediately after their birth. The last of them, miraculously saved, was named Morand (2) and later became famous as a jurist <note>term: *jurisconsulte* — a legal expert or specialist in the interpretation and application of laws.</note>; he is often called Morand mac Main, after his adoptive father, the blacksmith Maen, who eventually returned him to the king, his biological father (3).

> "...the following effects: ... Judgment, proof, and testimony belong to the master over the pupil, as to the father over the son, as to the church over the monk (1)."

It is from this right of paternal jurisdiction that the right of life and death <note>original Latin: *jus vitae necisque*</note> emanates; it is absolute, and, if the father kills his child, no one can demand a compensation <note>term: *composition* — a financial payment made to settle a legal dispute or crime, common in early Germanic and Celtic law to prevent blood feuds.</note> for this murder.

Primitive Indo-European custom appears to have everywhere recognized the father's right of life and death over his minor children (2); however, as a general rule, the marriage of children, which usually took place at puberty, brought an end to paternal power <note>term: *puissance paternelle* or *patria potestas* — the legal authority held by a male head of a household over his descendants.</note> (3). In Roman law and in Celtic law, paternal power lasted as long as the father's life. This alignment between the two legal systems was noted by the Roman legal expert Gaius, who lived in the second century of our era. The Celts had carried as far as Asia Minor the national law which regulated the power of the father over—

(1) "This is the relationship of foster-care between the pupil and the teacher... judgment and proof and testimony belong to the teacher of instruction over the pupil, and to the father over his son, and to the church over its monk" <note>original Old Irish: *Is i lanamnacht athfhethair itir in dalta ocus int-aite forcetail... breithemnus ocus imdenam ocus fiadnaise don oite forcetail for in dalta, ocus don athair for a mac, ocus don eclais for a manach*</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 348, lines 20, 21, 28-30).

->### END OF PATERNAL AUTHORITY.<-

...the son in a manner identical to Roman law (1).

For the Romans, this agreement between the two legal systems was all the more striking because Greek law, like Germanic law, set the end of paternal authority at the son's majority. This was fixed at seventeen or eighteen years by the law of Athens (2), and at fourteen years by Germanic custom. It is the age for military service—which is nearly identical to the age of puberty—that determines the date of emancipation for male children among the Greeks and Germans. The same custom reached the Welsh during the Middle Ages:

> "When the son has reached fourteen years of age," says the *Venedotian Code*, "the father presents him to the lord, <term>argluyd</term> <note>A Middle Welsh term for a lord or patron to whom a young man owed service.</note>...; then the son can <term>stand in justice</term> <note>Original: *ester en justice*—to have the legal standing to act as a party in a lawsuit.</note> in any lawsuit whatsoever; he can be a property owner; his father no longer has the right of correction over him (3)."

In ancient India, adoption was celebrated with the approval of the king, in the presence of the king and the relatives of the adopter (1). Adoption was originally, among all Indo-Europeans, a solemn act to which the relatives of the adopter could object, as seen in Ireland (2).

There was no exception to this rule, even in Irish law, in cases where the adopted person was the son of the adopter’s sister; he was then called a *<term>gor-mac</term>* <note>literally "pious son" or "dutiful son"; here specifically a nephew adopted to perform duties for his maternal uncle</note> (3), a compound word whose meaning is different from *<term>mac gor</term>* <note>literally "dutiful son"; a biological son who supports his parents</note> (p. 247). The *<term>gor-mac</term>* was entitled to the usufruct of the maternal inheritance, plus—in the event of the family's extinction—to a slave woman, a *<term>cumal senorba</term>* <note>literally "a slave woman of the old inheritance"; a standard unit of value in Irish law tied to land rights</note> (4), when the relatives had not given their consent to his adoption; with their consent, he could receive seven slave women <note>equivalent to seven *cumals*</note> like any "son of protection," or *<term>mac foesma</term>* <note>an adopted son who receives protection and legal standing in exchange for providing care to an elderly or infirm man</note> (5).

Thus, in Celtic law, there are three formally stated cases where one can kill a person without being liable to pay a <term>composition</term> <note>a legal fine or "blood money" paid to a victim's family to prevent a feud; known as "wergild" in Germanic traditions</note>: the killer of a thief, the victor in a regular duel, and the father who kills his child owe no composition.

Anyone can kill him without running the risk of paying a composition for murder.

The husband has the right of life and death over the slave who serves as his concubine; this slave is his property, she is not a person. But as for the legitimate wife—in Irish <term>cétmuinter</term> <note>literally "first of the household"; the primary wife who held higher legal status than concubines</note>, the equivalent of the Roman <term>materfamilias</term> <note>original Latin: "mother of the family"; the female head of a household</note>—if the husband kills her, the wife's family will take vengeance for this crime (2).

SECOND PART. CHAP. I. § 1.

force to the court. In Ireland, it is by the seizure not of a person, but of a thing, that the procedure begins.

The *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Custom," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon laws.</note> presents us with two types of seizures: movable seizure and immovable seizure. Movable seizure is carried out in two ways: 1st, with delays, or, to use the language of the *Senchus Mór*, "after length;" 2nd, without delay and immediately.

The language of Irish law generally expresses the idea of seizure through the word <term>tobach</term> <note>Old Irish for "levying" or "distraint."</note>, which designates both movable and immovable seizure. Movable seizure is properly called <term>ath-gabail</term>, literally "re-taking." Movable seizure, like the duel and the combat of many, takes place without the prior authorization of a judge. This is the <term>pignoris capio</term> <note>Latin: "taking of a pledge." A procedure in early Roman law where a creditor could seize a debtor's property without a prior court ruling.</note> that the Roman law of the historical period authorized only by exception (1). Traces of it are also found in the oldest Germanic laws. However, these traces consist mainly of texts that restrict or abolish the primitive right, and according to which authorization previously given by the judge is an indispensable condition of validity for any seizure (2). ### MOVABLE SEIZURE BY WOMEN. ###

The first four [types of seizure], those of one night, three nights, five nights, and ten nights, are for the use of men; however, the treatise on movable seizure <note>In legal history, "movable seizure" or "distress" refers to the legal right to take a debtor's property to compel them to pay a debt or fulfill an obligation.</note>, despite this addition, retains its original title in the manuscripts of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The *Senchus Mór* (Great Custom) is the primary collection of ancient Irish "Brehon" laws, traditionally said to have been compiled in the 5th century.</note>: "**Of the four species of movable seizure (1).**" This title excludes the fifth species of movable seizure—that is, the two-night seizure, or feminine seizure; and, consequently, the passages concerning it are more recent than the title itself.

There are two such passages. The first contains a mistake that testifies to the editor's carelessness; this passage is found at the beginning of the treatise on movable seizure, where the author provides a list of the various kinds of seizures he is about to discuss. These are, he says first, the seizures involving a delay of one night, three nights, five nights, and ten nights. Curiously, the movable seizure involving a delay of two nights—the feminine seizure—is not found in the place where one would naturally expect to find it (after the one-night seizure and before the three-night one); instead, it is mentioned after the ten-night seizure. It is, therefore, an addition to an older list.

If one could doubt this, the following would prove it: immediately afterward, the author has placed the announcement of the twelve-night seizure practiced by the—

# SEIZURE WITH DELAYS.

When movable seizure <term>movable seizure: also known as distraint, the legal practice of seizing property (usually livestock) to satisfy a debt or obligation</term> is practiced with delays—or in other words, "with duration"—one can distinguish eight successive steps:

1. Notice to pay, *aurfocre*;
2. The delay separating the notice and the seizure, *apad* (2);
3. Seizure, *athgabail*;
4. The delay during which the seized object remains in the hands of the debtor, *anad*;
5. Removal (in Irish, *toxal*) of the seized object, which is placed in a pound, *forus*;
6. Notification given to the person whose property was seized to inform them where the impounded object has been taken; this notification is called *fasc*;
7. The delay during which the seized object remains in the pound; the name for this delay is *dithim*;
8. The date from which ownership of the impounded object is gradually transferred from the defendant to the plaintiff; this date is called *lobad*, which means "destruction" <note>original: *lobad*; this term signifies the "decaying" or "extinguishing" of the original owner's rights until the property is fully forfeited</note>.

The delays can be extended by a dilatory exception <term>dilatory exception: a legal plea intended to delay or postpone a trial or action, usually due to an external obstacle</term>, *turbaid*, which occurs when an obsta—

# SEIZURE WITH A FIVE-NIGHT DELAY.

night. But, in the Irish procedure we are discussing here, the interval between the formal demand and the seizure lasts five nights (1); this interval is what is called <term>apad: the notice period between the initial demand and the actual seizure of property</term>.

The seizure made at the expiration of the *apad* is followed by a second delay, <term>anad: a stay of execution</term>, of a duration equal to the first: five more nights during which the seized objects remain at the defendant's home (2). During this time, the defendant is the legal custodian of the property, whereas in French law, he is only an optional custodian and can be rejected by the seizing party (*Code of Civil Procedure*, art. 598).

At the expiration of this second delay, the creditor, through an act called <term>toxal: the physical removal of the property</term>, carries away the seized objects; he places these objects in a pound and gives the defendant a new formal notice, <term>fasc: a notice of removal</term>, which serves as the starting point for a third delay, <term>dithim: the period during which the property is held in the pound before forfeiture</term>. This third period is sometimes double the length of each of the first two (3), but is usually the same length as each of them—another five nights (4).

### PART TWO. CHAPTER I. SECTION 1.

It is at the expiration of this third and final delay that the debtor's loss of rights over the seized objects begins; the creditor acquires a certain quantity of these objects on the first night, a second quantity on the second night, and so on until they become the owner of everything: this acquisition is called <term>lobad: a term meaning "decay" or "destruction"</term>; what is "destroyed" is the defendant's legal right to the property. This legal phenomenon takes the place of the sale prescribed by French law. The oldest historical Irish law, as we find it in the <term>Senchus Mór: the "Great Custom," one of the primary collections of ancient Irish law</term>, does not recognize "sale" in the strict sense, since its <term>currency of account: a unit used to measure value rather than a physical coin</term> consists only of movable objects: female slaves, horned cattle, and sacks of barley. Minted silver appears for the first time in the <gloss>scholarly explanations</gloss> of the *Senchus Mór*, and in treaties of a more recent date than the *Senchus Mór*, such as the <term>Book of Aicill: an ancient Irish legal text attributed to King Cormac mac Airt</term> (1).

In the Irish procedure in question, the total of the delays that elapse between the first notification and the moment when the person whose property was seized begins to be stripped of their rights over the movable objects removed by the creditor, amounts to fifteen nights; it is triple the number of nights that gave its name to this procedure: the "five-night seizure." ->IMMEDIATE SEIZURE. FIVE-NIGHT RESPITE.<-

When all the delays are thus observed, the procedure for the seizure of movable property takes the name of "seizure after delay," <term>athgabail iar fut: literally "seizure according to length"</term> (1); if the seizure is immediate, <term>athgabail tul: "immediate seizure" or "front-on seizure"</term>, the first two delays do not exist; there is no <term>apad: the notice period between the formal demand and the actual seizure</term>, that is to say, no interval between the command and the seizure; likewise, there is no <term>anad: the waiting period where the seized property remains with the debtor</term>, meaning that the seized object is immediately removed and put into the pound; the only delay is that which was called <term>dithim: the interval during which the object remains in the pound but still belongs to the debtor</term>, that is to say, the interval during which the object in the pound remains the property of the person whose goods were seized. The duration of this kind of respite is equal to the number of nights that gives the seizure its name (2).

Thus, when the five-night seizure is immediate, only five nights elapse between the start of operations and the moment when the seized objects begin to become the property of the person performing the seizure; whereas if the seizure had been what was called *athgabail iar fut*, "seizure after delay,"

If one risked their fortune during the irregularly executed preliminary operations, they could compromise it even more when it came to the actual act of the seizure itself.

The *Senchus Mór* <note>Literally "The Great Tradition," this is one of the most important collections of ancient Irish "Brehon" laws</note> advises the distrainer <note>the person seizing property to satisfy a debt</note> to be accompanied by a lawyer, who is both sufficiently educated to ensure the regular fulfillment of formalities, and competent enough in the art of speaking to explain before the judges how everything took place. He who seizes property irregularly owes the seized party five <term>horned beasts: cattle, which served as the standard unit of value and currency in early Ireland</term> as indemnity (2); but the Irish legal experts allow that the presence of one of their colleagues, called and naturally paid by the distrainer, acts as an obstacle to the collection of this kind of fine when the irregularity results from an error made by the legal expert (3). ### PART TWO. CHAPTER I. § 1.

— that "wolves do not eat each other." <note>This refers to the French proverb *les loups ne se mangent pas entre eux*, suggesting that legal experts protected one another from fines incurred by procedural errors.</note>

In Irish law, seizure <term>distraint: the legal act of taking property to enforce a debt</term> is considered a kind of contract between the two parties; its effect is to allow the claimant to acquire a right similar to a <term>pledge: a piece of property held as security for a debt</term> over the seized movable goods. One cannot perform a seizure if they lack the capacity to enter a contract: this implies that the individual is neither under <term>guardianship: the legal control of one's affairs by another</term> nor subject to paternal authority; furthermore, they must be solvent—that is, among the class of men who can serve as a <term>surety: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or behavior</term> (1). Finally, to be legally entitled to seize a debtor’s property, one must possess movable assets equal in value to those being seized (2). A seizure carried out by a slave, a domestic servant, or a person lacking mental capacity would be null and void by right; conversely, any seizure practiced against such individuals would be illegal (3).

One might perhaps, without too much boldness, venture here an expression foreign to Irish law and say that the power to seize was granted

This provision leaves a considerable number of Ireland's inhabitants in a position where it is impossible to obtain justice without the intervention of a third party more powerful than themselves. <note>This "third party" refers to a patron or lord who would act on behalf of a person lacking full legal standing.</note>

However, a rule that one might call democratic seems to provide a kind of benevolent corrective to this exclusion of the poor and the weak. The leaders of the public assembly—kings, heirs apparent to kings, and royal advisors—are forbidden from personally carrying out a seizure; the impossibility of standing up to them would make their power tyrannical (2). When they wish to have a debtor’s movable property seized, they are represented in this operation by a subordinate agent: a <term>substituted tenant: known in Irish as an *aithech fortha*</term>, and it is against this agent that those subject to their jurisdiction bring legal action when, conversely, the leaders are the ones who owe a debt (3).

We have little to say here regarding the <term>anad</term>—that is, the period of delay during which, in a seizure "after a length of time," the seized objects remained in the hands of the defendant. We have already discussed this on page 265. However, we must emphasize one point: this delay was the period during which a solvent debtor could provide <term>pledges: security or collateral</term> to the creditor to obtain the <term>release: the legal lifting or discharge</term> of the seizure. In contrast, the period called <term>dithim: the period of the pound</term> was the timeframe in which the solvent debtor was required to pay the debt in full. The pledges given by the defendant during the <term>anad</term> served as a guarantee that they would either pay or, if they contested the debt, appear before an arbitrator at the expiration of a delay of forty nights (1).

After the <term>anad</term> came the <term>toxal: the physical removal</term> (2) of the seized objects. To remove the seized objects, three people were required, and the objects had to be received into the <term>pound: a secured enclosure for seized livestock</term> by four people (3). The witness, the <term>naidm</term> (or <term>snaidm</term>) and the surety cannot be chosen from among persons of servile condition—that is to say, from among those who have received from a chief, along with livestock, their honor-price. However, the plaintiff ran a great risk if he placed the seized objects in a pound at his own home if they were of a value higher than his own <term>honor-price: the legal value assigned to a person's status</term>. When their value exceeded this price, he had to choose as a pound the residence of a personage whose honor was valued higher than his own. The common man took as a pound the enclosure, <term>faithche: the open field or green surrounding a residence</term>, of one of the members of the aristocracy. Seven ranks were distinguished within the aristocracy; there were therefore seven categories of enclosures which could serve to impound the objects seized by the members of the common people (2). It was even sometimes prudent to lodge the seized objects in fortresses to spend the night there when there was reason to fear that they might be carried off by brigands, for the person performing the seizure was responsible for their preservation until the moment when the <term>lobad: the period of legal forfeiture</term> made him the owner (3).

### MEANING OF THE NOTIFICATION.

The plaintiff owed the defendant a new notice; there was an obligation for the distrainor to inform the distrainee of the location to which the seized objects had been transported. The act of giving this information was called <term>fasc: a formal legal notification or notice</term>. The distrainor brought this notification to the distrainee himself; but he was not to be alone; custom required that he be accompanied by two witnesses (1), and one of the two witnesses was a law-agent (2).

The notification called *fasc* had to inform the distrainee of three things (3): it was necessary for the distrainor, speaking in a loud voice (4), to say: 1st, what debt was the cause of the seizure; 2nd, where the seized objects

It is strange that the translator did not see this when he translated the gloss: <note>original: "Raither no aisnethur dias as test"</note> "It is said or stated that two persons are to bear witness" (*Ibid.*, p. 302, l. 12-13; p. 303, l. 16; vol. The omission of even one of these three statements gave the <term>distrainee: the person whose property was seized</term> the right to demand five horned cattle as an indemnity (1). When the seized objects belonged to a person other than the one at whose residence the seizure had taken place, two formal notifications or *fasc* were required: one at the residence where the seizure was carried out, and the other at the residence of the actual owner of the impounded objects (2).

From this notification began the final delay of the seizure, the *dithim*. This was, it was said, the payment period and, for the debtor, a kind of grace period (3). However, this delay was burdensome in that, since the seized objects were usually livestock, their food and the costs incurred by the care given to them were the responsibility of the defendant (4).

<header>PART TWO. CHAP. I. § 2.</header>

immovable property could be acquired by means of seizure, <term>tellach: a formal legal entry onto land to claim possession</term>. It was necessary for the act called *tellach*—that is, the act of occupation performed in the legal form—to be repeated three times; upon the third time, the person performing the seizure was invested with a right called *tuinidhe*, or more correctly *tuinnige* (1), which can be translated as "possession." By virtue of this right, he had, as we shall see, the authority to exercise most of the prerogatives of a definitive owner.

The act called *tellach* (2) presents itself in the form—

---

(1) From the second meaning of <note>original: *tonn, tond*</note> "surface," particularly "surface of the earth," <note>original: *tond talman*</note> (Windisch, *Irish Texts*, I, p. 838, col. 1), is derived <note>original: *tuinnim*</note> "I stay" or "I dwell," literally "I am on the surface [of the earth]" (*ibid.*, p. 856, col. 1). From this comes <note>original: *tuinneach*</note> "one who stays," and finally <note>original: *tuinnigim*</note> "I stay," "I dwell," and <note>original: *tuinnige*</note> "the act of staying or dwelling somewhere," hence "possession." <term>Selb: a term for absolute ownership</term> (in Welsh <note>original: *helw*</note>, *Celtic Grammar*, 2nd ed., p. 130, line 5) designates a right more firmly established than *tuinnige*. *Selb* seems to mean full ownership; Tirechan <note>a 7th-century Irish bishop</note> used it with the sense of "appurtenances" (*Celtic Grammar*, 2nd ed., 243, line 6). The derivative *selbad* designates the right of a master over a slave in a passage from the Würzburg manuscript (*Celtic Grammar*, 2nd ed., 861, line 21). Finally, the following text seems decisive: <note>original: *inti dobeir na techta seilb, as e doron co fiachaib taige*</note> "He who gives what he does not own makes himself, by this act, a debtor for the damages due for theft" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. (2) *Tellach* is properly the act of taking something. Other examples of the use of the suffix *-ach* to form abstract nouns are collected *ibid.*, p. 810. On the etymology of the verb *tellim*, see Whitley Stokes, *Proto-Celtic Vocabulary*, p. 130.

the occupation of immovable property by the seizing party was accomplished from atop a war chariot.

The claimant <term>saisissant: the person initiating the legal takeover of property</term>, therefore, holds two horses in his hand (1). These two horses are under a yoke and draw a chariot. Under the eyes of a witness, a man who accompanies him, the claimant crosses the ditch that encloses the property with his horses (2), then he stops without unharnessing them. Then, raising his voice, he demands that his rights be granted according to the law, if there is justice to be had. If this summons obtains no response, or if the response is not satisfactory, he departs, only to return soon (3).

It will be recalled that the seizure of movables <term>saisie mobilière: the legal taking of personal property to settle a debt</term>, when it is done in full form—that is to say, "after a delay" <note>original: *iar fut*</note>—involves: 1st, three periods of delay which may be of five nights each; 2nd, three acts requiring verbal interactions between the seizing party and the person whose property is being seized. The second of these acts is the seizure itself <note>original: *athgabail*</note>, which ends the first delay and serves as the starting point for the second delay. <header># MALE SEIZURE OF IMMOVABLE PROPERTY #</header>

at the closing of the second delay and at the beginning of the third delay (p. 263).

The <term>saisie immobilière: the legal process of taking possession of land or buildings</term> involves, like the seizure of personal property, three distinct periods of delay. The only difference lies in the duration of each delay: they are always ten nights long instead of the five nights specified in the example we provided on pages 264–268; this results in a total of thirty nights instead of fifteen. The number of operations required of the person seizing the property is also three.

The first occupation, known as <term>cét tellach: the "first entry" or initial ritualized arrival upon the land</term> (1), and the demand that accompanies it—"Grant me my rights according to the law, if there is justice to be had"—correspond to the formal command to pay, or <term>urfocre: a legal summons or notice given to a debtor</term>. Two other occupations are required: the one called the "middle" occupation, or <term>tellach medonach: the second entry onto the property</term> (2), which takes place in the middle of the second ten-night delay; and finally, the occupation known as the "entry of two tens" (meaning two sets of ten nights), which consists of the middle ten nights and the final ten nights, known as <term>tellach da dechmad: the third and final entry</term>. This final occupation occurs thirty nights after the first, and fifteen nights after the second (3). The *middle entry* can be compared to the <term>athgabail: the actual seizure of cattle or goods in personal property law</term>, and the *entry of the two tens* can be compared to the transport of goods to the pound and the <term>fasc: the public notification of a seizure</term>. It is this third occupation, the *entry of the two tens*, which establishes the definitive change of ownership, or <term>tuinnige: the legal vesting of possession or "settling" on the land</term>. Thus, the transport to the pound and the *fasc* open the final delay which—

In the seizure of land <note>French: *saisie immobilière*</note>, the two final acts of occupation are carried out in a manner similar to the first. The only difference lies in the solemnity, which increases with each stage. During the second occupation, the number of horses brought by the seizing party is four instead of two. The seizing party does not stop at the edge of the ditch; he advances beyond it and unyokes his horses (1). This symbolic ceremony requires the presence of two male witnesses instead of the one that sufficed the first time. It must be performed when five nights of the second ten-day period <note>term: *dechmaid* — a ten-day unit of time used in early Irish law to measure legal delays</note> have elapsed (2); it is immediately followed by a second summons to fulfill the legal claim, and the seizing party waits for a response for a period of three nights (3).

The third act of occupation takes place at the end of the final ten-day period (1), that is to say, thirty nights after the start of this procedure: the seizing party brings eight horses and three male witnesses, and advances all the way to the house (2). He issues a final summons, demanding an immediate judgment if the debtor wishes to grant him his rights (3). In the absence of a satisfactory response, he takes possession by bringing a herd of horned cattle onto the seized land (4), and may even go so far as building a shed or a stable there; he may, at his discretion, either shelter his animals there during the winter, or leave them there only for the summer to bring them back to his former home on the 1st of November <note>This date marks Samhain, the traditional beginning of the winter half of the year in the Gaelic calendar</note>; finally, his right can extend to encumbering this land with a rent for the benefit of a chief (5).

The <term>seizure of real property</term> <note>the legal process of taking possession of land to settle a debt or claim</note> by women is much less ancient than the seizure of real property by men. Like the seizure of real property by men, it requires three successive acts of occupation of the property. For the first occupation, the two horses are replaced by two ewes (1) and the male witness by a woman. At the second occupation, instead of four horses, four ewes are required, and the two male witnesses are replaced by two women (2). The third occupation is carried out not with eight horses but with eight ewes. As for witnesses, it would seem that three women—

When a vagabond has taken possession of a piece of land, but without having either a hearth or a home there, he can be expelled in three nights and one has the choice between two procedures. One is that of real property seizure, in which the waiting periods are then reduced from thirty nights to three (3). [The glossators] estimate the **male yearling** <note>original: *colpach firend*</note> at four silver **scruples** (1), or in kind as four sacks of barley (2), and the **female yearling** <note>original: *dartaib boinend*</note> at three sacks of barley (3); this is likely half the price of the **three-year-old heifer** <note>original: *samaisc* (4)</note>, which itself is worth half of a **shelter-set** <note>original: *clithar sét*; high-value livestock such as milch cows</note>. One text states that the **shelter-set** is the "first choice," or the **best of all** <note>original: *forgu na n-uile*</note>; as for the "last choice," or **the worst** <note>original: *digu*</note>, this text does not mention the **fork-sets** <note>original: *sét gabla*; the lowest category of livestock used in legal payments</note>; according to it, the last choice is—

---

(1) <note>original: "*Colpaige firinne .i. ceithri screpall*"</note> "A male yearling, i.e., four scruples" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 260, line 4; cf. p. 134, line 5). The **scruple** is the twenty-fourth part of the Roman ounce; it weighs 1.137 grams (cf. *Revue celtique*, vol. XIII, p. 406); consequently, four scruples weigh 4.55 grams; a weight 0.45 grams less than that of our [former] French one-franc piece, which weighed 5 grams. The weight of the scruple exceeds by 137 milligrams that of our [former] 20-centime piece, which weighed one gram. The scruple would be worth a bit less than 23 centimes in French silver, and the four scruples, 91 centimes. <note>The author is comparing these ancient values to French currency of the late 19th century.</note>
(2) <note>original: "*Agh loighe da miach .i. adh damba logh da screpall*"</note> "A calf of the price of two sacks," that is to say, "a calf whose price is two scruples" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 246, lines 26-27). — <note>original: "*Agh loige ceithri miach .i. ceithri scripaill is fiu*"</note> "A calf of the price of four sacks, that is to say, it is worth four scruples" (*ibid.*, vol. II, p. 250, line 7). On page 254, line 13, the four sacks drop to three scruples <note>original: *tri scripuill*</note>. Two scruples would be worth 45 centimes in French silver; three scruples, 68 centimes; and four scruples, as we have seen, 91 centimes.
(3) <note>original: "*Dartada .i. agh tri miach*"</note> "Of a heifer, that is to say, a calf of three sacks" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 258, line 17).
(4) <note>original: "*Bo con a-fosair... ocht meich bracha*"</note> "A cow with its accompaniment... eight sacks of malt" (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. II, p. 250, lines 22, 26). Its value in silver would be eight scruples, or 1 franc 82 centimes. Different figures are proposed by O'Donovan, *ibid.*, p. 134, note 1. According to Cormac's Glossary, under the entry **shelter-set** <note>original: *Clithar sét*</note>, the average value of the **set** <note>unit of value</note> in the **Great Custom** <note>original: *Senchus Mór*; the primary collection of ancient Irish laws</note> is half an ounce, or 2 francs 73 centimes. <meta>This page continues the discussion of legal proceedings in early Ireland, specifically focusing on the transition from the seizure of property to the arbitration phase. It clarifies the role of the "forty-night" delay mentioned at the end of page 291.</meta>

<header>PART TWO. CHAP. I. § 3.</header>

...appears to have usually been forty nights (pp. 145, 150). We say *before an arbitrator*.

It was seen above, on page 156, that judgment, when it concerns private interests, is purely a matter of arbitration in Celtic law. The two parties only appear before the judge if they have reached a mutual agreement to do so; now, in a seizure involving delays, the period when this agreement should regularly occur is the timeframe known as <term>anad</term> <note>original: *anad*; a legal stay or period of "waiting" during which the debtor could settle the claim or agree to arbitration</note> (1). Then, at the end of a forty-night period, the judgment must take place; however, public force does not compel the parties to submit to the judge's decision. Until the moment the judgment is accepted by both parties, each of them has the right to resort to arms, either in the form of single combat, <term>comrac</term> <note>original: *comrac*; a duel or judicial combat</note> (2), or in the form of a battle between several people, <term>cath</term> <note>original: *cath*; a battle or group conflict</note> (3). In such cases, the solution provided by the sword overrides the sentence that the judge has pronounced.

Normally, the judgment was rendered by the king based on the report of the legal expert or <term>brehon</term> <note>original: *brehon*; an ancient Irish jurist and judge</note> and in agreement with the assembly of citizens. The kings of Ireland were discussed in some detail earlier, on pages 99-105; a chapter of the *Course on Celtic Literature*, Volume I, pages 296-298, has already been devoted to the duties of those among the <term>fili</term> or <term>file</term> <note>original: *fili* (plural *file*); a class of elite poet-scholars who also served as legal experts</note> who—

The fairs, <term>óenach</term>, are one of the most important institutions of ancient Ireland. Their organization is based on the division of the Celtic year and the periodic celebration of pagan festivals with which the name of the druids is associated by formal texts.

The Celtic year is divided into two equal parts: winter and summer, each subdivided into two also equal sections: winter (taken in the narrow sense) and spring; summer (taken in the narrow sense) and autumn (2).

Winter, <term>gam</term>, or <term>gaim-red</term> in Old Irish, <term>gaem</term>, <term>gayaf</term> in Old Welsh (3), begins on November 1st and ends on January 31st. The 1st of Novem—

### DIVISIONS OF THE CELTIC YEAR.

-man or *samhain* derived from *sam* "summer." The name *Beltene* <note>Modern Beltane</note> still survives in modern Irish, in Scottish Gaelic, and in the Manx dialect. This is what May 1st is still called in these languages. *Beltene* formerly served to designate one of the important festivals of Irish paganism.

Autumn began on August 1st, a day called in Irish *Lug-nasad*, that is to say the games, festival, or anniversary of Lug (1) <note>Lug, or Lugh, is a major deity in Irish mythology, often associated with light and many skills</note>. It ended on October 31st, the day of *samfuin* or *samhain*, the "end of summer," of which autumn was only a subdivision. Autumn is called *fogmur* in Irish, meaning "under winter," and in Old Welsh *kynnhaeaf*, "before winter"—two words which, without being identical, express the same idea.

What allows us to consider this fourfold division of the year not only as Irish, but as Celtic, is that it is found first in the oldest law of Wales. The <term>Venedotian Code</term> <note>A collection of medieval Welsh laws associated with the kingdom of Gwynedd</note> divides the year, from a judicial point of view, into four sections: from November 9th to February 9th, one can plead in court; from February 9th to May 9th the courts are closed; they reopen on May 9th and the public can address them until August 9th, when the course of justice is suspended, only to begin again on November 9th (2).

(1) *Cormac's Glossary* <note>original Latin/Irish: "Glossaire de Cormac"</note>, in *Three Irish Glossaries*, p. 23; *Sanas Chormaic* <note>Cormac's Glossary</note>, p. 99. The name *Lugnasad* is still maintained in Scottish Gaelic and in the Manx dialect.

(2) Book II, chapter 11, § 1-5; *Ancient Laws and Institutes of Wales*, folio edition, p. 68; octavo edition, vol. I, p. 141-142.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the division of the Celtic year into four quarters, comparing the Welsh judicial calendar with the Irish seasonal system and connecting these traditions to ancient Gaulish festivals.</meta>

<page-num>298</page-num>
->**SECOND PART. CHAPTER I. SECTION 4.**<-

The Welsh judicial year is thus divided into four sections, each of three months, corresponding to the sections of the Irish year. There is only one difference between the two systems: the sections of the Irish year each begin on the first of a month of the Roman calendar, while the sections of the Welsh judicial year begin on the 9th of the same months. The Welsh did not establish the concordance of their calendar with the Roman calendar in exactly the same way as the Irish. This discrepancy is of no importance.

Finally, one can hardly help being struck by the resemblance that exists between the Gaulish festival of Augustus at *Lugu-dunum* <note>The Roman name for Lyon, France</note>, that is to say the fort of *Lugu-s* <note>Lugus is a major pan-Celtic deity</note> (on August 1st) and the *Lug-nasad* or festival of Lug, in Ireland (1), on the same date. This idea will be developed further on pages 316-317.

The festivals of the beginning of summer or *Beltene* <note>Modern Beltane, observed around May 1st</note>, of the beginning of autumn or *Lugnasad*, and of the end of summer *sam-fuin* or *samhain* <note>Modern Samhain, the precursor to Halloween, observed around November 1st</note>, provided the Irish with the dates for their most important fairs, known as <term>óenach</term> <note>A traditional gathering or assembly in ancient and medieval Ireland that served social, commercial, and legal functions</note>. These were at once assemblies for pleasure, commerce, and public business, as has already been stated.

# THE FESTIVAL OF BELTENE, MAY 1st.

->Let us provide some information regarding each of these festivals.<-

According to a gloss preserved in the *Glossary of Cormac* <note>An early Irish encyclopedic dictionary attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin, a king-bishop of the 9th century</note>, the pagan Irish supposedly had a god called *Bial* in the nominative case, and *Bil* in the genitive: from this comes the word *Beltene*, which would mean "fire of *Bial*" (1). This *Bial*, who obviously has no connection to the Semitic god Bel <note>A title meaning "Lord" used for various deities in ancient Mesopotamia</note>, seems identical to the *Belenus* of the Gauls, whom the Romans equated with their own god Apollo. Elsewhere, according to the *Glossary*, *Beltene* is composed of *bil*, "happy," and *tene*, "fire," which does not agree with the first etymology; but here is what the *Glossary* adds: "On that day, the druids, while singing great magical songs, lit two fires between which they made the livestock pass, and it was a preservative against <term>epizootics</term> <note>Outbreaks of infectious diseases among animals, similar to epidemics in humans</note> until the following year (2)."

There is an almost identical nature between this ceremony and that of the *palilia* <note>The Parilia, an ancient Roman festival of rural character aimed at cleansing sheep and shepherds, held on April 21st</note> which was celebrated in Rome nine days earlier, on April 21st. At the *palilia*, a single fire was lit and the livestock, and even the men, were made to jump over it: "Through the flames the flock has leaped, the farmers have leaped," <note>original Latin: "Per flammas saluisse pecus, saluisse colonos"</note> says Ovid in the *Fasti* <note>A Latin poem by Ovid explaining the origins of Roman holidays</note> (3). In Rome, they ran the risk of burning the livestock and the men—

### PART TWO. CHAP. I. § 4.

...mes; in Ireland, livestock passing between two fires were out of danger.

There is a solar myth at the origin of this ceremony: we know that Apollo, the Greek god of the Sun, and at the same time of Death and Medicine, was born at Delos at the beginning of May (1). The festival of Beltene thus belongs, by its origins, to the common heritage of the Greco-Italo-Celtic group, which is the most western branch of the great Indo-European family.

This festival of the first of May holds an important place in Irish mythology. The legendary tales that serve as a preamble to the authentic history of Ireland speak of a mysterious Partholan <note>A mythical figure in the Lebor Gabála Érenn (Book of Invasions) who led the second group of settlers to Ireland after the Great Flood</note> who supposedly preceded the current Irish race in Ireland. Partholan, it is said, established his family in Ireland, which consisted of several thousand people (2).

...which, in its entirety and without exception, was carried off in a single week by one of the most terrifying epidemics mentioned in legendary history. This epidemic began on the day of Beltene (1), which is to say, as we have seen, at the time of the birth of the Greek solar god <note>Apollo</note>. Reading the Celtic account, one seems to hear the whistling—as in the *Iliad*—of the arrows that Apollo, from his silver bow, shoots at the Greeks, bringing death into their camp, or those which, fired by the hands of Apollo and Artemis, took the lives of the twelve children of Niobe (2). Partholan appears to be a double of Niobe <note>In Greek myth, Niobe boasted of her children, leading Apollo and Artemis to kill them all; here, the author compares the total destruction of Partholan’s race to this Greek tragedy</note>. It was also on the day of Beltene that there landed in Ireland first the **Tuatha Dé Danann**, or gods of the day (3), and later the **sons of Míl**, who are the ancestors of the island's current population (4). The festival of Beltene thus belongs to the mythological history of the Irish.

### BELTENE FESTIVAL, MAY 1st, AT UISNECH.
<meta>catchword: Under</meta>

Uisnech was originally named *Mide*. According to legend, Midé is a man's name. Midé was the first of the descendants of <term>Milé<gloss>The Milesians, the final legendary race of invaders to settle in Ireland</gloss></term>—that is to say, the first of the Irish—who lit a fire on the hill of Uisnech; this fire burned for seven years, and all the great fires, the sacred fires of Ireland, originated from it (1). It is most likely that *Mide* is a Celtic adjective identical to the Latin *medius*, *media* <note>meaning "middle"</note> (2). This adjective is found again, developed by means of a suffix, in neo-Celtic dialects.

Used as a place name to designate the central point of Ireland where an annual assembly was held, this Celtic adjective expresses the same idea as the Latin adjective in a famous phrase by Caesar:

> "Every year, at a fixed date, the
> druids meet in a consecrated place
> in the territory of the Carnutes,
> *which region is considered the* MIDDLE
> *of all Gaul* <note>original Latin: "quae regio totius Galliae MEDIA habetur"</note>; there, those
> who have disputes gather from
> all sides, and they obey their decrees
> and their judgments (3)."

This is what Caesar reports.

--- Page 332 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the god Lug (Lugh), picking up from the previous page's introduction where the author was beginning to cite Julius Caesar's observations on the Celtic pantheon.</meta>

<page-num>306</page-num>
<header>PART TWO. CHAP. I. § 4.</header>

Roman Mercury <note>original: "Mercure romain"</note>: "He is," says the great captain <note>Julius Caesar, in his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*</note>, "according to the Gauls, the inventor of all the arts." Lug, in Ireland, is surnamed *samh-ildánach*, "he who possesses many crafts at once (1)." When the *Tuatha dé Danann* <note>The "People of the Goddess Danu," the divine race of Irish mythology</note>, that is to say, the gods of the sky and of light, are about to fight the second battle of *Mag-Tuired* <note>Moytura</note> against the *Fomoré*—that is to say, the gods of the sea and of death, the equivalent of Hesiod’s Titans—Lug, arriving from distant travels, comes to offer his assistance to the *Tuatha dé Danann*. He presents himself at the gate of the palace of Tara.

—Who are you? asks the porter.
—I am a carpenter, cries Lug.
—We have a very good carpenter, replied the porter; go away.
—But, Lug resumes, I am an excellent smith.
—We have a very good smith, replies the porter.

Lug offered himself successively as a professional warrior, as a harper, as a poet, historian, and jurist, as a sorcerer, as a physician, as a cupbearer, and as a worker in bronze and precious metals; each time the porter replied that the position was filled. 

"But finally," said Lug, "go and ask the king if he has anyone near him who can practice all these crafts with equal competence." 

The king happily accepted Lug’s assistance; and before the battle, Lug reviewed all the craftsmen or <term>fir dána<gloss>Literally "men of skill" or "men of art," referring to the professional class in ancient Ireland</gloss></term>, as they were called in Irish: the carpen-

The Irish Lug, identical to the *Lugus* of the continental Celts, was therefore the god of all tradespeople, among whom were included men of letters. This is why Caesar calls him the inventor of all the arts. He was, Caesar adds, the guide of travelers: <note>Latin: *viarum atque itinerum ducem*</note> "the leader of ways and journeys"; indeed, according to Irish legend, he was a traveler himself. When he arrives at Tara, the capital of Ireland, he comes from abroad and no one knows him (2); one of his father’s names is *Cian*, which means "distant" or "far off" (3). Lug thus possessed the necessary experience to properly guide travelers. According to Caesar, the Gauls attributed to their Mercury great power over financial gains and markets: <note>Latin: *Hunc ad quæstus pecuniæ mercaturasque habere vim maximam arbitrantur*</note> "They consider him to have the greatest influence over the acquisition of money and over trade" (4). On the day of Lug’s festival, the day called *Lug-nasad* <note>Lughnasadh, the traditional Gaelic harvest festival</note>, the Irish hold fairs, <term>óenach<gloss>A traditional assembly or fair that served political, judicial, and commercial purposes</gloss></term>, which are not only political and judicial assemblies, but places where commerce plays a significant role, as we shall see on pages 312 and 315. There is, therefore, an identity between the Irish Lug and Caesar’s Gallic Mercury (5).

<note>The following text is a continuation of footnote (5) from page 307, discussing the god Lug.</note>
Spain, dedicated a monument (*Corpus of Latin Inscriptions* <note>original Latin: *Corpus inscriptionum Latinarum*</note>, vol. II, no. 2818), are identical to the Irish Lug. As the patron of all craftsmen, Lug was necessarily the patron of shoemakers. Mr. Mommsen <note>Theodor Mommsen, a famous 19th-century classical scholar</note> found the divine name *Lugoves* inscribed on a marble in the Museum of Avenches (*Inscriptions of the Helvetic Confederation* <note>original Latin: *Inscriptiones confœderationis helveticæ*</note>, no. 161). L.*, XII, 3067, 4101, 4218). According to the legend reported by the Pseudo-Plutarch in the treatise *On Rivers* <note>original Latin: *De fluviis*</note>, the site where Lyon was founded was said to have been indicated by two ravens, and *lougos* <note>original Greek: λοῦγος</note> was said to be the name for these ravens in the Gaulish tongue. One can suppose that these ravens might have been a form taken by the god Lugus. In Irish mythology, we often see the gods appear in the form of birds. There are examples of this in the legend of Cûchulainn <note>The hero of the Irish Ulster Cycle</note>; see among others, *Course on Celtic Literature* <note>original: *Cours de littérature celtique*</note>, vol. V, p. 178. The same legend, *ibid.*, pp. 26, 33-35, shows us an appearance of Lug preceded by the arrival of mysterious birds that hunters pursue in vain. However, it is not proven that the Celts had a word *lougos* <note>original: λοῦγος</note> meaning "raven," and *lougos* cannot explain the name *Lugu-dunum* <note>The Latin name for Lyon</note>. The ending of the linguistic stem *lugo-* is not identical to that of the first term of *Lugu-dunum*. If it were demonstrated that the etymology proposed for the name of Lyon by the pseudo-Plutarch in *On Rivers* was known and accepted in Lyon in the second century of our era, it would prove that Gaulish, at that date, was little cultivated in this Roman capital of Gaul. One could presume this for other reasons; for instance, it was in Greek and not in Gaulish that Irenaeus <note>Saint Irenaeus, an early Church Father</note>, the famous bishop of Lyon, wrote at that time. Cf. below, pp. 316-317.

But Christianity did not succeed in erasing the memory of the founders' original idea. This idea was that Carman was a cemetery, that kings and queens had been buried there, and that the games and horse races, which gave the fair its main attraction, had been instituted in honor of the dead whose graves the assembled multitude trod underfoot. The same doctrine is found at the fairs of <term>Tailtiu</term> and <term>Cruachan</term> <note>Cruachan: the ancient capital of the kingdom of Connacht and a major burial site</note>: <term>Tailtiu</term> and <term>Cruachan</term> were cemeteries before serving periodically for gatherings of business and pleasure.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Irish funerary games and festivals, moving from the legendary origins of the fairs at Carman and Tailtiu to a specific historical instance of "funeral races" in the tenth century and a comparison with Greek epic traditions.</meta>

<page-num>314</page-num>
->PART TWO. CHAPTER I. § 4.<-

A detail from the war sustained in the tenth century by the Irish against the Scandinavian <note>The author refers here to the Vikings, often called "Norsemen" or "Danes" in Irish chronicles</note> pirates and conquerors shows that, at that time, horse races were still considered in popular opinion to be an honor rendered to the dead. The Irish, having taken Limerick and made prisoners of the Scandinavians who inhabited that city, massacred a portion of them and reduced the others to slavery. Then, joining an insulting irony to the violence of this vengeance, the Irish commander-in-chief, Cathal, son of Féradach, gathered the captive women on a hill, had them arranged in a circle, and forced them to crawl on all fours, each carrying one of the young victors on her back. This, he said mockingly, was for the salvation of the souls of the dead Scandinavians. This funeral march was called the "race of the son of Féradach" (1). This took place in 968.

The custom of horse racing in honor of the dead is not uniquely Celtic. Compare the horse races in honor of Patroclus <note>A hero of the Trojan War and close companion of Achilles; his funeral games are a cornerstone of Greek epic literature</note> in the twenty-third book of the *Iliad*, lines 262-649. In the Homeric text, the horses competing for the prize are harnessed to chariots and not ridden. We know that riding in Greece, as among the Celts, is a relatively modern practice (2).

At Carman, there were seven races, which is to say one per day for as long as the fair lasted. But that was not all. Here, people concerned themselves with the judgment of lawsuits: they spoke of legal claims, of the <term>seizure</term> <note>The legal process of taking possession of assets to satisfy a debt</note> of property, of debts, and of the denial of justice. In one area, musicians played the harp and wind instruments; further along, the *<term>filé</term>* <note>A class of elite Irish poet-scholars who held high social rank and served as keepers of history and genealogy</note> or poets and scholars recited the histories they knew by heart; others, who possessed less memory but had learned to read, read aloud accounts of war, plunder, murder, and love. According to these scholars, the fair of Carman had been held nine times thirty times—or two hundred and seventy times—by the time Saint Patrick arrived; it would thus have dated back to the year 378 before our era (1). These indications seem to show us the germ of a system in Ireland similar to that which gave the Greeks the era of the <term>Olympiads</term> <note>The four-year periods between Olympic Games used as a dating system in ancient Greece</note> (2).

But let us return to the fairground:

There were three markets: food was sold in the first; in the second, one found livestock; in the third, gold and precious fabrics brought by foreign merchants. The Christian author, who gives us these—

It was difficult to strip the Irish of the old habits that national tradition associated with these ancient festivals. However, Christianity had banished from the fair of Carman the pagan religious ceremonies that formed the fundamental element of the original program. According to the new program, the second day of the fair was to be dedicated to the saints of Ireland, to prayer, and to fasting (3). He appears to have delivered these judgments with absolute and unchecked authority. But that was during the mythological period. In the heroic period, which begins with the cycle of Conchobar and Cúchulainn, the *file* are reduced to being simple advisors to the assemblies and kings. This is their historical role. This reform took place, it is said, on the occasion of the trial known by the name of *Acallam in dá suad*, "Dialogue of the Two Sages," <note>original: "Acallam in da suad"</note> in the time of the epic king Conchobar. The obscurity of the judgment delivered by the *file* caused them, it is said, to be stripped of the monopoly they had enjoyed until then (2).

### SECOND PART. CHAPTER I. § 5.

...to obtain the agreement of the assemblies and the kings for their decisions, the <term>file</term> <note>The elite class of poet-scholars and legal experts in early Ireland</note> were obliged to explain these ancient maxims. The judgments contained in the *Senchus Mór* <note>Literally "The Great Custom," the primary collection of early Irish Brehon Law</note> are presented as the collective work of legal experts and the assemblies or kings.

In the first of these documents, the legal expert is Sen Mac Aigé. The *Senchus Mór* says that this figure "carried" (*berta*) judgments (*bretha*) (1) in an assembly of the three free races of Ireland; and here, it adds, are the decisions that "were carried" (*bretha*) by this assembly.

Thus, the same verb is used to designate both the act of Aigé, who proposes a judgment, and the act of the assembly that adopts and promulgates it: *berta* is an active aorist <note>A Greek-style grammatical term used by early scholars to describe a simple past tense in Irish</note> of the verb *beru* "I carry" in the third person singular, while *bretha* is the passive preterite <note>The past tense</note> of the same verb in the third person plural (2).

In another instance, the judgment is presented as being rendered jointly by a legal expert and a king: the verb *fuigillim* <note>An Old Irish verb meaning "I adjudge" or "I refer for judgment"</note> expresses this collective act; but the king’s name is placed first, and the verb preceding the subject is in the singular, as if there were only one subject—the king: *co fuigled Conchubur imbi ocus Sencha* "until [it was judged by] <term>Conchobhar</term> <note>Conchobar mac Nessa, legendary King of Ulster</note> and <term>Sencha</term> <note>Sencha mac Ailella, the chief poet and judge of Ulster in the Ulster Cycle of mythology</note> concerning it," until...

# THE BREHONS, THEIR ROLE.

But the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Custom," the primary collection of early Irish law</note> provides an example where the advice of the legal experts and the acceptance of this advice by the political authority are expressed by different verbs. In the case in question, the act of the legal experts is indicated by the verb *ruccim*, a synonym of *beru* "I carry" (2); and the act of the people by the verb *fuigillim* "I judge": it concerns a three-day delay in a matter of seizure; it was Brigit Briugad <note>A famous female figure in Irish legal tradition known for her wisdom</note> and Sencha who "carried" (in the singular), *ro-s-uc*, the sentence that the inhabitants of Ulster were to render—literally "would judge," *fo-n-gelltais Ulaid* (3).

In general, when one wishes to distinguish in Old Irish law between the act of the legal expert who proposes a decision and the act of the people or the king who accepts and imposes that decision, the expert's act is expressed by the formulas *beru breith*, *ruccim breith* "I carry judgment" (4), or by the

### SECOND PART. CHAP. I. § 5.

verb *midiur* "I think, I estimate (1)" and the act of the people or the king by the verb *fuigillim* "I decide" or by the noun *fuigell*, "sentence, decree" (2). The technical term that designates the <term>jurisconsult</term> <note>A legal expert or specialist in law</note>, *brithem*, in the plural *brithemon*—or "brehon" using the English spelling of the modern Irish pronunciation—derives not from *fuigell*, the decision of the people or the king, but from *breth* (in the accusative singular *breith*), which is the technical name for the solution proposed by the legal expert.

A legendary tale, published by Mr. Whitley Stokes in the *Celtic Review* <note>original French: *Revue celtique*</note>, vol. II, p. 382, depicts the future King Solomon judging the people near the throne of his father David, and criticizing the slowness with which that prudent prince decided to pronounce sentences. The sentence solemnly rendered by the king upon his throne is expressed by the word *fuigell*, while the act of the legal expert (here Solomon) who proposes this sentence is noted differently: *midiur* "I think" and *beru bretha* "I carry judgments." In Ireland, the jurisconsult delivered the verdict, and the people delivered the ruling, which was then pronounced by the king (4).

The *file*, who practiced the profession of <term>jurisconsults</term> <note>Professional legal experts who provided advice and interpreted the law</note>—that is to say, the <term>brehons</term> <note>From the Irish *brithem*, meaning a judge; these were the hereditary legal masters of medieval Ireland</note>—owed an enormous influence to this popular credulity. A few members of the Christian clergy occasionally exercised an influence similar to that of the *file* <note>The *filid* (plural) were an elite class of poet-seers in ancient Ireland who held legal and religious roles</note>. The most famous example was provided in the year 580 AD by Saint Columba, when at the Assembly of Druim Cetta <note>A major political convention held in County Londonderry to settle disputes between Irish and Scottish Gaelic leaders</note> he was chosen as arbiter between the High King of Ireland and the *file*, whose leader Dallan son of Forgall was exaggerating the privileges of his order (1). But this is a case where the exception proves the rule. The Christian clergy, though victorious over Druidism, never succeeded in supplanting those *file* who specialized in law. These *file*, or, as they are called, the “Brehons” (*brithemon* <note>Old Irish: *brithem*, meaning "judge"</note>), still preserved their authority when, in the seventeenth century, the English conquest—hitherto only nominal—became a reality.

Thirteen years ago, I wrote in the *New Historical Review of French and Foreign Law* <note>original: "Nouvelle revue historique de droit français étranger"</note> (4th year, p. 159) that there were not, in my view, good reasons to reject the Irish tradition regarding the origin of the *Senchus Mór*. According to this tradition, the text of the *Senchus Mór* would predate Saint Patrick, except for some revisions due to the influence of the famous apostle of Ireland, and carried out by a commission of nine members, of which he was a part <note>Tradition holds that a committee of three kings, three bishops (including Patrick), and three poets revised the laws to align with Christian principles</note>. A deeper study of the first volume of the *Ancient Laws of Ireland* has caused me to abandon this opinion which, moreover, was not personal to me: it was the opinion of the editors of the *Senchus Mór*.

I do not, however, share in any way the viewpoint of the skeptics who say: the oldest of the manuscripts of the *Senchus Mór* dates from the fourteenth century, therefore the *Senchus Mór* is the Irish custom of the fourteenth century. This way of reasoning would lead one far astray if applied to the *Digest* <note>The *Digest* is a primary source of Roman Law; though the law dates to antiquity, our surviving copies are from much later periods</note>! As for the *Senchus Mór*, this doctrine—accurate perhaps for a portion of the gloss <note>explanatory notes and commentary added by later medieval scribes in the margins or between lines</note> which may indeed date from the fourteenth century—is false if applied to the glossed text itself, which is much older. This text already existed around the year 1100; it is cited in a manuscript of that date, the *Book of the Dun Cow* <note>original: "Lebor na hUidre"</note>, p. 11, col. 1, and in a nearly contemporary manuscript, the *Book of Hymns* <note>original: "Liber Hymnorum"</note> of Trinity College of

According to the glossator, *faig* means "he sewed" or "he wove," *ferb* signifies "word of teaching," and the meaning of *fithir* is "father of science." The glossator then adds that *ferb* has three meanings; one of these three meanings, he says, is "cow"; for example: "three white cows, Assal took them from the slave of Nûadu" <note>original: "teora ferba fira do-sn-acht Assal ar mog Nuadat"</note>. #### § 2. — *The Senchus Mór and metallic currency.*

Another sign of antiquity in the text of the *Senchus Mór* is that it never mentions metallic money. The <term>currency of account: a standard unit used to measure value in trade and legal fines, rather than a physical coin</term> found there is the female slave, or <term>cumal: the highest unit of value in early Ireland, originally representing the worth of one bondwoman</term>; the horned beast, or <term>sét: a medium unit of value, typically worth half a cumal or the value of a young heifer</term>; and the sack of barley, or <term>miach: a dry measure of grain used as a smaller unit of currency</term>. Metallic money—specifically the silver <term>pinginn: the Irish word for penny, a term of Germanic origin</term>—appears only in the <gloss>glosses: explanatory notes written between the lines or in the margins by later medieval commentators</gloss>. However, Irish coinage dates only from the second half of the tenth century, and was unknown to the original author of the *Senchus Mór*. It was during this second half of the tenth century that the silver penny was minted in Ireland by Viking kings—if not for the first time, then at least in significant enough quantities to influence established customs (1). See above, pp. 266, 289-291.

Before the use of metallic currency became common, the *cumal* and the *sét* could be replaced by their equivalent in gold or silver weighed on a scale. The *Book of Armagh* <note>An important 9th-century manuscript containing some of the oldest surviving specimens of Old Irish</note>, from the ninth century, mentions a horse sold for a *cumal* of sil[ver]... <note>original: "ar[gent]"—the text cuts off at the end of the page</note>

->SECOND PART. CHAP. II. § 3.<-
->336<-

From the two observations contained—one in the present chapter, the other in the preceding—it follows that the text of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Custom," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Laws</note> is earlier than the eleventh century. It is unlikely that such a substantial document was written in the ninth or tenth centuries, during which Ireland was constantly put to fire and sword by Scandinavian conquerors <note>The Viking Age in Ireland, roughly 795–1014 AD</note>. One may therefore, without being overly bold, suggest the year 800 as the probable date of the *Senchus Mór* text.

# DATE AND MANUSCRIPTS OF CORMAC'S GLOSSARY.

—beginning of the seventh that we find the first mention of a work written in Irish (1). Even then, this mention may well be merely legendary. It was around the same period that the traditional legends of Ireland were recorded in writing for the first time. In the ninth century, scribes took advantage of the blank spaces remaining between the lines of manuscripts to explain, through glosses <note>Brief marginal or interlinear notes providing a definition or explanation of a word</note>, the obsolete words that already filled these narratives, which were by then two to three hundred years old. <term>Cormac Mac Cuilennáin: King-Bishop of Cashel and a renowned scholar of early medieval Ireland</term>, a bishop who was killed in battle in 907 (2), had the idea to make a selection of these glosses. He divided them into seventeen chapters, each titled with a letter of the alphabet, and he grouped within each of these chapters the words beginning with the letter that provided the chapter's title.

The oldest complete manuscripts of *Cormac's Glossary* are: 1st, ten pages of the manuscript known by the name *Leabhar Breacc* <note>Literally the "Speckled Book," a major 15th-century Irish manuscript containing religious and historical texts</note>, "Speckled Book," folios 263-272, of which a facsimile was published by the Royal Irish Academy in 1876; this manuscript dates from approximately the year 1400; 2nd, the first ten pages of another

The *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Custom," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Laws</note> is therefore earlier than *Cormac's Glossary*. Another observation establishes this:

The *Senchus Mór* provided materials for *Cormac's Glossary*. The author of the *Glossary* <note>Traditionally attributed to Cormac mac Cuilennáin, king-bishop of Cashel (d. 908)</note> had at his disposal the three elements of this legal document: the text, the introduction, and the gloss <note>The "glose" or commentary added to explain the archaic language of the original laws</note>. Thus, when *Cormac's Glossary* was written, the *Senchus Mór* was already provided with an introduction and a gloss. 

I speak first of the introduction:

In the article *Noes* of the *Glossary* (2), the words *nó-fhiss*, that is, the knowledge of nine persons <note>original: "*nó-fhiss .i. fis nonbair*"; this refers to the tradition that nine people—three kings, three bishops (including St. Patrick), and three poets—revised the Irish laws</note>, were taken from the introduction (3), and the article itself in its entirety merely reproduces in another form the ideas already expressed in seven lines of the introduction, at the bottom of page 16, volume I of the *Ancient Laws of Ireland*. The name *Cáin Patraic* <note>Patrick's Law</note>, used to designate the *Senchus Mór* in the article *Clithar sét* <note>Shelter of valuables/chattels</note> of the *Glossary* (4), is also borrowed from the introduction to the *Senchus Mór* (5).

**FERB.** <note>Old Irish for "cow"</note> *As it is in the Senchus Mór*: *Three true cows <note>original: Teora ferba fîra</note>, that is, three white cows <note>original: tri ba finda</note>* (1). The phrase *three cows <note>original: teora bai</note>* from the gloss, modernized by the scribes, became *three cows <note>original: tri ba</note>* in the *Glossary*. The meaning is the same.

# BOOKS IN THE GLOSS OF THE SENCHUS MÓR. #

The loss of a gloss <note>a marginal or interlinear commentary</note> is not something that should surprise us, and there is no doubt that the passage of the <term>Senchus Mór</term> <note>The "Great Custom," a foundational collection of ancient Irish laws</note> cited in this article was indeed a gloss. In fact, it is a piece written in regular six-foot verses; however, the main text of the *Senchus Mór* does not contain such poetic pieces. Conversely, several pieces of regular verse are found interspersed within the glosses of the *Senchus Mór*.

Thus, the text of the *Senchus Mór*, which Cormac used at the end of the ninth century or the beginning of the tenth, was already glossed.

This is the point to highlight a fundamental difference between the Irish civilization as shown to us by the original text of the *Senchus Mór* and the civilization presented to us by the glosses of the *Senchus Mór* and <term>Cormac’s Glossary</term> <note>An early medieval Irish dictionary attributed to King-Bishop Cormac mac Cuilennáin</note>. The original text of the *Senchus Mór* does not cite any books of civil law; yet books of civil law appear both in the glosses of the *Senchus Mór* and in *Cormac's Glossary*.

The text of the *Senchus Mór* sometimes relies on judicial rulings; we provide examples of this on pages 324-327 and 381, but nowhere does it mention a written work of law. However, in a single passage, the gloss informs us of the titles of nine works of law:

1. *The Court's Debate* <note>original: Imard airechta</note>, by Connla;
2. *The Law of Emain* <note>original: Ai Emnach</note>, by Fithel;

Another important detail.
The word for book, *leabar*, borrowed from the Latin <note>original Latin: "liber"</note>, is foreign to the language used in the original text of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish laws</note>. It is already found in the introduction, where it is used to designate the *Senchus Mór* itself (2), and it reappears in the glosses <note>Explanatory notes added to the margins or between the lines of a manuscript</note> (3). In the portion of the *Senchus Mór* text (vol. III, pp. 2-79) which primarily contains Christian additions due to the influence of the clergy, the word *litir* ("letter"), used in the genitive case *litre*, characterizes canon law <note>The law of the Church</note>, *recht litre* <note>literally "law of the letter"</note>, as opposed to Irish customary law, *recht aicnid* (4); the power of habit caused these two expressions to retain their ancient meaning in the introduction (5), even though, by the time the introduction was composed, the *Senchus Mór* was a book written in letters, *leabar*, just like the records of canon law (6).

### PART TWO. CHAP. II. § 3. ###

We can conclude that the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Antiquity," the primary collection of ancient Irish laws</note> is: 1st, older than *Cormac's Glossary* which was written around the year 900; and 2nd, more recent than certain books of Irish canon law <note>Laws governing the Church</note>, probably the "Canonical Collection" <note>The *Collectio Canonum Hibernensis*</note> compiled around the year 700. It appears to be the oldest book of civil law in Ireland. The date of approximately 800 that we attributed to it on page 336 seems, therefore, to be justified.

What confirms this theory is this: *Cormac's Glossary* speaks of the penny, *pinginn* <note>A silver coin introduced to Ireland via Viking trade and Anglo-Saxon influence</note>, which was struck for the first time in Ireland in the ninth century; however, as we have seen above, the *Senchus Mór* is not aware of metallic currency (1).

Palladius <note>The bishop sent to Ireland in 431 AD, prior to Saint Patrick</note> was writing. They were preserved in one of the three churches that Palladius had founded.
