1. a short *Treatise on Immediate Distress*, composed after the introduction of Christianity (5th century), but prior to a council recorded around the year 700 in the *Irish Collection of Canon Law* (1);
2. a *Treatise on Distress with Delays*, written after this council. In a number of cases, the doctrines set forth by one of these treatises contradict the doctrines formulated by the other: the author of the *Senchus Mór* did not see these contradictions; indeed, for his first book, whose subject is distress, he adopted the title of the first of these treatises, "Of the four types of distress," without perceiving that he was presenting in this first book a doctrine irreconcilable with that title, as seen on p. 258–261, cf. below, p. 350, 352–356, 382, 383.

->### IMMEDIATE DISTRESS. PRIMITIVE TREATISE.<-

...nights <note>The text continues from the previous page: "a respite of one, three, five, or ten nights"</note>: rules fix the duration of this grace period <note>original: "répit"</note>, at the expiration of which the seized objects become the property of the seizor. The length of this duration depends on the reasons for the seizure, or the circumstances in which it occurs. Here are some examples:

If an heir wishes to compel his co-heir to a partition <note>original: "partage"; the division of an inherited estate</note>, he performs a seizure, and the seized objects, placed in a pound <note>original: "fourrière"</note>, remain there during a respite of one night—that is, one clear day—during which the defendant can, if he consents to the partition, regain possession of the movable property that was taken from him (1).

A king has summoned his subjects for a military expedition: some do not appear. The king sends agents who proceed with a seizure against the recalcitrant subjects; the seized objects remain in the pound during a respite of three nights—that is, three clear days. If, during this respite, the summoned warriors join the body of troops they are meant to be part of, the seized objects will be returned to them (2).

The duration of the respite in the pound is fixed, in this case as in the previous one, by the nature of the disputes that provoked the seizure; in the first case, it concerns a request for partition; in the second, it is a matter of the obligation of military service. # SECOND PART. CHAP. III. § 1.

...those circumstances in which the seizure occurs result in the respite in the pound <term>pound: original "fourrière," a secure enclosure where seized cattle or goods were held</term> being lengthened.

The debtor is dead: one wishes to compel his heir to pay, and a seizure is proceeded with against this heir. The heir will be treated more favorably than the deceased would have been. The seized objects will remain in the pound during a respite of five nights; consequently, the heir will have five clear days <note>original: "cinq jours francs"</note> to pay what he owes or to offer a sufficient pledge <term>pledge: original "gage," a physical object given as security for a debt</term> and by this means regain possession of the seized objects (1).

The seizure is practiced outside the territory of the city <note>original: "cité," likely referring to the *túath* or tribal territory in the Irish context</note> to which the seizor belongs: it is within the territory of the seizor's city that the seized objects have been placed in the pound. These objects will remain in the pound during a respite of ten nights; the defendant will thus have ten clear days to pay his debt or offer sufficient pledge and retake possession of the seized objects (2).

From these examples, it follows that there are, in immediate seizure <note>original: "saisie immédiate," referring to the legal process of distress</note>, four possible durations for the respite in the pound: one, three, five, and ten nights. From this comes the Irish idea that there are four species of seizure: and from this comes the title of the first book of the *Senchus Mór* <term>Senchus Mór: The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Laws</term>: *Di chethar-shlicht athgabala* (3) <note>original Irish: "Of the four paths of distress"</note> "Of the quadruple species of seizure."

### SEIZURE OF MOVABLES WITH DELAYS. PRIMITIVE TREATISE.

...of seizure." This was the title of the oldest treatise on seizure—that is to say, the *Treatise on Immediate Seizure* <note>original: "saisie immédiate," the legal process of "distress" where property is taken to compel a debtor to meet an obligation</note>—a treatise which consisted of a nomenclature of cases where seized objects were taken away immediately. The duration of the respite in the pound <term>pound: original "fourrière," a secure enclosure for seized livestock or goods</term> was: 1st, one; 2nd, three; 3rd, five; and 4th, ten nights. The duration of this respite determined the species of the seizure: 1st species of seizure, one night of respite in the pound; 2nd species of seizure, three nights of respite; 3rd species of seizure, five nights of respite; 4th species of seizure, ten nights of respite. One night constitutes one clear day <note>original: "un jour franc," a full 24-hour period</note>.

The seizure with delay differs from immediate seizure in that the removal of the seized objects and the placement in the pound are preceded by two delays. The procedure begins with a command <term>command: a formal legal summons or notice, called "aurfocre" or "apad" in Old Irish</term>, followed by a first delay; then comes the seizure, and the debtor is appointed as the guardian of the property during the duration of a second delay <term>stay: the text uses the term "anad," a period where the seized goods remain with the debtor before being moved</term>. The duration of each of these delays is equal to the length of time during which the seized objects, having finally been removed, remain in the pound (1); the result is that the procedure for seizure with delays takes the creditor three times as long as that of the immediate seizure...

We also see from chapter 20 that the daughter has the usufruct of the entire paternal inheritance when the father leaves no male children. ### SECOND PART. CHAP. III. § 1.

...date of 600, when the council was supposedly held that granted women the right to inherit from their father. Indeed, this treatise does not only admit the right for daughters to inherit from their father; it recognizes the right of the daughter's son to retain the inheritance at least in part, and even to transmit it to his own son. Such is the doctrine of article 35, § 32 (p. 202, l. 3-4): there, we see foreseen the case where a legal action will be pursued for the partition of the succession of the son of a nephew born from a sister: *concerning the division of the inheritance of a sister's son* <note>original Old Irish: *im orba mic niath do comruind*</note>. This case—the 32nd of those involving a seizure with a delay of ten nights <term>seizure with delay: a legal process in Old Irish law where property was seized to compel a defendant to come to court, but held in a pound for a set period before being forfeited</term>—would be impossible if one strictly followed the text of the *Irish Canon Collection* <note>a 7th/8th-century compilation of ecclesiastical laws</note>, according to which the sons of a sister must restore their mother's inheritance to their male-line relatives (1); this case is therefore the result of a jurisprudence <term>jurisprudence: the practical application of law and the patterns of court decisions over time</term> which developed the right of succession attributed to daughters by canon law. 

Now, this case is not mentioned in the corresponding part of the *Treatise on Immediate Seizure* (art. 47, p. 246, l. 18-22), where nine cases of immediate seizure with ten nights in the pound are listed. This treatise does not even offer us any indication relating to the right of succession obtained by women; we can therefore consider it to be prior to the council which, around the year 600, established this right of succession.

<meta>This page continues the chronological analysis of early Irish law, specifically using linguistic and ecclesiastical evidence to date the "Treatise on Immediate Seizure" after the "Treatise on Seizure with Delays."</meta>

# DATE OF THE TREATISE ON IMMEDIATE SEIZURE.

Furthermore, the *Treatise on Immediate Seizure* was written after the establishment of Christianity in Ireland. Article 42, § 26 (page 232, line 4; page 234, lines 27-29) mentions among the causes for an immediate seizure with a three-night respite in the pound, "altar furniture" <note>original Old Irish: *aidme altoire*</note>. The word *altoir* ("altar") is not a Celtic word; it is the Latin word *altare* <note>Latin: "altar"</note> pronounced as *altóre* by the Britons of the fifth century and introduced into Ireland around that time along with Christianity.

The *Treatise on Seizure with Delays* does not only foresee the situation where altar furniture is a matter of dispute; it employs a formula that includes more than just the furniture of the altar—meaning the chalice, the candlesticks, and the missal <term>missal: a liturgical book containing all the instructions and texts necessary for celebrating the Mass throughout the year</term>. It says (article 20, § 11; page 122, line 12; page 126, lines 28-30) "church furniture" <note>original Old Irish: *intreb n-ecalsa*</note>. This formula includes choir books, their stands, and the lamps or torches that provide light during the night office, etc. This phrasing transports us to an era when religious worship was more completely organized than at the date when the *Treatise on Immediate Seizure* was written.

Curiously, in this instance, the *Treatise on Seizure with Delays* does not extend the duration of the procedure; in this, it is exceptionally in contradiction with the general law it observes everywhere else. Regarding the seizure of three nights without delay—that is to say, with a respite of three nights, or three full days in the pound—as provided for by the *Treatise on Seizure*...

The *Treatise on Seizure with Delays* consequently demonstrates a very special favor for the clergy: it does not increase the duration of delays against them, whereas, as a general rule, it triples them against every creditor in the interest of the debtor. Thus, the provisions of the *Treatise on Seizure with Delays* relating to ecclesiastical furniture belong to a date when the influence of the Christian clergy was greater than at the time when the *Treatise on Immediate Seizure* was written. However, the Christian clergy did exist at the time when this latter treatise, the older of the two, was drafted: the use of the word *altoir* ("altar") proves it.

# DATE OF THE TREATISE ON IMMEDIATE SEIZURE.

Later, the influence of written language caused the *n* of *cinsus* to be restored in pronunciation on the European continent. At the same time, the initial *c* was assimilated—meaning it took on the sound of *ts*: from this we get the German word "*Zins*" <note>meaning "interest" or "tribute"</note>. The French word "*cens*" <note>a feudal quit-rent</note> is a more scholarly term, resulting from the restoration of the *e* by returning to the classical Latin spelling *census*.

The Christian clergy devised the use of *cis* (equivalent to *census*) to designate the dues owed to a lessor by a tenant of "servile livestock" <term>cheptel servile: a legal arrangement where a lord provided cattle to a tenant of lower status in exchange for rent and specific labors</term>. ...begins with a command, *apad* <note>original: "apad"; a formal legal notice or warning served to a debtor</note> or *aurfocre* <note>original: "aurfocre"; a public announcement or proclamation of legal intent</note>, followed by a period of ten nights after which there is: 1st, seizure; 2nd, the appointment of the defendant as the guardian of the seized objects; then a second period of ten nights passes: when it has expired, the seized objects are removed and put in a pound: in the pound, they remain for ten nights the property of the seized defendant, then they become the property of the seizing party. This procedure therefore involves three periods of ten nights: now, among the cases where this procedure must be employed, is that in which the person whose property is seized is summoned to appear at any assembly that is to be held beyond the borders—that is to say, outside the limits of the territory <note>The author uses the word "cité" (city/state) to translate the Irish *túath*, the basic political and jurisdictional unit</note>—*im cach n-dál críche* <note>original: "im cach n-dál críche"; meaning "in every boundary assembly"</note>. The rule prescribing this complicated procedure is irreconcilable with § 3 of article 47, since in the same case that paragraph allows for proceeding by immediate seizure; that is to say, without having given a prior command, or immediately after the command, and without having appointed the defendant as guardian of the seized object, the creditor removes this seized object which, once placed in the pound, begins after ten nights to become the property of the said creditor. The expropriation of the defendant takes place after ten full days in the system of article 47, and only after thirty full days according to article 33: this is the first additional example of a contradiction.

### § 3. — *Collection of examples taken from Book I of the Senchus Môr (the definitive Irish treatise on the seizure of movable property) which attest to the incompetence of its author.*

One cannot, therefore, reconcile the *Treaty on Distraint with Delays* and the *Older Treaty on Immediate Distraint*. By reproducing them one after the other without noticing the contradictions, the author of the *Senchus Môr* <note>The *Senchus Môr* (Great Custom) is the primary collection of ancient Irish law, traditionally said to have been compiled in the 5th century</note> gave proof of great ineptitude: many other such instances can be found in his work.

### SECOND PART. CHAP. III. § 3.

The procedure of fasting is a modification of the procedure for <term>distraint with stay</term> <note>original: "saisie avec délais"; a legal seizure of property where the debtor is given a grace period before the assets are forfeited</note>: the formal notice, <note>original: "aurfocre" or "apad"; Old Irish legal terms for the summons or warning notice</note> which begins the procedure for distraint with stay, is replaced by a fast when the debtor belongs to the aristocracy. This fast is performed at the door of the debtor by the creditor for the duration of one day; it constitutes a more polite formal demand than a summons, but it carries a much more severe penalty: if, after the creditor’s fast, the debtor does not pay—or at least does not promise to pay or to appear before an arbitrator and does not provide <term>pledges</term> as security—the debt is doubled, and this recalcitrant debtor loses all his own claims to any debts owed to him.

In the era when distraint with stay was unknown, and when <term>immediate distraint</term> <note>original: "saisie immédiate"; a seizure of property where the assets are taken to the pound without a grace period</note> was the only practice, no formal notice was given, or more accurately, the notice was immediately followed by the notification of seizure and the removal of the seized items: there was no room for fasting. The highest dignitaries of the aristocracy who did not pay their debts were exposed to immediate seizure, though this seizure involved ten nights in the <term>pound</term> <note>original: "fourrière"; the enclosure where seized livestock was held during a legal dispute</note>. The first paragraph of article 47, which deals with immediate seizure of ten nights, concerns this important case: "seizure against a high-privileged person," <note>original: "athgabail ardneime"</note> (p. 246, l. 18-19). The scribe to whom we owe Harleian manuscript 432 in the British Museum, which serves as the basis for Volume I of the *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, has

The meaning of this maxim is that, when it concerns the <term>honor-price</term> <note>original: "prix de l'honneur"; a value assigned to every free person based on social rank, used to determine fines and legal standing</note> due to the seizing creditor, the creditor has the right to use the procedure of immediate seizure, and to refuse the debtor the favor of <term>distraint with stay</term> <note>original: "saisie avec délais"; a seizure where the debtor keeps the property for a set period before it is moved to a pound</note>, *apad* <note>formal notice</note>, *anad* <note>the stay or grace period</note>. What is especially characteristic of distraint with stay is the *anad*, that is, the delay during which the seized objects remain in the hands of the debtor, who is appointed as their guardian. In immediate seizure, this delay does not exist; the only respite the debtor has is the period called *dithim* <note>the time during which seized property is held in a pound before ownership is legally transferred to the creditor</note>, during which the seized objects are in the <term>pound</term>, *forus*, and the creditor has possession of these objects while waiting to acquire ownership of them (Art. 37, p. 210, l. 20-29).

->PART TWO. CHAP. III. § 3.<-
372

Now, according to Articles 19 and 43, there would be no <term>stay</term> <note>original: *anad*; a grace period during which seized property remains with the debtor before being moved to a pound</note>, meaning one should not use distraint with delay when the purpose of the seizure is to force the debtor to pay the <term>honor-price</term> <note>original: *prix de l'honneur* / *enech-lann*; the legal value of a person's social status, used to calculate compensation for insults or injuries</note> owed to the creditor. This is the meaning of the maxim "honor-price does not suffer delay," *ni daim enech-lann anad*. This maxim represents an attempt at reconciliation between the procedure of immediate seizure and the procedure of distraint with a stay: it was introduced by legal experts who sought to maintain both procedures side-by-side, even though the procedure of distraint with a stay had been designed to replace the procedure of immediate seizure.

However, the text of the *Treatise on Distraint with a Stay* is formally irreconcilable with the maxim "honor-price does not suffer delay" (*ni daim enech-lann anad*). Indeed, among the legal causes that lead to a one-night seizure with a stay, we find mentioned the "honor-price of a virgin," <note>original: *lóg n-enech n-oige*</note> (Art. 20, § 36; p. 124, l. 2). Here the author, to express the idea of honor-price, did not use the word *enech-lann*; he used the formula *lóg-enech*. But we know that *lóg-enech* is simply the translation of *enech-lann* into a slightly less archaic language. Even the <gloss>commentary</gloss> <note>original: *glose*</note> of this passage uses the archaic *enech-lann* as a synonym for *lóg-enech* (see p. 132, l. 17-18): *im inuclund dlighus in oig in a sarugha*, meaning "for the honor-price to which the virgin is entitled because of her violation."

# HONOR AND THE STAYS OF DISTRAINT.

Thus, according to the *Treatise on Distraint with a Stay*, the father and, in the absence of the father, the agnate <note>a relative whose kinship is traced exclusively through the male line</note> who claims the price of honor for a violated virgin must resort to the procedure of distraint with a stay: this requirement cannot be reconciled with the maxim "honor-price allows no stay."

After presenting the portion of the *Treatise on Immediate Distraint* which lists the cases where seized objects remain for one night in a pound <note>original: *fourrière*; a place where distrained livestock or goods are kept</note> before becoming the property of the person performing the seizure, he asks a question: "Why do these distraints allow no stay, <term>anad</term> <note>a legal grace period during which the debtor keeps the seized property</note>?" He provides two reasons: one is that "honor-price allows no stay, <term>anad</term>." Whether this reason is particularly sound matters little here; what is certain is that in this instance the word <term>anad</term> is used in its proper legal sense, and the author of the *Senchus Mór* is speaking as a jurist.

But he does not do so in Article 19 (p. 120, l. 19-20). There, he attempts to comment on the *Treatise on Distraint with a Stay*: he intends to list, according to this treatise, the cases where seized objects must, for a stay (<term>anad</term>) of one night, remain in the hands of the debtor (who acts as a guardian). The most singular explanation is found in Article 48 (p. 250, line 15 and following). Two adversaries were preparing to fight a duel; they agreed to grant themselves a delay, or <term>anad</term> <note>a legal stay or waiting period granted to a debtor before property is permanently forfeited</note>, of an indeterminate duration. This is said to be the origin of the immediate distraint of five nights; yet, one of the distinctive characteristics of the immediate distraint of five nights is that, in the procedure for this seizure, the delay known as *anad* does not actually exist.

Here is the other explanation (Article 45; p. 238, lines 6-14): <term>immediate distraint</term> <note>original: "saisie immédiate," a legal seizure of property where the claimant takes the goods to a pound without a prior waiting period</note> of five nights is that which one proceeds with when the defendant is sued for a crime committed by either his father, his son, his grandson, his brother, or his wife; father, son, grandson, brother, and wife make five people, and these five people could have committed the crime to be settled in five different ways: they could have committed it with the hand, with the foot, with the tongue, with the lips, or with the eye. # ALLEGED ORIGIN OF THE FIVE-NIGHT DELAY.

[The verses previously mentioned] are a kind of supplement to the *Treatise on Immediate Distraint* <note>original: "Traité de la saisie immédiate"</note>: they fix the duration of the stay in the <term>pound</term> <note>original: "fourrière," a secure enclosure for seized property, typically livestock</note> at five nights when the <term>distraint</term> <note>original: "saisie," the legal seizure of property to settle a debt or crime</note> affects a close relative who is held responsible in place of the culprit or an <term>insolvent debtor</term> <note>a person unable to pay their debts</note>. These rules can be reconciled with the *Treatise on Immediate Distraint*.

According to the *Treatise on Immediate Distraint* (art. 47, § 4, p. 246, l. 20, 21), when a family is sued for the crime of one of its members who avoids responsibility by fleeing, immediate seizure is permitted with ten nights of stay in the pound: this applies to cases where the kinship is distant (p. 248, l. 25); however, when the kinship is close, the duration of the stay in the pound is five nights, in accordance with the aforementioned legal maxims.

In the *Treatise on Distraint with Delays*, the system is different: the delays are three nights when the creditor proceeds by seizure against a close relative of the culprit, or generally, of the debtor (art. 26, § 9, p. 156, l. 29-30; p. 160, l. 18-26); the duration of the delays increases to five nights when the person whose property is seized is a distant relative (art. 31, p. 182, l. 22 and following). Thus, the numbers are three and five—each repeated three times—when practicing distraint with delays, and five and ten—without repetition—when practicing immediate distraint.

To return to our starting point, it is absurd to explain the five nights in the pound for immediate distraint by the "number five" of persons for whom the responsible relative can be prosecuted—

<summary>This page analyzes the conflicting rules for the duration of livestock "stays" in the pound during legal distraint, comparing the treatment of close versus distant relatives. The author argues that the symbolic numerical explanations provided by medieval commentators are illogical and contradict different sections of the Irish legal treatises.</summary>
<keywords>Senchus Mór, distraint, Irish law, pound, kinship, legal liability, immediate distraint, distraint with delays</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Senchus Mór commentary, specifically focusing on the arbitrary numerical justifications for the length of time seized property remains in the pound. It completes a sentence from the previous page regarding the classification of crimes and the duration of legal delays.</meta>

->DEUXIÈME PARTIE. CHAP. III. § 3.<-

by way of <term>immediate seizure</term> <note>original: "saisie immédiate"</note> with five nights in the <term>pound</term> <note>original: "fourrière," a secure enclosure where seized livestock or goods were kept</note>, and by the number five of the crimes that these persons may have committed.

The explanation for the three nights in the pound in Article 42 (p. 230, l. 20 and following; p. 232, l. 1-6) is no better. According to the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Law</note>, the duration of the <term>respite</term> <note>original: "répit," the period during which the debtor could reclaim their property before it was forfeited</note> in the pound is three nights in the cases provided for by this article, because these cases can be categorized under three heads: law, honor, and soul (art. 41, p. 230, l. 3-7). That is to say: "law" <note>original: "droit"</note> refers to the duty toward a chieftain to whom one owes military service, rent, food-provision, etc.; "honor" <note>original: "honneur"</note> refers to a violation of status, for example, by striking the son, the slave, or the wife of the <term>plaintiff</term> <note>original: "demandeur," the person bringing the legal claim</note>; "soul" <note>original: "âme"</note> refers to cases where one has endangered their spiritual salvation by seizing the furniture or property of a church. The truth is that the considerations which led the legislator to shorten or lengthen the procedural delays are sometimes the interest of the plaintiff and sometimes the interest of the <term>defendant</term> <note>original: "défendeur"</note>. It is in the interest of the plaintiff when it concerns demanding the delivery of an object for which the plaintiff has an urgent need, such as a dairy cow whose milk he relies on for sustenance; it is in the interest of the defendant when, for example, he is being sued for a debt that is not his own and which was contracted by a relative. Relating the three nights in the pound to three heads under which various causes of seizure can be classified is not a genuine <term>legal doctrine</term>; it is merely a <term>mnemonic device</term> <note>a tool used to help memory, rather than a functional legal principle</note>.

<summary>This page critiques the Senchus Mór's attempt to justify legal delays (like the three-night stay in a pound) using symbolic categories like "law, honor, and soul." The author argues these are mere memory aids rather than functional legal reasons, which actually depended on the practical needs of plaintiffs and defendants.</summary>
<keywords>Senchus Mór, Irish law, distraint, legal delays, pound, plaintiff, defendant, mnemonic devices, Brehon law</keywords>

->THE DOCUMENT CALLED BRATHCHÆ.<-

### § 4. — *The Bráthchæ or Judgment of Cae.*

I cannot conclude without saying a word about the document called *Bráthchæ* or the *Judgment of Cae* <note>Cae was a legendary judge in Irish tradition, sometimes associated with the time of Moses</note>, which is cited by the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish Brehon Law</note>, art. 37 (p. 210, l. 27-29); this document is mentioned twice by Cormac’s Glossary: an excerpt from this document is found in that glossary under the entry *clithar sét* <note>A technical term referring to certain protected categories of property or "sheltered valuables"</note> (1), and the same glossary devotes an article to this document, where the name is written as *Brathchaei* (2). The *Bráthchæ* predates the *Senchus Mór*, since the author of the *Senchus Mór* speaks of it, and it is later than the two treaties on immediate seizure and seizure with delays, of which it sought to determine the fundamental difference:

> "To the various durations of the delay that 
> " precedes the removal, when an interval separates 
> " the seizure from the removal, is equal the duration 
> " of the respite during which the removed object remains in 
> " the pound when no delay has preceded the remo-
> " val of the seized object," literally "the <term>anad</term> <note>A legal stay or waiting period between the formal notification of seizure and the actual moving of the property</note> 
> " of every seizure after a duration, is the <term>dithim</term> <note>The period of time the property sits in the pound before the debtor loses ownership rights</note> 
> " of every immediate seizure without any *anad* at all."

The consequence of this maxim is that the basis for classifying the causes of seizure with delays is not the duration of the respite in the pound, but the duration of the delay, *anad*, placed between the seizure and the removal.

Such is, in our view, the meaning of the rule laid down by the *Bráthchæ*.

This rule may appear, at first glance, to be devoid of interest: what use is there in taking the duration of the *anad* as the basis for classification rather than that of the *dithim* in seizure with delays, since as a general rule in this type of seizure the duration of the *dithim* is equal to that of the *anad* (p. 176, l. 28-30)? The reason is that, when it concerns female seizure where the *anad* is two nights, the duration of the *dithim* is double (art. 22; p. 144, l. 23-24; p. 146, l. 21-25; cf. p. 150, l. 1-2); now, the interpolator who inserted female seizure into the Treaty on Seizure with Delays placed it between the seizure of one night and that of three: if he had taken as the basis of his classification—

### § 5. — *Conclusion.*

The observations gathered in the preceding pages establish, we believe, in a sufficient manner the interest offered by that part of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Tradition," the primary collection of ancient Irish law</note> where the author has interpolated the *Primitive Treaty of Immediate Movable Seizure*. This treaty would have been composed before the end of the sixth century of our era. The <term>unintelligent compiler</term> <note>A critique of the medieval scribe who assembled the larger Senchus Mór from older, sometimes contradictory, sources</note> to whom we owe the *Senchus Mór* reproduced this treaty exactly as he found it, without seeking to bring it into agreement with the rest of his work on movable seizure, and without appearing to notice the contradictions: he furthermore framed it with assertions, most of which are inept, in the midst of which one recognizes two verses borrowed from a versified treaty of immediate movable seizure, and by which the primitive prose treaty is completed (1). Such is the result of our second part.

But, some readers will say, what is the use of studying the rules of such a complicated procedure? What practical importance can the regularity of a procedure have when the defendant has the power to oppose its effects by force, even if the plaintiff commits no breach of this regularity? The answer to this question is easy. The plaintiff, who has right and <term>form</term> <note>The specific, required legal rituals and procedures</note> on his side, is supported first by his family, then by public opinion. The members of the defendant's family do not risk their lives to yield to the whims of a relative whose wrongs are obvious; and if the latter takes it into his head to kill a plaintiff whose right is clear and who was acting within the proper forms, it is certain that he will be lynched. The human spirit has always had the same laws, and where individuals do not obtain from public authorities the calm and cold protection to which the <term>Roman tradition</term> <note>The system of state-enforced civil law that replaced tribal/customary systems in much of Europe</note> has accustomed us for twenty centuries, popular indignation and fury are the violent sanction of <term>customary law</term> <note>droit coutumier: law based on community tradition and social pressure rather than written statutes enforced by a central government</note> when it is despised by the irritating and foolish pride of the unjust and wicked man.

### IMMEDIATE SEIZURE. FIVE-NIGHT DELAY. ###

...three nights; in a seizure of three nights, it rises to nine nights; finally, in a seizure of ten nights, the total delays amount to thirty nights. <note>In ancient Irish law, the "seizure after delay" typically tripled the base number of nights named in the legal category.</note>

When all delays are thus observed, the procedure for the seizure of movable property <note>In this context, usually livestock such as cattle.</note> is called **seizure after delay**, <term>athgabail iar fut<note>Old Irish: *athgabail iar fut*. This was the standard procedure allowing the debtor several windows of time to settle the debt before the cattle were taken.</note></term> (1); if the seizure is immediate, <term>athgabail tul<note>Old Irish: *athgabail tul*, meaning "front" or "immediate" distraint, used for specific high-priority legal claims.</note></term>, the first two delays do not exist. There is no <term>apad<note>Old Irish: *apad*; a formal notice or summons served to the debtor.</note></term>, which is to say there is no interval between the command and the seizure. Likewise, there is no <term>anad<note>Old Irish: *anad*; a "stay" or waiting period where the property remains in the debtor's possession after the notice.</note></term>, meaning that the seized object is immediately removed and put into a pound. The only delay is the one called <term>dithim<note>Old Irish: *dithim*; the "delay in the pound." This is the period during which the seized property is held in a neutral enclosure before it starts to forfeit to the creditor.</note></term>, which is the interval during which the object in the pound remains the property of the person who was seized. The duration of this species of respite is equal to the number of nights that gives its name to the seizure (2).

Thus, when the seizure of five nights is immediate, only five nights pass between the commencement of operations and the moment when the seized objects begin to become the property of the seizing party; whereas if the seizure had been the one called <term>athgabail iar fut</term>, "seizure after delay,"

### PART TWO. CHAPTER I. § 1.

...the interval between the start of the operations and the beginning of the debtor's expropriation would have been fifteen nights.

Immediate seizure of one night's duration was particularly rigorous: the plaintiff, without prior warning, removed movable objects belonging to his debtor, and, at the end of the one-night grace period, began what was called in Irish *lobad* <note>original: *lobad*; this term refers to the "decay" or forfeiture of the right of ownership, effectively the final transfer of property to the creditor</note>, meaning the expropriation of the debtor for the benefit of his creditor (1).

From this explanation of general principles, we will move on to detailed observations regarding some of the eight stages we have identified in the procedure of Irish movable seizure.

The first stage is the summons, *aurfocre* <note>original: *aurfocre*; a formal legal notice or demand for payment</note>. In principle, every movable seizure must be preceded by a summons. In the section of the *Senchus Mór* <note>The "Great Custom" or "Great Tradition," one of the primary collections of the *Brehon Laws* (ancient Irish law)</note> concerning movable seizure with delays, we find an exception to this rule. This

<margin>(1) The list of cases for immediate seizure covers twenty pages of Irish text in the edition of the *Senchus Mór* (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, Vol. I, pp. 120, 210-250, namely: seizure of one night, pp. 120, 210-230; seizure of three nights, pp. 230-236; seizure of five nights, pp. 236-246; seizure of ten nights, pp. 246-250. It should be noted that there is no immediate seizure of two nights; in other words, this procedure is not used by women, who must always act by *athgabail iar fut* <note>original: *athgabail iar fut*; meaning "seizure after a delay" or "lengthy seizure"</note>, seizure after a length of time. Of the four types of immediate seizure, the most common was that of five nights: *athgabail cuicthi in dul is gnathu dogres oldas cach athgabail* <note>original Irish quote translates as: "a five-day seizure is the one that is more usual than any other seizure"</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, Vol. I, p. 250, lines 15-16).</margin>

->### SUMMONS. THE CREDITOR'S FAST.<-

An exception occurs when the person against whom the seizure is to be carried out belongs to the aristocracy—that is, the category of people that Irish law designates by the adjective <term>nemed <note>original: "nemcd"; this is a common OCR error for *nemed*, meaning privileged or sacred.</note></term>, the meaning of which is "sacred." These include kings, the <term>aire <note>A member of the noble class or a freeman of rank.</note></term> or members of the nobility, <term>flaith <note>A lord or ruler.</note></term>, and the men of letters or scholars—storytellers, poets, and legal experts, the <term>fili <note>A class of elite poet-scholars who held high social standing.</note></term>—who are treated as their equals.

Whether the claimant is of common status or belongs to the same upper class as his opponent does not matter: Irish etiquette forbids addressing a formal summons to those called *nemed*; instead, one must go and fast at their door (1). The debtor before whose door his creditor fasts must offer him food (2) and promise either to pay him or to have the matter judged; as a guarantee, he must provide him with a solvent <term>surety <note>A person who takes responsibility for another's debt or behavior.</note></term> or hand over pledges (3). Otherwise, his debt is doubled; he also owes five horned beasts in damages (4), and he is...

(*Senchus Mór*, in *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 112, lines 14-16; cf. the gloss, same page, lines 19-26, and p. 114, lines 6-8).
(2) *Senchus Mór*, in *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 114, lines 10 and following.

### SECOND PART. CHAPTER I. § 1.

— that "wolves do not eat each other." <note>This proverb suggests that members of the same legal or social class were expected to follow specific codes of conduct toward one another.</note>
Seizure <term>distress: the legal seizing of property to satisfy a debt</term> among the Irish is considered a kind of contract between the two parties; its effect is to allow the claimant to acquire a right similar to a pledge or security on the seized movable goods. One cannot perform a seizure if they are not legally capable of entering into a contract: this implies both that the person is not under guardianship, nor subject to paternal authority; furthermore, they must be solvent, meaning they belong to the class of men who can serve as a surety or guarantor (1). Finally, to have the right to seize a debtor's property, one must possess movable assets equal in value to those being seized (2). A seizure carried out by a slave, by a domestic servant, or by an insane person would be void by law, and conversely, any seizure practiced against them would be illegal (3).

One might perhaps, without too much boldness, venture to use here an expression foreign to Irish law and say that the power to seize was attributed

(1) "They do not take [distress]... those forbidden from suretyship or unfit for a bond" <note>original: *Ni-s-gaibet... aurcuillte ratha na ecoir nadma*</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 84, lines 27-28; p. 86, lines 1-3, 8-9). *Aurcuillte ratha* means "one who cannot be a surety." *Ráth* <term>surety: a person who takes responsibility for another's debt</term> appears synonymous here with *deo-rad*, "foreigner," and is the opposite of *ur-rad*, literally "good surety," which is translated into English as *native*. On the capacity to act as a surety, see above, p. 109, 110. — From *naidm*, "contract" or "bond," there is a more complete form, *snaidm* (Windisch, *Irish Texts*, I, 783; Whitley Stokes, *Proto-Celtic Vocabulary*, p. 315).

(2) "He does not sue who does not exchange from the stock of the residence" <note>original: *Ni acair nad caemclai o croib in forais*. This refers to the requirement that the person seizing property must have equivalent wealth to what they are taking.</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 102, lines 26-27; p. 104, lines 27-29).

(3) *Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 84, lines 28-29; p. 104, lines 35-36.

<summary>This page describes the legal requirements for "distress" (seizure of property) in ancient Irish law, emphasizing that the person seizing must be a free, solvent, and legally independent "native" of equal wealth to the debtor.</summary>

The Irish text uses a paraphrase: "Seizure is forbidden to anyone who does not have the right to take part in the public assembly which judges based on the report of a <term>jurisconsult</term> <note>a professional legal expert or jurist</note> (1)." This provision leaves a considerable number of Ireland's inhabitants unable to obtain justice without the intervention of a third party more powerful than themselves.

But a rule that one might call democratic seems to provide a kind of benevolent corrective to this exclusion of the poor and the weak. The leaders of the public assembly—kings, heirs presumptive to kings, and royal advisors—are forbidden from personally practicing seizure: the impossibility of standing up to them would make their power tyrannical (2). When they wish to seize a debtor’s movable property, they have themselves represented in this operation by a subaltern agent: an <term>aithech fortha</term> <note>original Irish: "substitute plebeian" or "tenant of substitution"</note>, and it is against this agent that those subject to their jurisdiction bring an action when, conversely, they are the creditors (3).

## PART TWO. CHAP. I. § 1.

We have little to say here regarding the *anad* <term>anad: a stay or delay where the seized property remains with the debtor</term>, that is to say, the delay during which, in the seizure known as "after delay," the seized objects remained in the hands of the defendant. We have already spoken of this on page 265. We will, however, insist on one point: this delay was the period during which the solvent debtor could give pledges to the creditor and obtain the release of the seizure; the delay called <term>dithim</term> <term>dithim: the "delay in pound" where the property is moved to a neutral enclosure</term> or the period of the pound was when the solvent debtor was required to pay. The pledges given by the defendant during the *anad* constituted the guarantee either that he would pay or that, if he contested the debt, he would appear before an arbitrator at the expiration of a period of forty nights (1).

After the *anad* took place the removal, <term>toral</term> <note>toral: the act of carrying away the seized goods</note> (2), of the seized objects. To remove the seized objects, three people were required, and the seized objects had to be received into the pound by four people (3). The three people who cooperated in the removal were: 1st, the man of law, <term>aigne</term> <note>aigne: a legal advocate or agent who oversaw the process to ensure it was lawful</note>, serving as—

***

(1) *The period of staying is the period of giving gages; and the period of distress is the period of paying debts* <note>original Old Irish: "Cum[b]a e uidi anta a uidi gellta; ocus uidi ditma cum[b]ad e uidi ica fiach"</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 176, lines 29-30). On the period of forty nights, see above, p. 145.

(2) It is also called <term>táin</term> <note>táin: a driving or taking of cattle/property; the same word used in the famous epic "Táin Bó Cúailnge"</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 264, l. 23; p. 288, l. 9; p. 298, l. 5).

(3) *Three to carry off, four to receive* <note>original Old Irish: "Do foxla triar do cethrur"</note> (*Ancient Laws of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 266, lines 2-3; p. 288, lines 19 and following; p. 290, l. 29 and following; vol. II, p. 18, l. 8).
